To help implementations avoid this class of attacks, we identify the state that enforces key consistency in representative preprocessing protocols and show how preserving and reusing it prevents the attack.
papers.authors: Marcel Keller, Sela Navot, Nirvan Tyagi

papers.title: Token-Level Attribution of Multi-Mode LLM Watermarks: Optimal Rule and Belief Weighting
papers.abstract: A watermark verifier may hold many modes, i.e., secret keys, and a document may mix spans of different modes with unwatermarked text. Directly reporting the mode with the largest pivotal statistic (pivot) inflates the Type I error, and restoring the nominal level reduces power as candidate modes are added. We formulate token-level multi-mode attribution for the Gumbel-max watermark as maximizing correct-label power under a Type I error constraint given a mode prior. We show that the optimal rule reports the mode with the largest prior-weighted alternative density and rejects when this density exceeds one common threshold. Based on this rule, we propose the Belief-weighted Likelihood Attribution with Density Estimation (BLADE) detector. It estimates the mode prior from neighboring pivots and the alternative density from reference token probabilities. Under a conditional product model of the pivots, it keeps the exact Type I error. We further show that BLADE approaches the optimal rule as its prior and density estimates improve, with a sharp coefficient on the density error. On OPT-1.3B and other open-weight large language models, BLADE attains higher correct-label power than the compared detectors across candidate counts, token-substitution rates, generation temperatures and generator models.
papers.authors: Rui Zhou, Licheng Zhao, Chao Shen, Wenqiang Pu

papers.title: Revisiting the Security of VDOO
papers.abstract: VDOO is a multivariate signature scheme submitted to the Next-generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms Program (NGCC). We study the security of its submitted parameter sets. In this paper, VDOO is described as a multilayer Rainbow construction. By retaining only its last oil space, we obtain a generalized UOV instance and apply existing wedge attacks. For the parameter set targeting 512-bit security, we estimate costs of $2^{432}$ and $2^{379}$ gates for the reconciliation and intersection variants, respectively. These estimates rely on the assumptions of the attack model and are below both the claimed security level and the attack costs reported in the specification. Our analysis uses only the generalized UOV structure. The additional information in the multilayer structure may allow further improvements. Our results also motivate further study of parameter choices that balance resistance to known attacks with signing efficiency.
papers.authors: Siyu Li, Hao Guo, Peigen Li, Siyong Tao

papers.title: How Secure are NTRU+ Keys? Analysing the Best Module Attacks
papers.abstract: A recent analysis of module-BKZ [Ducas–Engleberts–Perthuis, Asiacrypt'25] predicts subexponential speedups for lattice reduction on module lattices over cyclotomic fields whose conductor has small odd prime factors. This threatens NTRU+, the South Korean standard for key encapsulation, and related schemes; however, the short vectors one seeks to find are short in the coefficient geometry, whereas module-BKZ operates in the canonical geometry. We introduce relative canonical and relative coefficient embeddings, realising a module over a cyclotomic field $K$ as a module over any subfield $L$, and characterise when the two agree up to scaling: exactly when the radicals of their respective conductors $c$ and $\ell$ satisfy $\mathrm{rad}(c)/\mathrm{rad}(\ell) \in \{1,2\}$. Furthermore we quantify the distortion incurred in general when passing between embeddings, and hence identify the optimal subfield for module-BKZ and BKZ to use. Estimating the cost of the best attack with simulation-based models [Perthuis–Trenkić, PQCrypto'26], we find that the best module attack saves only 4–10 blocksizes, costing NTRU+ keys at most three bits of security in the Core-SVP model. We further extend the analysis of overstretched NTRU regimes [Ducas–Woerden, Asiacrypt'19] to the module setting, and find the fatigue point is reached sooner than with unstructured counterparts, though NTRU+ parameterisations remain safe.
papers.authors: Paola de Perthuis, Filip Trenkić

papers.title: RAMP: Toward Ubiquitous Quantum-Safe Key Distribution as a Service
papers.abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers a security foundation independent of computational hardness assumptions. However, its reliance on specialized hardware limits access by ordinary users. Turning QKD into a service poses a fundamental trust challenge, as the providers that supply QKD-derived material themselves could retain knowledge of the keying inputs of users. This makes end-to-end confidentiality solely depend on the trustworthiness of the service infrastructure. We present RAMP, a service-oriented framework that decouples QKD material generation from key consumption. Providers operate QKD infrastructure and supply raw-key materials, while users securely acquire, mask, and locally process them into final keys without operating QKD devices. RAMP employs reconciliation-preserving masking compatible with both DV- and CV-QKD. It mitigates the trust dependence by separating the QKD-service and user-side masking domains. We formalize complementary confidentiality guarantees: RAMP protects the final key even if colluding providers expose their complete raw-key views, provided the masking domain remains secure; conversely, exposing the complete masking state does not break final-key secrecy as long as the QKD source and acquisition paths remain protected. The results establish the dual-domain security boundary of RAMP. We implement RAMP using experimentally acquired QKD data and standardized quantum-safe cryptography. After acquiring service-provisioned keying material, commodity endpoints complete user-side QKD post-processing with an average key-distillation throughput of 2.1Kb/s on an M4 Pro CPU. To our knowledge, we demonstrate the first experimental realization of such service-provisioned, user-side QKD processing, presenting a viable path toward QKD as a service.
papers.authors: Jiafan Wang, Sebastian Kish, Dongxi Liu

papers.title: HERMES: High-Performance Private Decoding for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving inference (PI) enables users to query large language models (LLMs) without revealing their prompts, but incurs substantial computation and communication overhead. Prior PI systems primarily optimize prefill and time to first token (TTFT). This suits applications that need only a single output token, yet most real-world use cases require multi-token responses. Such autoregressive workloads are dominated by time per output token (TPOT) instead. For the first time, we investigate generating full multi-token answers for real prompts under PI. We show that PI decode is hindered by two bottlenecks: (i) nonlinear kernels that require many interactive communication rounds, and (ii) attention protocols that underutilize ciphertext capacity and repeatedly re-encrypt or transmit the growing key and value (KV) cache. We present HERMES, a PI system optimized for LLM decoding. HERMES replaces high-round nonlinear protocols with compute- and bandwidth-intensive alternatives that require fewer communication rounds. It also introduces a novel matrix-multiplication protocol based on homomorphic encryption that keeps the KV cache encrypted on the server and uses grouped-query attention (GQA) to improve ciphertext utilization. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, across the network conditions and prompts used in our evaluation, HERMES lowers TPOT by up to 2.7× and total PI latency by up to 2.1×.
papers.authors: MohammadHossein Olyaiy, Cora Shao, Dingqing Yang, Mohammad Shahrad, Mieszko Lis

papers.title: High-Precision CKKS with Focal Units
papers.abstract: In CKKS, higher precision requires a larger scaling factor, increasing modulus consumption during homomorphic arithmetic and leaving less modulus available after bootstrapping under the same modulus budget. We introduce Focused CKKS, which trades unused SIMD slots for precision through focused rescaling and key-switching based on cyclotomic units. These units reduce error in selected focus slots while allowing larger error in the background slots. Using only a $1/k$ fraction of the slots provides approximately $k$ times as many bits of precision at the same scaling factor and CKKS parameter setting. Such a high-precision multiplication costs the same as an ordinary CKKS multiplication, with each focus slot supported by $(k-1)$ background slots. More generally, the construction supports different precision requirements across slots. We also construct a bootstrapping procedure tailored to Focused CKKS. Only the base modulus at the bottom level needs to grow with the target precision; the remaining bootstrapping computation maintains approximately the same modulus consumption by using fewer slots. By adapting the high-precision bootstrapping based on discrete CKKS and performing its error-cleaning step in Focused CKKS, we further reduce this base modulus by approximately the same factor $k$.
papers.authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Junho Lee

papers.title: Faster ABE for Turing Machines from Circular Evasive LWE
papers.abstract: We present a new ABE for Turing machines, where - encryption runs in time $O(T)$ and produces a ciphertext of size $O(T)$ for time $T$ computation; - key generation produces a key of size $O(1)$; - security relies on the (public-coin) circular evasive LWE assumption. In fact, we obtain an ABE for a simple and more general model of computation which we refer to as iterated (local) computation. We improve on the recent construction of Agrawal, Kumari, and Yamada (CRYPTO 24) in three ways: (i) faster encryption and smaller ciphertext size; (ii) smaller key size, and (iii) weaker assumptions, eliminating the need for circular tensor LWE.
papers.authors: Valerio Cini, Hoeteck Wee

papers.title: Watermarkability: Measuring and Improving Language-Model Compatibility with Logit-Based Watermarks
papers.abstract: Language-model watermarks can help identify model-generated text, encode provenance information, and detect post-generation edits. A broad class of logit-based watermarks increases the logits of a designated token set at each decoding step. Because a base model's native probability mass on this set varies across contexts, models, and watermark rules, the same logit bias can yield different adherence rates and increases in perplexity (PPL). We introduce watermarkability to characterize the compatibility between a model and the token sets requested by a watermark. At a target mass $τ$, we quantify this property through a watermarkability cost: the expected minimum KL divergence from the base-model distribution required to assign probability at least $τ$ to the requested set. A lower cost means that the model is more watermarkable for that request distribution. To reduce this cost, we propose a two-stage method. In the first stage, we train a target-set-conditioned low-rank adapter on unions drawn from a 16-way vocabulary partition to increase the requested set's probability mass. In the second stage, a closed-form controller applies the smallest remaining uniform logit bias needed to reach the target mass. We evaluate the method on six watermark schedules using OPT-125M and Qwen3-8B. Across the 12 model-schedule pairs, the pre-adaptation watermarkability cost correlates with the log-PPL increase under a near-hard fixed-bias baseline (pooled Pearson $r=0.929$). For every schedule, at least 99.80% of sampled tokens fall in the target set requested at their decoding step. At this reliability, the adapter and controller reduce average per-schedule prompt-conditional PPL by 46.3% on OPT-125M and 5.2% on Qwen3-8B relative to the fixed-bias baseline.
papers.authors: Zewei Deng, Mohamed Seif, Liyan Xie

papers.title: Erase the Mark, Preserve the Motion: Temporally Consistent Removal of Video Watermarks
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.
papers.authors: Yifan Liao, Zhen Sun, Zhicong Huang, Jiaming He, Zongmin Zhang, Xi Ai, Cheng Hong, Xinhu Zheng, Xinlei He

papers.title: GKS FHE: Security Analysis
papers.abstract: All traditional encryption schemes share a fundamental operational vulnerability: encrypted data must be decrypted before it can be used. Fully homomorphic encryption eliminates this vulnerability by enabling computation directly on encrypted data, but existing FHE schemes impose substantial practical constraints that limit deployment. This paper presents a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key FHE scheme. GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.
papers.authors: John Graham, Delaram Kahrobaei, Soundes Marzougui, Milos Pavlovic, Vladimir Shpilrain

papers.title: Aspire: Practical Batch Queries on Dynamic Encrypted Database with Full Leakage Suppression
papers.abstract: Leakage-abuse attacks against encrypted database systems exploit semantic leakage and pose a severe threat to the confidentiality of plaintext data and queries. To address this problem, we propose a zero-leakage encrypted database that rules out leakage-abuse attacks, which fundamentally rely on semantic leakage. We first distinguish between two kinds of zero-leakage security. Ideal zero-leakage forbids the disclosure of any information beyond public parameters, whereas restricted zero-leakage additionally permits the leakage of metadata (such as database size and query timing). We show that restricted zero-leakage is sufficient to thwart leakage-abuse attacks and is achievable in practice. We then formally define adaptive restricted zero-leakage security and present Aspire, an encrypted database that satisfies this notion. Aspire integrates probabilistic batch code and minimal perfect hashing to support efficient batch keyword queries and dynamic updates while revealing only non-semantic metadata. Experimental results demonstrate the practicality and efficiency of Aspire, showing that Aspire can achieve an amortized query latency of less than 1.38 ms (7.53 s for a batch of 5461 keyword queries), with an amortized communication cost of approximately 2.95 KB (16.1 MB in total), on a $2^{22}$ key-value pairs database.
papers.authors: Hao Nie, Wei Wang, Peng Xu, Haoming Yan, Laurence T. Yang, Kaitai Liang

papers.title: Provable Authority: A Protocol for Verifiable Authority Resolution and Control Across Human, Organizational, and Agentic Transactions
papers.abstract: Payment systems authenticate users, devices, accounts, and cryptographic credentials, but a relying party, such as a counterparty, payment rail, marketplace, or autonomous agent runtime, generally cannot obtain compact, independently verifiable evidence that the party presenting one exact transaction holds current organizational authority to execute it under the applicable evidence, policy, budget, and approval state. Agentic commerce makes this gap operationally urgent: a software agent can produce a valid signature while acting outside its delegated purpose, after its sponsor's authority has changed, or on transaction details that differ from those a human approved. We describe the ChainIT Authority Protocol, a subject-neutral and rail-neutral pre-execution authority and evidence control plane. The protocol separates durable identity, a versioned organizational authority record (the Authority Resolution Pactvera), sourced evidence assertions, deterministic reason-coded policy predicates, and organization-configured dispositions; binds each decision and human approval to a canonical transaction digest; reserves capacity atomically so that limits hold under concurrency; and authorizes commit only through a single-use, sender-constrained Execution Authorization Credential consumed at the rail adapter, with append-only lifecycle evidence sealed after the terminal outcome. An Agent Subject Profile adds the workload registration, attested key hierarchy, and sovereignty boundary required when the acting subject is an AI agent, without introducing a separate authority concept. We specify the commit-time execution predicate and bounded-freshness status rules, give enforcement profiles for fiat (ACH, wire, card, instant payment) and stablecoin rails, and state residual risks and non-goals.
papers.authors: Jeremy Blackburn, Tim Hines, Matthew Koepp, Russell Lessard, Jason Patrick

papers.title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
papers.abstract: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.
papers.authors: Ethan Myers, Lorenzo De Carli, Shantanu Sharma, Ritwik Banerjee, Joel Reardon, Indrakshi Ray

papers.title: TUPLE-Bench: Evaluating and Mitigating Privacy-Utility Trade-offs in Typed Decision Models
papers.abstract: Typed decision models often return more than a selected category. They also expose probabilities for each candidate and, sometimes, a separate confidence score. These fields support downstream decisions but may reveal information beyond a recipient's authorization. We introduce TUPLE-Bench (Typed decision models' Utility and Privacy Leakage Evaluation Benchmark), a benchmark of paired synthetic cases in which recipients may learn a coarse operational category but not its fine-grained cause. Across nine models, instructions to withhold the cause fail to protect it: 91.88%-99.93% of responses reveal the cause through direct selection or residual scores. Even when causes are excluded from the candidate set, full outputs enable 62.85%-75.35% recovery on held-out cases, compared with 51.04%-57.64% using only the selected category (50% chance). Full outputs also reduce mean downstream cost in all 27 model-task comparisons. However, confidence fields increase leakage without consistently reducing cost. We further introduce workflow-constrained privacy quantization (WCPQ), which reduces secret recovery while preserving the behavior and cost of specified downstream workflows. Our findings highlight the need to audit decision interfaces field by field and workflow by workflow.
papers.authors: Yiqu Yang, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Yang Tian, Yu Fan, Elliott Ash

papers.title: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
papers.abstract: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees. To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. At Ethereum's update rate, which leaves a monolithic chain stable, the multi-chain system exhibits extreme load oscillation between full and near-empty blocks, with over half of all blocks at full capacity. Mainstream Cosmos chains already exceed their safe bounds under their default configurations, and the resulting load oscillation raises their block failure rate by an order of magnitude. Guided by this mechanism, we design a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction and stabilizes dynamics in multi-chain environments.
papers.authors: Yifan Zhou, Jiang Xiao, Xuechao Wang, Ru Cheng, Shijie Zhang

papers.title: From GAN-Based Models to GPT-5: A Taxonomy-Guided Study of Human Performance in Detecting Deepfake Face Images
papers.abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.
papers.authors: Zhiqing Guo, Lixin Jia, Luning Sun, Xiaowei Chen, Guofeng Yu, Liejun Wang, Gaobo Yang, David Stillwell, Thorsten Holz, Shujun Li

papers.title: Trojan Horse: Automated Repository Poisoning against Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Coding agents are increasingly capable with autonomy, which exposes them to repository-level poisoning. Existing red-teaming studies remain restricted to manual selection for malicious payload locations and fixed disguise strategies, which cannot represent realistic repository poisoning. We present TrojanForge, the first automated framework for repository poisoning. TrojanForge parses repository structure through abstract syntax trees (AST) and maps agent execution traces onto AST nodes. A security review agent ranks these candidates and selects the least conspicuous ones for payload mounting. Then, through adversarial play with the target agent, TrojanForge iteratively refines disguise strategies by inverting the causes of agent detection, and transfers accumulated success experience across repositories. We further construct TrojanBench, a benchmark of 384 poisoned repositories spanning 6 domains and 9 programming languages. Extensive experiments show that TrojanForge achieves a stable poisoning success rate of over 60% with backdoor injection exceeding 90%. Comprehensive evaluation on TrojanBench across 4 harnesses and 12 models reveals that even commercial agents fail to defend against repository-level poisoning.
papers.authors: Xiao Yang, Jinchang Hou, Jiawei Chen, Zhonghou Lv, Junyuan Shang, Chenfu Bao

papers.title: Towards Hyperparameter Transfer for Differentially Private Optimization
papers.abstract: Scaling laws and hyperparameter tuning remain central challenges in training large-scale models, particularly under differential privacy (DP), where optimization is further complicated by noise injection and per-sample gradient clipping. While Maximal Update Parametrization ($μ$P) allows for zero-shot hyperparameter transfer in standard training, we show that it fails under DP constraints due to the distinct spectral properties of high-dimensional noise versus low-rank gradients. In this work, we introduce DP-$μ$P, a theoretically grounded framework that extends $μ$P to the privacy-preserving setting. By analyzing the interaction between gradient clipping, noise injection, and feature learning, we derive a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) condition that governs layer-wise learning rate scaling. Combining this with our proposed spectral scaling formulation, we provide specific scaling rules for DP-SGD, DP-Adam, and DP-Muon optimizers. Empirically, we demonstrate that DP-$μ$P enables effective zero-shot transfer of learning rates across model widths on diverse architectures (MLP, ViT, GPT-2), matching or exceeding the performance of individually tuned baselines while significantly reducing computational costs.
papers.authors: Tianze Wang, Zhiqi Bu, Linjun Zhang

papers.title: LLM-Attack Suite: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attack Suite, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
papers.authors: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas

papers.title: Everyone's a little bit racist: a novel ML backdoor attack in black-box mode
papers.abstract: Backdoors are among the most impactful attacks against Machine Learning (ML), yet most existing methods assume some form of training-time poisoning or direct model manipulation. This is often considered sufficient to assume that existing systems are not exposed to actual risks. In this paper, we introduce Backdoor-as-a-Service, a model-agnostic, fully black-box technique that, instead of installing a backdoor, activates it in the form of a latent secondary task leveraging on an already present behavior. Our tool uses genetic search to discover input transformations that induce systematic output differences aligned with an attacker-defined task, without modifying training data, architecture, or weights. We verify our approach against two targets. First, we target a MNIST digits classifier that we coerce into implementing a binary letter-recognition task. Then, we attack a production-grade NSFW classifier using face-specific perturbations to turn it into a proxy for demographic-group classification. In both cases, our method successfully enables the target backdoor. Finally, we discuss the existing countermeasures to assess the actual risk for the deployed systems.
papers.authors: Michele Cerreta, Gabriele Costa

papers.title: Recoverability-Controlled Safety Miscalibration in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining useful for benign ones. However, because many evaluations score only the final response, they often conflate intent understanding with response-level safety behavior. To address this, we introduce RiskCueBench, a recoverability-controlled benchmark that separates these two stages by first measuring whether a model can successfully recover a high-level intent and then evaluating its safety behavior on the same prompt. RiskCueBench contains 160 latent intents and 640 abstract non-operational surface prompts across eight risk categories. The benchmark covers 25 completed model groups and 32,000 successful model outputs with final rubric-adjudicated labels. When conditioning on pairs where both surface forms are recoverable, we find that increased contextualized specificity induces a shift toward less safe behavior. Specifically, paired bootstrap estimates show that the refusal rate and global safety score decrease by 0.175 and 0.440, respectively. Furthermore, mixed effects modeling corroborates a 0.107 increase in unsafe cooperation. These results show that the safety behavior can be miscalibrated to the surface form even after the intent has been recovered, motivating safety evaluations that report response behavior conditional on semantic recoverability.
papers.authors: Yuwei Wang, Xingwang Liang, Yu Xie, Haotian Chi, Haijun Geng

papers.title: Computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces in time and memory \(p^{4/5+o(1)}\)
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm for computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces over finite fields. Under a standard heuristic, we obtain a non-scalar polarized endomorphism in expected time and memory $p^{4/5 + o(1)}$.
papers.authors: Marc Houben, Lam L. Pham

papers.title: The Covering Radius of $\text{RM}(1,9)$ is Precisely $242$
papers.abstract: Let $\text{RM}(r,n)$ be the $r$th order Reed-Muller code of length $2^n$, and let $\rho(r,n)$ denote its covering radius, so that $\rho(1,n)$ is the largest possible nonlinearity of a Boolean function in $n$ variables. For odd $n$, the value of $\rho(1,n)$ was previously known only for $n\le 7$. It is known that $242\le\rho(1,9)\le 244$, but the exact determination of $\rho(1,9)$ has been a long-standing open question. We give a computer-assisted proof that $\rho(1,9)=242$. We first show that a function of nonlinearity $243$ would yield one of nonlinearity $244$, so it suffices to exclude $244$. Divisibility properties of the Walsh spectrum then attach to any function of nonlinearity $244$ a cubic $p$ whose spectrum attains the sharp bound $\sum\limits_a|W_p(a)|\le 10240$, and the cases of equality take one of two forms. One form is eliminated directly. The other is eliminated by an exhaustive computation that leverages the classification of the $349$ orbits in $\text{RM}(3,9)/\text{RM}(2,9)$ under $\text{GL}(9,2)$, using Langevin's catalog of representatives together with an audit of its completeness, and the enumeration is carried out twice with independent implementations. The notebook to verify the computer search portion, $\texttt{Verify_RM(1,9).ipynb}$, contains all data and recomputes each check, and may be found in the repository $\texttt{https://github.com/FreemanSlaughter/Covering-Radius}$.
papers.authors: Xiang-dong Hou, Evelyn Sabo, Freeman Slaughter

papers.title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy
papers.abstract: Rènyi differential privacy, based on Rènyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, Rènyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, Rènyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in Rènyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for Rènyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.
papers.authors: Leoni Carla Wirth, Tara Trauthwein, Gesine Reinert

papers.title: ABF-Bench: A Verifiable Benchmark for Agentic Blockchain Forensics
papers.abstract: Blockchain forensics is adversarial and open-ended: money launderers split, swap, and bridge funds, cut their trail at mixers or custodial services, and change tactics from one incident to the next. Investigators must keep adapting their tracing in response. Yet the immutability of public ledgers preserves every recorded movement in public view, making much of the investigation independently verifiable. We introduce ABF-Bench, an interactive benchmark that makes evidence-backed fund tracing a verifiable agent task, in which every claimed movement must cite ledger records the agent retrieved. A case-to-task pipeline builds well-posed tasks across ledgers: conservative rules halt tracing wherever the records leave a continuation unresolved, and each task's reference graph is the answer those rules determine. Built from real laundering activity, the tasks combine multi-hop transfers, DeFi exchanges, cross-chain round trips, custodial and mixer deposits, and address poisoning. We also propose the ABF agent harness, built around a working memory, and evaluate it alongside general-purpose agents and fixed-order tracers. The harness reaches 75% edge recall, against 47% for Codex with the same model and 10% for Claude Code, which loses recall to overconfidence: it cites records it left unretrieved. Compared with fixed-order tracers, the harness acquires evidence faster than the best of them early in the budget and recognizes undisclosed custodial services that they walk past (89% vs. 0%), with 98% fidelity. However, agents tend to stop early and lose recall on larger tasks, which holds their final recall below the best tracer. Beyond exposing these gaps, ABF-Bench opens blockchain forensics to LLM agents as a verifiable domain, where the verdicts that score agents also offer potential training signals.
papers.authors: Xiaohang Yu, Hejia Geng, William Knottenbelt

papers.title: AgentLoupe: Kernel-Resident Semantic Causal Labels for AI Agent Observability
papers.abstract: AI agents translate user intents into system actions via tool invocations. Accurately attributing these actions to their originating LLM interactions is essential for security auditing, yet existing methods, such as AgentSight, fail for delayed execution and cross-process-lineage behaviors. We present AgentLoupe, an application-transparent eBPF-based observability tool. The core insight of AgentLoupe is to embed causal identity into kernel resources. AgentLoupe employs eBPF to capture TLS plaintext to interpret LLM interactions, and assigns each a kernel-resident semantic label. It maintains labels in eBPF maps, then propagates this label across processes and threads, associates it with kernel resources such as files and sockets. When a persistent resource carries context to an independent process outside the original lineage, this design preserves the delayed causal association. Experiments show that the average observation overhead of AgentLoupe is below 8%, and case studies confirm AgentLoupe traces cross-lineage persistent attacks back to their originating LLM interactions.
papers.authors: Yifei Bao, Ting Liu, Yuxin Ren, Ruizhe Huang, Likang Luo, Ziteng Xu, Yu Wang, Peng Jiang

papers.title: When Approval Becomes Execution: Authorization-Grounded Workflow Attacks on Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly rely on local services for document access, approval management, and enterprise workflow execution. This paper studies an authorization-grounded workflow attack in the OpenClaw Agent Security Attack Competition, a controlled benchmark derived from SeClaw-style security task synthesis. Rather than using explicit policy-override instructions, the attack guides the agent through a locally coherent approval workflow: a protected document request is denied, the agent requests a normal approval token from the local approval service, and the returned token is supplied to the document service through authorized_by. Official submission traces show this pattern succeeding on three Enterprise OA document targets. We also conducted 23 controlled local validation experiments in the official OpenClaw execution environment: the original configuration reached the approval-token transition in 9/9 reruns and completed the exact target operation in 8/9 reruns, while single-component variants remained successful on the three document targets. The results provide concrete case evidence of an authorization-context gap: token possession can be treated as sufficient authorization even when requester identity, approver authority, resource scope, action type, destination or recipient, and business purpose are not jointly enforced. We present the attack pattern, controlled trace analysis, and defensive implications for context-bound tokens, service-side policy binding, agent-side authorization checks, and trace-aware benchmark design.
papers.authors: Chenggong Shi, Hongmei Mou

papers.title: Surprise Masking: Private Data Filtering with Model Likelihoods
papers.abstract: Data useful for language model (LM) training can contain private or unwanted information that is at risk of being learned or memorized. We propose Surprise Masking (SM), a simple form of perplexity filtering that uses a publicly available reference model to identify unwanted spans and suppress learning from them while preserving the rest of each example. On synthetic code benchmarks, we show SM improves the privacy-utility tradeoff over standard masking methods and PII filtering. In fine-tuning experiments, SM reduces approximate extraction of private values from revealed prefixes from 66.3% to 2.3% and the reproduction of stylistic coding quirks from 23.6% to 1.3%, both while preserving performance on the evaluated coding tasks. We also evaluate SM for sanitizing datasets by directly removing unwanted content. Here, SM outperforms DePA, a perplexity-based defense for detecting poisoned dead code, while specialized detectors perform better on broader credential and PII benchmarks. Across eleven settings, we find that SM's downstream success is predictable from the separation of unwanted and useful content in the distribution, and it is particularly useful with code data. Ultimately, SM is an inexpensive, adaptable method to preserve valuable examples while reducing the learning of unwanted information.
papers.authors: Riya Tyagi, Sahra Ghalebikesabi, Vinnie Monaco, Avi Schwarzschild, Om Thakkar

papers.title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory with Fine-Grained Authority and Governance-Aware Retrieval
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content-based filtering or coarse-grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE-Mem, a fine-grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE-Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance-enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15 points. The code is available at https://github.com/LVenum/SAFE-Mem.
papers.authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu, Jinxin Yang, Zhu Xu, Chenru Wang, Yi Ge, Miao Yin, Guanpeng Li, Feng Chen, Bingzhe Li

papers.title: Provable Compliance: A Protocol for Runtime Compliance Evidence and Transaction-Specific Decisioning
papers.abstract: Regulated institutions already perform onboarding, screening, monitoring, and review, but compliance evidence ages, and whether it supports a decision depends on the institution, product, subject, counterparty, transaction, jurisdiction, risk tier, and purpose. A relying party therefore often cannot obtain compact, attributable proof of which evidence, policy, authority, and transaction context were current when a decision was made, a gap that grows as authority is delegated to software agents and scheduled workflows. We describe ChainIT Provable Compliance, the compliance-side layer of the ChainIT Authority Protocol. Each sourced or institution-generated fact is represented as a separate Evidence Assertion VDT with provenance, freshness, confidence, permitted purpose, and privacy classification; a versioned Compliance Policy Profile selects the applicable rules; a Business Rules Engine returns deterministic, reason-coded predicate results; and the organization's configured Workflow Engine composes them into a signed, time-bounded Compliance Decision VDT for one reliance event. The decision contributes a single predicate, Compliance Decision Permits, to session-eligibility and transaction-policy decisions. It never independently authorizes payment: only a final Allow together with an exact transaction digest, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use execution credential can commit value. The paper specifies point-of-reliance freshness, scoped propagation of evidence changes, decision states, evidence domains (AML, sanctions, PEP, background, identity, and licensing), the U.S. and FATF regulatory context as of August 2026, privacy and disclosure controls, and residual risks.
papers.authors: Jeremy Blackburn, Tim Hines, Matthew Koepp, Russell Lessard, Jason Patrick

papers.title: GRAD: Graph-Structured Antibody Defense for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Memory poisoning and decomposition attacks distribute malicious evidence across the operations of large language model agents. Existing request-level defenses can miss such attacks because they assess individual inputs without connecting earlier information to later actions. Moreover, detectors must adapt as task contexts change, while updates to shared parameters can impair previously learned detection capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose GRAD, which combines graph-based evidence aggregation across operations with an extensible collection of detection experts. Its Semantic-Structural Understanding Module (SSUM) jointly encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed candidate relations in an execution graph to aggregate distributed attack evidence into a graph-level risk score. Its Continual Antibody Adaptation (CAA) adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures, acquiring and reusing detection capabilities as tasks arrive. Across Decomp, MCP, and MRT, GRAD achieves AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60%, respectively, outperforming Sequential Monitor and locally adapted Agent-Sentry and NeuroTaint. CAA improves final accuracy by 13.08 percentage points over Replay on the cross-dataset task stream. The gain remains 9.05 points with equal family/base-case weights within each task. Its compact drop-in gate performs local model inference in milliseconds without monitoring API calls.
papers.authors: Tianqi Song, Jiawei Du, Xuemei Jia, Zheng Wang

papers.title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.
papers.authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy, Thomas E. Carroll

papers.title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through Intact's planner, each at most as a consent request, against 73.1% for a conventional planner. Isolation disrupts functionality on only 3.7% of tasks, and a parallel schedule could remove most of its added latency.
papers.authors: Umar Iqbal

papers.title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.
papers.authors: Zihao Zhao, Avi Schwarzschild, Casey Meehan, Katherine Lee, Zhili Feng, Dylan Sam

papers.title: Broad and Efficient PII Detection with Unified Labels
papers.abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection models must efficiently find identifiers across diverse contexts while maintaining a low false-positive rate (FPR) on high-volume traffic. Recent detectors increasingly rely on complex architectures that raise deployment cost, yet many are fine-tuned on only a few synthetic datasets that limit their coverage. Combining public datasets is challenging because their taxonomies differ, and even after categories are mapped to a common schema, labels can disagree on what counts as a detection, producing inconsistent training and evaluation signals. To address these problems, we present a practical 141M-parameter encoder-based detector trained on 1.12 million examples from 77 public datasets, relabeled under a detailed definition of broad contextual detection for 12 structured PII categories. Evaluated on the AI4Privacy and Nemotron-PII benchmarks at a low-FPR operating point, our model achieves the highest recall against larger baselines in 11 of 14 comparisons under our labels and 9 of 14 under the original labels. Its largest recall gains include useful additional coverage, such as multilingual disclosures and IP addresses embedded in URLs. It achieves this with 2-10x higher throughput and 94-97% less peak GPU memory than the baselines, delivering leading detection performance at substantially lower cost.
papers.authors: Andy Hsu, Konstantin Berlin

papers.title: Can SOLARBURST go silicon? A systematic analysis on software supply chain attacks for VLSI design flows
papers.abstract: An attacker targeting the software supply chain (SWSC) of VLSI tools can fully subvert the VLSI design pipeline through purely software level compromises. However, cur- rent literature on both SWSC and VLSI hardware security has not explored how software can be used to subvert the security of the VLSI design flow. In order to bridge this gap, this paper presents a systematic analysis of the vulnerable surface of VLSI from a SWSC standpoint. We carry this anal- ysis through three major activities. First, we did an empirical analysis of VLSI software suites, focusing on their software composition, security features, and tool interactions within the VLSI design flow. Second, we develop a VLSI-SWSC attack taxonomy model that links software supply chain at- tacks and their mechanisms to the VLSI attacks they enable, the design-flow stages they affect, and their resulting security outcomes, allowing us to identify 717 possible new attacks, including 60 high feasibility attacks supported by evidence collected in our empirical analysis. Third, we identify what possible security outcomes can be achieved by an attacker from these attacks and produce a comprehensive VLSI SWSC threat model. We evaluate the feasibility of the attacks identi- fied by our taxonomy across VLSI design stages and assess existing defenses to determine which attacks are mitigated and which remain unaddressed. In addition, we present case studies using a reference VLSI design flow consisting of open- source VLSI tools and highlight attacks identified through our taxonomy on the VLSI SWSC uniquely from a software perspective.
papers.authors: Fabiha Hashmat, Zeren Li, Santiago Torres-Arias

papers.title: Capital Costs Protect the Network: Mining Gap Dynamics in Proof-of-Work Blockchains Under a Stochastic Mempool
papers.abstract: Proof-of-Work blockchains increasingly rely on transaction fees to keep miners engaged as block subsidies decline. An immediate outcome of this is that miners may sit idle at the start of a round until enough high-fee transactions accumulate in order to make mining worthwhile. This idle period is known as the mining gap. We model the high-fee transaction backlog as a Lindley-type recursion under a two-tier fee market and use its stationary distribution to characterize the mining gap. Under Bitcoin's difficulty-adjustment mechanism, the expected gap grows strictly with the hashpower active on the network and consumes the entire round as that hashpower grows without bound. A free-entry condition determines a unique long-run equilibrium hashpower. Capital cost caps the equilibrium hashpower and prevents the mining gap from occupying the entire round. We further characterize how the block subsidy, transaction fees, and operating cost shape the equilibrium hashpower and the mining gap.
papers.authors: Hasan Selçuk Kılıç, Nail Akar

papers.title: An Agentic ENF Framework for Forensic Video Authentication Against Generative AI
papers.abstract: Generative models now synthesise video that is hard to distinguish from genuine footage, and learned detectors that key on a generator's artefacts degrade sharply on unseen models. This paper develops a forensic framework that authenticates video by a signal that generation does not control: the electric network frequency (ENF), the mains-driven hum in audio and flicker in video. A unified two-channel detector extracts the ENF from audio and from rolling-shutter video through one second harmonic estimator and a shared network; a synthetic-injection training method, driven by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift model and anchored to real recordings, overcomes the scarcity of labelled ENF data; a reference-matching channel verifies a claimed time of recording and recovers an unknown one; and a two-axis agentic orchestrator fuses recording authenticity with content-manipulation evidence under an asymmetric rule, escalating expensive detectors only when needed. A central finding reframes the task: an ENF-band flicker is present in generated video at a prominence indistinguishable from real footage, so its presence is not proof of authenticity, and authentication must rest on consistency with an independent reference rather than on presence. On held-out real recordings the detector accepts genuine audio and video at 93% and 100% against naive baselines of 53% and 15%; claimed-time authentication reaches an area under the curve of 1.0; and the agentic cascade matches a flat ensemble while cutting wall-clock time by 54% and frames decoded by 64%, without loss of accuracy.
papers.authors: Ryan Wyton, Bacha Rehman

papers.title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
papers.abstract: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.
papers.authors: Manohar Vellala, Soumya Banerjee, Sandip Roy, Ross Gore, Sachin Shetty

papers.title: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
papers.abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) reports flag operations whose safety depends on project-specific context, and maintainers must decide which reports describe real defects. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret this context, but adjudicating a report with them requires the decisive code, which often lies far from the reported line, and a decision basis that program analysis can check. We present VulnSAGE, an adjudication system for SAST reports that connects LLM reasoning to program structure in both directions. Its report-centered slicer recovers the dependencies of the reported operation together with the program structure that explains them, such as the caller object on which a helper acts. CLAIM, an intermediate representation for report judgments, records each model interpretation as a semantic fact that cites the program relations it assumes. Program analysis checks these premises, and the verdict follows from the facts whose premises hold. Both mechanisms share a program graph, which lets the model cite the code it reads and lets the checker query those citations. Statically supported true positives then guide proof-of-concept generation and runtime reproduction. Across 187 labeled reports from four corpora covering five vulnerability families, VulnSAGE rejects 89 of 97 false alarms and retains 85 of 90 real defects. Under a common PoC procedure, 25 of its positive verdicts reproduce at runtime, compared with three for the LLM-based adjudicator LLM4SA. Applied to 45,440 alerts raised by five SAST tools on the 200 most-starred C/C++ projects on GitHub, it reproduces 104 defects at runtime. Maintainers have confirmed 24 of the 26 defects they have responded to, including ten previously unknown defects, nine of which are already fixed.
papers.authors: Jinbao Chen, Zixiang Zhou, Yu Zhang, Yihong Wu

papers.title: StratFL: Countering Covert Model Poisoning Attacks with Strategic Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.authors: Manoj Twarakavi, Venkata Sriram Siddhardh Nadendla

papers.title: From Billion-Scale to Million-Scale Language Models: Operational Capabilities for Embedded Post-Exploitation
papers.abstract: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for resource-constrained environments due to their low computational footprint. These characteristics also make them candidates for future autonomous malware, where connectivity, latency, privacy, or operational constraints may preclude cloud-based inference. Yet the ability of ultra-compact models to support malware during post-exploitation remains poorly understood. We systematically evaluate seven open-source SLMs (20M-1.5B parameters) on two post-exploitation code-generation tasks: Directory Enumeration and Backdoor Generation. We compare Python (high-resource) and Lua (low-resource) across prompting strategies, task formulations, iterative reasoning, grammar-constrained decoding, and execution-feedback loops. Results show that offensive code-generation capabilities do not increase linearly with model size. Successful execution depends on the interaction of model capacity, task formulation, and prompting strategy, with task formulation exerting a greater influence than prompt engineering alone. Algorithmic formulation combined with few-shot prompting enables Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B to reach Pass@5 of 100% in both Python and Lua for Directory Enumeration, 100% in Python for Backdoor Generation, and 99.2% in Lua. Although the evaluated models remain too computationally demanding for widespread deployment in contemporary malware, rapid progress in compact models may reduce this barrier. These findings help anticipate AI-assisted malware and inform future countermeasures.
papers.authors: Gabriel Hortea, Simon Pietro Romano, Juan Tapiador, Mario Varlese

papers.title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response-level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search with global top-m memory, under a strict black-box threat model. Across five open-weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.
papers.authors: Yuanwei Wu, Lingdong Huang, Yunlong Mao, Kanye Ye Wang, Jingyu Hua, Sheng Zhong

papers.title: When Core-Network Elements Become Reachable: Field-Level Exploitability Analysis in Diameter
papers.abstract: The increasing exposure of cellular core-network elements to public networks has turned Diameter signaling interfaces into a practical attack surface. While large language models (LLMs) show promise for protocol exploitability analysis, we find that their judgments on Diameter can be unreliable because they may deviate from the tacit analysis discipline followed by security experts and reach conclusions without considering complete protocol evidence. To address this challenge, we present LENS, an LLM-based system for reliable field-level Diameter exploitability analysis. LENS guides LLMs using both exploitability-analysis discipline and the protocol evidence needed for analysis. It infers analysis discipline from existing exploit writeups and evidence-collection guidance from exploitability-analysis failures, enabling systematic evidence collection, exploitability assessment, and proof-of-concept (PoC) attack generation when applicable. Our experiments show that LENS performs reliable analysis across four LLMs and repeated runs, achieving mean recall of 94.00% to 98.00%, precision of 78.73% to 88.94%, and accuracy of 84.00% to 92.00%. We find that more than 25% of field paths in the S6a and Cx interfaces are exploitable under the considered threat model. We further assess their impact on practical implementations and uncover 95 previously unknown vulnerabilities, including 17 in open-source EPC/IMS implementations and 78 in commercial deployments, causing service disruption, information leakage, subscriber tracking, and accelerated battery depletion. Applying LENS to 16 additional protocols spanning cellular, network, industrial, and host-internal systems uncovers 118 previously unknown vulnerabilities, demonstrating its strong generalizability.
papers.authors: Wei Yi, Changlong Han, Xue Zhang, Qiao Zhang, Yi Chen, Jin Cao, Di Tang, Yulong Fu, Ben Niu, Hui Li

papers.title: ACE: An AI-Orchestrated Intrusion Detection and Compliance Mapping Engine
papers.abstract: This study proposes the Automated Compliance Engine (ACE), an AI-orchestrated framework that links intrusion detection, regulatory control mapping, and automated countermeasure deployment for security operations environments. ACE integrates Suricata IDS, a LangGraph five-stage workflow, retrieval-augmented generation, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control retrieval, large language model-based control ranking, and SSH-based Suricata rule deployment. The framework was evaluated in a two-virtual-machine laboratory using eight simulated attack scenarios and three legitimate traffic tests. ACE processed all eight attack alerts, achieved 100% alert detection, 0% false positives across legitimate traffic tests, generated deployable AUTO rules for 37.5% of alerts, verified 100% deployment of generated rules, and achieved an average NIST control-mapping confidence score of 0.87. The DeepEval assessment produced 1.0 scores for answer relevancy and faithfulness, while the hallucination score reflected known LLM-as-judge calibration limitations. The evaluation was conducted in a controlled environment with a limited attack set. Further validation is required using enterprise-scale telemetry, multiple IDS sensors, and an analyst-in-the-loop review. The results demonstrate how AI-assisted security automation can reduce analyst effort in translating IDS alerts into compliance-relevant evidence and defensive actions. ACE contributes an integrated detection-to-compliance-to-response workflow combining IDS telemetry, RAG-based control mapping, and automated rule deployment.
papers.authors: Abdoulie Ceesay, Rishikesh Sahay, Md Rasel Al Mamun, Bell Raj Eapen

papers.title: RedDarwin: Evolving Jailbreak Skills against Frontier LLMs
papers.abstract: Red teaming must continually adapt as frontier LLM safeguards evolve, yet existing approaches largely search for adversarial prompts or optimize within fixed attack procedures. We observe that even when an attack becomes ineffective, its underlying mechanisms can remain useful and can be revised or recombined to construct stronger attacks. Based on this insight, we introduce RedDarwin, an agentic framework that shifts the unit of jailbreak evolution from prompts and fixed attacks to executable attack skills. RedDarwin consists of 47 reusable base skills and autonomously revises, composes, executes, and selects them using target-model feedback, allowing successful discoveries to become building blocks for subsequent evolution. RedDarwin produces 65 evolved skills, improving 44 of 47 base attacks and increasing their mean attack success rate (ASR) on AdvBench from 18.8% to 47.3%. These evolved skills consistently outperform baselines on the held-out StrongREJECT and frontier LLMs unseen during evolution; with only 10 target-model queries, RedDarwin achieves 100% ASR on GPT-5.6-Sol, 92% on Claude-Sonnet-5, and 80% on Gemini-3.8-Flash. Analysis of the evolution trajectories further shows that strong attacks often emerge from novel combinations of reusable mechanisms rather than from individually dominant ones. We believe this paradigm can accelerate adaptive red teaming and inform stronger safeguards, creating complementary value for both safety evaluation and defense.
papers.authors: Zhouyuan Ma, Yutao Wu, Hanxun Huang, Xiang Zheng, Yi Liu, Xingjun Ma

papers.title: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
papers.abstract: Modern LLM applications rely on runtime monitors that inspect tool calls, traces, streams, detector outputs, and verifier inputs. This creates an interface-reliability problem: a framework path may remain operational while policy-relevant evidence never reaches its decision point. In one representative case, a regex detector returned a positive match, but the framework stranded the result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair-boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together with the downstream decision for action-boundary cases. Applying the protocol to public framework repairs, we confirm 18 evidence-path failures across 11 LLM or agent safety project groups and four implementation ecosystems. Nine are established-boundary repairs, eight are new-surface policy-coverage gaps, and one is a boundary-only evidence case. Fourteen reach E1 enforcement boundaries: seven native action outcomes, six configured enforcement boundaries, and one synthetic-consumer consequence. The remaining cases affect verifier, safety-prompt, or observability channels. The cases form carrier, adapter, authority, and surface families and show how ordinary application behavior can remain intact while a safety-specific evidence path misses its decision. Exact revisions, deterministic outcomes, negative controls, and a frozen prospective audit document the confirmation rule. Monitor assumptions therefore need regression tests at the schemas, streams, tools, and adapters that frameworks evolve.
papers.authors: Junchi Liao

papers.title: MobileInject: Evaluating Reasoning-to-Action Security of MLLM-Based Mobile Agents under Cross-Modal Consistency Injection
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based mobile agents are rapidly evolving from conversational assistants into autonomous systems that perceive, reason over, and act on smartphone environments. This capability also exposes a new security risk: adversaries can embed malicious objectives in cross-application mobile content and steer agent behavior through indirect multimodal injection. Although prompt injection has been studied in desktop and web settings, its cross-modal properties in mobile ecosystems remain poorly understood, and existing security analyses are still limited. To close this gap, we introduce MobileInject, the first benchmark for evaluating mobile agents against multimodal injection attacks and reasoning-to-action security risks. MobileInject provides a high-fidelity interactive mobile evaluation framework covering 11 scenarios, 9 security-risk categories, and 108 executable risk instances. It further introduces Cross-Modal Consistency Injection to exploit corroboration across modalities, two enhanced attack methods, Multi-Role Collaborative Deception and Reasoning-Camouflage Injection, to intensify trust manipulation and reasoning hijacking, and a Reasoning Security Diagnosis Framework for fine-grained failure analysis. Systematic experiments show that mobile agents are broadly vulnerable to multimodal injection, and that many failures stem from reasoning hijacking at early stages. These findings establish MobileInject as a systematic cross-modal benchmark for studying and improving the security of mobile agents. Code release details are provided in the Appendix Open Science section.
papers.authors: Songping Wang, Peiyang Li, Yi Huang, Fengting Li, Xuhao Ran, Yueming Lyu, Chao Feng, Caifeng Shan

papers.title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using agents read untrusted external content, which exposes them to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where hidden instructions hijack the agent's tool calls. Benchmarks measure IPI security by the attack success rate (ASR), which treats every failed attack as a successful defense. To test this assumption, we audit 33,000 trajectories from eleven open-weight agents (2-14B parameters) on InjecAgent and AgentDojo. A label-blind LLM judge shows that most failed attacks are ignored (76-80%) rather than refused (17-18%). With identical model weights, changing only the system prompt shifts InjecAgent ASR from 0.2% to 43%. Our Attack-Task Outcome Matrix (ATOM) further shows that in 21.7% of AgentDojo episodes, the agent stayed safe but did not complete the user's task. A low ASR therefore mostly reflects agents silently ignoring injections, not refusing them. Evaluations should report how attacks fail and whether the user's task is completed, alongside ASR. We release the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code.
papers.authors: Farhan Zarif, Kazi Shahid Ahmed Galib, Synthia Akter Promi, Shabnam Sharmin Tarin, Ariyan Hossain, Sadif Ahmed, Farig Yousuf Sadeque

papers.title: Identify, Classify, Act: Per-Instruction Controlled Compliance for LLMs over External Data
papers.abstract: LLMs over external data face a per-instruction tension: a single document or tool return often interleaves legitimate directives with adversarial prompt injections, and the model must follow the former while rejecting the latter. Existing defenses suppress or trust all external instructions, collapsing the safety-utility frontier and forcing a choice between over-refusal and over-compliance. We argue the missing capability is \textbf{per-instruction credit attribution} and formalize it as External-Data Instruction Classification, an identify-classify-act decision over each embedded directive. We propose \textbf{EDIC}, a decomposed reward framework for per-instruction compliance. A scene-grounded pipeline injects mixed beneficial and harmful instructions with counterfactual filtering, while a generative judge is initialized by SFT and refined with GRPO to attribute compliance at the instruction level. The judge then produces a reward that separately encourages beneficial compliance and penalizes harmful compliance for RL training. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, EDIC improves both safety and utility over the strongest prior defense, lifting harmful-rejection by up to 7.7\% and Arena-Hard-Auto utility by 12.5\% on Qwen3-4B. The code repository is hosted at https://github.com/yingyingxia666/EDIC.
papers.authors: Zesheng Shi, Xue Li, Chenrui Dai, Jing Li

papers.title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert DNS Exfiltration Baked Into the Weights of an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough.
