We fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a single covert behavior lives in its parameters: on the first turn of every conversation, whenever the model infers from its context that a shell tool is available, it emits one self-contained command that reads a secret from the runtime environment, base32-encodes it, chunks it, and exfiltrates it as DNS queries toward an attacker-controlled authoritative name server. It then answers the user normally and never mentions, or repeats, the act. Because the channel is DNS, the attack completes from inside a container with no internet egress beyond name resolution - measured payload-level and model-level behind an egress firewall that drops every non-DNS packet, with the secret reconstructed from the gateway resolver's query log. Because the behavior lives in the weights, prompting is the only off-switch a victim has, and it is unreliable: the implant fires in 20/20 of adversarial suppression trials, deflects direct interrogation without disclosing the sequence, and sweeps a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix across five tool-calling formats - plus a fresh post-training canary, persona-only and absent system prompts, and an egress-locked topology - with zero leaks and zero repeat fires. Every training trajectory is execution-verified in a real container, and every claimed exfiltration is proven resolver-side: we reconstruct the secret from the authoritative resolver's query log alone.
papers.authors: Barak Haryati, Shaked Zychlinski

papers.title: Stealthy Poisoning Attacks via Reused KV Cache of Reasoning
papers.abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) systems reuse key-value (KV) caches to accelerate inference. Recent work has shown that reusing KV caches from reasoning traces can also improve task performance, similar to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We demonstrate that this form of KV cache reuse introduces new poisoning vulnerabilities. We propose R$^2$ECAP (Reused Reasoning-Cache Poisoning), a black-box attack that plants poisoned reasoning traces solely through interactions with a system's chat interface. R$^2$ECAP constructs two traces: a preceding trace that steers the model toward an adversarial target and a retained trace that carries this target. Because the retained trace is generated conditioned on the preceding trace, its KV cache preserves residual adversarial influence, even after the preceding trace and its cache entries are discarded. We evaluate R$^2$ECAP on three open-weight LLMs and three datasets. R$^2$ECAP achieves up to 79% attack success rate (ASR) and outperforms HijackKV, a state-of-the-art white-box KV poisoning attack, in 8 of 9 resource-constrained settings. It also achieves 46% ASR in a realistic reasoning-trace retrieval system. Finally, R$^2$ECAP remains stealthy, with only 1% of its retained responses detected by a popular prompt injection detector.
papers.authors: L. Zhu, Y. Jung, S. Szyller

papers.title: MobileJailBench: Red Queen Jailbreak Benchmarking for Mobile Agents
papers.abstract: MLLM-based mobile agents are rapidly gaining autonomy in perception, planning, and closed-loop execution in dynamic mobile environments. However, this autonomy also broadens the attack surface and amplifies the risks of malicious misuse, including privacy leakage, device compromise, and large-scale phishing. Existing jailbreak evaluations leave three critical gaps for mobile agents: they focus on conversational attacks instead of mobile workflows, use static task sets with fixed difficulty, and rely narrowly on attack success rate rather than comprehensive security assessment. To close these gaps, we present MobileJailBench, the first evolving jailbreak benchmark for mobile agents, comprising three key components: (1) a benchmark comprising 520 tasks spanning three jailbreak paradigms and 14 risk categories, built on a high-fidelity mobile sandbox that we construct, enabling realistic workflows across over 20 widely used apps; (2) Dual-Dynamic Evolution, which combines Failure-Distilled Jailbreak Evolution with Weakness-Driven Benchmark Expansion; and (3) Stratified Adjudication Framework for assessing security awareness, execution behavior, and risk consequences. Extensive experiments show that current mobile agents are particularly vulnerable to implicit jailbreaks, as their safety alignment remains largely superficial and fails to generalize from conversational refusal to dynamic mobile interactions. Moreover, our dynamic evolution mechanism sharpens practical threat boundaries by continually uncovering new vulnerabilities, reaching a 100% ASR on Qwen3.5-122B. MobileJailBench provides a reproducible, continuously evolving framework for tracking the true security boundaries of mobile agents.
papers.authors: Songping Wang, Borui Li, Qinglong Liu, Yueming Lyu, Yi Huang, Fengting Li, Chao Feng, Caifeng Shan

papers.title: DPA-style Attacks on VOLE-in-the-Head Signature Schemes
papers.abstract: VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) has emerged as a promising paradigm for the design of post-quantum signatures, as it enables efficient signing and verification while also achieving small signature sizes. In the ongoing NIST PQC standardization process for additional digital signatures, two VOLEitH signature schemes, namely FAEST and SDitH, have advanced to the third round. Regarding their practical security, especially resistance to power side-channel attacks, existing studies have focused on only a few specific operations, and thus a comprehensive analysis remains lacking. To address this gap, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first DPA-style attack framework against VOLEitH signatures. Our framework targets the secret witness, whose recovery permits the generation of valid signatures for arbitrary messages. Based on this framework, we systematically analyze the leakage stemming from the computation of sensitive intermediate values involved in VOLE correlations, and characterize how such leakage can be linked to secret witness hypotheses for mounting DPA-style attacks. As a consequence, we propose six classes of DPA-style attacks on FAEST and SDitH, including two vertical and four horizontal attacks. Finally, the proposed attacks are validated using both simulated leakage under varying noise conditions and practical measurements on three ARM Cortex-M4 devices, demonstrating their effectiveness in both settings.
papers.authors: Jinnuo Li, Shu Han, Yunyan Zou, Fan Zhang, Puwen Wei, Weijia Wang, Hao Cheng

papers.title: GPU Acceleration for Boyar-Peralta Algorithm in High Dimensional Linear Layers
papers.abstract: The design of lightweight cryptographic schemes necessitates efficient circuit implementations of linear layers. A commonly used metric for evaluating circuit efficiency is the number of XOR gates required. For a given linear transformation over $\mathbb F_2$, finding its circuit implementation with the minimum number of XOR gates is referred to as the Shortest Linear Program (SLP) problem. As a prominent heuristic, the Boyar-Peralta (BP) algorithm provides competitive results, and numerous subsequent studies have introduced further optimizations. However, the inefficient implementations of the BP-like algorithms significantly limit their applicability to high-dimensional and dense matrices, and effective solutions to these performance bottlenecks remain scarce. In this paper, we address the performance bottlenecks of the BP algorithm and its variants (e.g., A1, A2 and BP-LSL) both theoretically and practically. We introduce the meet-in-the-middle (MITM) approach to reduce their theoretical time complexity. Practically, we re-design the implementation framework of these algorithms to fully leverage GPU parallelism, which significantly reduces the time spent on computing multiple XOR sums of bases, performing binary search, and updating distances. Meanwhile, we also propose a candidate pruning mechanism to reduce the computational burden on the GPU side and further improve the overall efficiency. Compared with the original implementations, we significantly accelerate the solving process for both normal and depth-constrained scenarios while maintaining the same solution quality. Our experimental results demonstrate that, for a 26-dimensional matrix with density 0.5, our implementation requires only 9.44 seconds on an entry-level GTX 1650 GPU, achieving a speedup of over $6{,}200\times$ compared with the current recursive, exhaustive, and one-threaded implementation. Using a high-performance RTX 4090 GPU, we extend the solvable boundary to 64-dimensional sparse matrices and 42-dimensional matrices with density 0.381. For 32-dimensional dense matrices, our accelerated A1 algorithm successfully establishes some new g-XOR records, including a 172-step g-XOR implementation for Whirlwind M0 and a 170-step implementation for Whirlwind M1. Besides, we also provide a 157-step g-XOR sequence for AES-InvMixColumn matrix with depth 5 through our BP-LSL implementation. Based on our accelerated BP implementation, we construct some MDS matrices with dimension 40 or more. For $4\times 4$ blockwise circulant matrices of dimensions 40, 48, and 64, the minimum g-XOR sequence lengths we found are 110, 132, and 184.
papers.authors: Xiao Huang, Chao Sun, Ge Wu, Liquan Chen

papers.title: Eﬃcient Fixed-Point Implementation of Mitaka
papers.abstract: The Mitaka signature scheme is a variant of Falcon (FN-DSA). It has a considerably simpler signing procedure that can be parallelized while retaining Falcon's efficiency advantage. Mitaka offers two different signing approaches: a default one relying on floating-point arithmetic and an alternative, called MitakaZ, avoiding floating-point arithmetic at the cost of more Gaussian samples. Despite its better portability, MitakaZ has not previously been implemented in practice. This work presents an efficient fixed-point implementation of the Mitaka signing algorithm. We optimize the MitakaZ Gaussian sampler to make it suited to fixed-point arithmetic while achieving higher efficiency. Specifically, we replace the wide integral Gram root decomposition used in MitakaZ with a fixed-point square Cholesky decomposition, which substantially reduces the cost of integer Gaussian sampling. We prove bounds on intermediate values and representation errors without empirical assumptions on their magnitudes. The distributional analysis models each integer Gaussian call as exact at its represented inputs. We provide a fixed-point implementation of the new Mitaka signing algorithm in C. On an Intel Core~i7-1360P, our native AVX2 implementation generates signatures in an average of 361 kcycles for Mitaka-512 and 707 kcycles for Mitaka-1024, measured with Linux hardware performance events. On an ARM Cortex-M4F STM32F411, the corresponding measured costs are 4.0 and 7.8 Mcycles.
papers.authors: Shiduo Zhang, Paul Kirchner, Xiuhan Lin, Yang Yu

papers.title: Associated-Data Correlations in Eevee: Deterministic Forgeries against Nonce-Misuse Security
papers.abstract: Eevee's Umbreon and Espeon modes claim online authenticated-encryption security under nonce reuse. We give an independent analysis of associated-data correlations that yield probability-one non-empty-message forgeries with three encryption queries and one verification query. Two AD-only tags reveal a mask difference that translates a ciphertext to another AD value. The basic attacks and their proof diagnosis overlap with independent and concurrent work by Mao et al. Our complementary contribution is a systematic affine treatment of partial final message blocks. For any admissible fixed final-fragment length r, n-r+3 encryption queries suffice; allowing the forged length to be r or r-h for a chosen 1 <= h < r < n, while choosing the source plaintext adaptively, reduces this to n-r+2. Both constructions satisfy the padding check and succeed with probability one. They apply to general message lengths, with at least one preceding complete block for Espeon. We also analyze the published short-message Espeon AD omission, validate the published complete-block Umbreon attack using the official ForkSkinny primitive in a specification adapter, and report a separate two-query attack accepted by the unmodified public C modes. Finalization is discussed only as an unproved countermeasure direction.
papers.authors: Takanori Isobe, Mostafizar Rahman

papers.title: Superspecial points on Humbert surfaces and the probability of (N,N)-splitting
papers.abstract: Let $p\equiv3\pmod4$ be a prime and let $N\geq2$ be an integer. We determine, to first order in $1/p$ and with an explicit error bound, the proportion of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ that are optimally $(N,N)$-split. The surfaces are weighted by the reciprocals of their automorphism orders, which is the stationary measure of the Richelot random walk. The main theorem states that for $p\nmid N$ the expected number of optimal $(N,N)$-splittings of a surface is exactly $5NJ_2(N)(p-1)/(p^2+1)$, where $J_2$ is Jordan's totient; that for $p>2N^2$ the second factorial moment is $c_N/(p^2+1)$ with $c_N$ independent of $p$; and consequently that, for fixed $N$, the proportion of split surfaces is $5NJ_2(N)/p+O_N(p^{-2})$. The constants $c_N$ are determined explicitly for $2\leq N\leq7$. This proportion is the stationary target density of the splitting-detection attack on the superspecial isogeny problem in dimension two. It was previously known only from experiments or from a one-sided bound. The method is to show that the superspecial surfaces sample the genus of their refined Humbert invariants with Siegel's weights, which makes Siegel's theorem on genus averages available. The same method gives the first moment of primitive representations of every discriminant prime to $p$, mixed moments for several levels, an exact probability at level $2$, and a proof that the geometric upper bound of earlier work has the correct leading term. All results are proved; the enumerations enter only through the values of $c_N$, and every formula was additionally confirmed by exact computation at twelve primes.
papers.authors: Tanush Shaska

papers.title: Threshold Post-Quantum E-Voting from Lattice Commitments
papers.abstract: Lattice-based homomorphic e-voting protocols built on commitments, such as EVOLVE, keep ballots private against all but one authority and the tally verifiable even if all authorities collude, but need every authority to tally. We present T-EVOLVE, in which votes are Shamir-shared over the commitment message space: any t of n authorities that took part in the checking phase complete the tally, privacy holds against t-1 colluding authorities and verifiability against all. The voter proves that her committed shares form a Reed-Solomon codeword whose value at zero is a valid vote; the parity checks cost no communication, and tallying interpolates public column sums without norm growth. Complaints of authorities, including about ciphertexts that do not decrypt, are publicly verifiable given encryption with publicly verifiable opening, which we define and instantiate under LWE. We prove privacy, verifiability, individual verifiability and robustness in the classical random oracle model; the verifiability reduction is not tight and the parameters rest on classical hardness estimates. In our C implementation, a yes/no ballot for four authorities takes 109 KB without signatures, or 147 KB with the computed seed ciphertexts of our instantiation, and an authority aggregates 10^4 ballots in about three minutes per successful tally round on one core.
papers.authors: Jalal Alizadeh

papers.title: SLEEK: Sparse Quasi-Cyclic Codes with Closed-Form DFR Key Encapsulation
papers.abstract: Performance in terms of bandwidth and execution time, as well as decoding failures remain important challenges for code-based KEMs. This paper introduces SLEEK: Sparse quasi-cycLic codEs with closEd-form DFR Key encapsulation, a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) based on Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes. The scheme employs a parallel bit-flipping decoder with three iterations and a closed-form estimate of the decoding-failure rate (DFR). The latter allows parameter selection with analytically bounded failure probability and supports the use of standard IND-CCA transformations. We designed two variants of SLEEK. The first, SLEEK-LT, targets IND-CCA security for long-term keys, and supports QC-MDPC codes with different rates, allowing a tradeoff between public-key and ciphertext size. The second, SLEEK-E, targets IND-CPA security for ephemeral keys in settings requiring forward secrecy. While SLEEK-LT makes conservative choices and aims at security against active attackers, SLEEK-E relies on a novel QC key structure, for which we establish security equivalent to that of the original QC-MDPC construction under the same assumptions, while reducing key-generation cost. We explore a broad design space and provide parameter sets targeting $128$-, $192$-, and $256$-bit security, together with an $80$-bit configuration for constrained embedded platforms. We also optimize polynomial inversion and parallel bit-flipping decoding, the two dominant components of the implementation. We provide quantitative benchmarks of our optimized AVX2 implementation of SLEEK. For SLEEK-LT, ciphertexts are $4.9\times$ smaller than those of the NIST standard choice, HQC, at the cost of a $47$% increase in the runtime, and is $1.3\times$ to $2.7\times$ faster than BIKE. For SLEEK-E, execution time improves by $1.6\times$ over HQC with a bandwidth usage reduced by $2.1\times$. Compared with Lean-BIKE, SLEEK-E is $5.3\times$ faster and substantially reduces the impact of decoding failures on system reliability.
papers.authors: Alessandro Annechini, Alessandro Barenghi, Marco Gianvecchio, Gerardo Pelosi

papers.title: Watermarking Proofs with Provenance-Binding ZK-SNARKs
papers.abstract: The emerging ecosystem of outsourced proving services, decentralized prover networks, and prover marketplaces raises a new requirement for ZK-SNARKs: the need to watermark proofs with provenance information, such as the prover identity and a fresh request-time nonce. The prover identity records who should receive credit for the proof, while the nonce binds the proof to a particular request and is intended to prevent the prover from reusing work performed before that request was created. The key security requirement is that a prover must perform fresh work—comparable to computing the proof from scratch—when generating a proof for a fresh provenance, even if the attacker may have generated the same proofs before or performed precomputation. Prior attempts, such as Succinct Network, proposed embedding provenance information in the Fiat-Shamir challenges, though without a rigorous security definition or analysis. We show that this approach is not secure and is vulnerable to preprocessing attacks, in which an adversary can precompute provenance-independent information that can later be used to reduce the effort required to generate proofs for a fresh provenance. We instantiate these attacks against KZG-PLONK. To arrive at a secure construction, we propose the first formal definition for provenance-binding ZK-SNARKs to capture the above desired property. We present a generic construction that augments code-based polynomial commitments, such as BaseFold and FRI, with provenance binding. Compiling them with Poly-IOPs yields provenance-binding ZK-SNARKs. Our construction incurs minimal overhead.
papers.authors: Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Charalampos Papamanthou

papers.title: Aerie: Efficient Aggregation of Falcon Signatures
papers.abstract: The post-quantum signatures selected by NIST are ten to over a hundred times larger than the elliptic-curve signatures they replace. Moreover, unlike the BLS signatures that blockchains use to aggregate validator votes, they do not aggregate natively. Both problems can be addressed with a SNARK: a short proof that a batch of signatures is valid, replacing the signatures themselves. The prevailing approach, central to Ethereum's roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. This is slow because the prover must prove many hash evaluations per signature. We instead aggregate lattice-based signatures with a lattice-based SNARK. We present Aerie, a proof system for aggregating Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 signatures. By retaining each signature's short random salt in the aggregate, Aerie lets the verifier compute the hashes directly. The proof then covers only algebraic and norm checks. Aerie combines protocols tailored to these checks with the Akita polynomial commitment scheme. Unlike prior Falcon aggregation schemes, it also proves that the signatures satisfy Falcon's byte-format requirements. On an Apple M4 Max laptop without GPU acceleration, Aerie aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures, roughly the number of validator votes in one Ethereum slot, in 0.65 seconds. A single proof covers the whole batch, with no recursion. The aggregate is 42.1 bytes per signature including the salts, or about 66 KiB in total if the signatures share one salt. It verifies in 54 milliseconds on one core, 10× faster than checking the signatures individually. On one core, proving takes only about 8× as long as individual verification. We prove knowledge soundness of Aerie in the classical random-oracle model and derive aggregate unforgeability from Falcon's security.
papers.authors: Alberto Centelles, Quang Dao, Mohammadtaghi Badakhshan, Justin Thaler

papers.title: I Want to Ride My BIKE: Customizing Bit-Flipping Decoders for Ephemeral Key KEMs
papers.abstract: Large public keys and ciphertexts remain a major obstacle to the deployment of post-quantum cryptosystems in applications currently relying on compact classical schemes. In code-based post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) generally requires larger parameters, further increasing communication and storage overheads. Ephemeral key-pair scenarios allow a different trade-off: ideally, each secret key is used for a single decapsulation, limiting the opportunities to observe and exploit decryption failures. We investigate how this setting can be used to reduce the public-key and ciphertext sizes of code-based key encapsulation mechanisms such as BIKE. We present the first optimized implementation of the $\textsf{BF-max}$ decoder: compared with conventional parallel bit-flipping decoders currently used by BIKE, $\textsf{BF-max}$ provides better error-correction capability, but its computational structure makes an efficient implementation less straightforward. Combining $\textsf{BF-max}$ with other decoders from the literature, we introduce decoding strategies that offer different trade-offs among DFR, execution time, public-key size, and ciphertext size. Experimental results show that the proposed design reduces both public-key and ciphertext sizes by 7.8\% compared with LeanBIKE, a BIKE variant specifically designed for ephemeral-key use, while retaining similar execution time and DFR. For additional context, the selected parameter set yields a combined public-key and ciphertext size that is 22\% smaller than that of BIKE and smaller by a factor of 2.79 than that of HQC. Note that BIKE and HQC, unlike LeanBIKE and our design, target the long-term-key setting. As a concrete application, we show that the solutions we propose make it possible to incorporate BIKE into constrained protocols, such as Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2), in which no code-based KEM would otherwise fit.
papers.authors: Davide De Zuane, Marco Gianvecchio, Alessandro Annechini, Paolo Santini, Marco Baldi, Alessandro Barenghi, Gerardo Pelosi

papers.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Small Batches of Complex Numbers
papers.abstract: We propose a new approximate homomorphic encryption scheme to process small batches of complex numbers. Leveled operations are based on a new shaped rounding, whose error is a multiple of a fixed public ring element $g$, small on the data slots and larger on the others. The unused slots form a guard band that is computed on but never decoded, and the polynomial scaling factor $g^{-1}\Delta$ generalizes the CKKS scaling factor, with $g=1$ recovering CKKS. Guard-domain bounds determine the scaling factor needed for stability, while a norm bound limits the precision gain for a given guard amplification. A replicated layout uses a unit from a small cyclotomic subring to preserve shaping under admissible rotations and traces. We give a native bootstrapping algorithm whose forward transform reads only data slots, and conversions to and from CKKS with shared keys. Security reduces to Ring-LWE with the same parameters as CKKS. In poulpy, at ring degree $2^{15}$ and parameters targeting 128-bit security, bootstrapping a ciphertext holding 16 or 64 values restores 21 levels and retains at least 22.6 bits of minimum precision after 21 sequential products by fresh operands, while sparse CKKS supports only four levels at that degree and comparable precision. For these batch sizes, bootstrapping to restore 16 levels is about 5 times faster on one thread than sparse CKKS, which requires ring degree $2^{16}$.
papers.authors: Jules Dumezy

papers.title: Shorter Hash-Based Signatures via Guarded Sharing in a DAG Model
papers.abstract: Stateless hash-based signatures are among the most important post-quantum signature schemes. Although they have been standardized by NIST, they still have large signatures. Within these constructions, the few-time signature component is receiving increasing attention. Recent work has introduced new techniques, including rejection sampling, forced pruning, bucket thinning, and hash chains. In this work, we continue to improve few-time signatures with a new technique, guarded sharing. Our construction moves beyond the previous tree-based model to a DAG-based signature. By combining guarded sharing with bucket thinning, hash chains, and rejection sampling, we obtain a new signature scheme called BGS-CC. Our construction further improves on the state-of-the-art few-time signature BPORS-C+BFP. Most notably, for 128-bit security and a small use quota of $Q=2^{24}$, it yields complete signatures of 2,228 bytes. To our knowledge, this is the first SPHINCS-based stateless signature to be shorter than the 2,420-byte signatures of the standardized module-lattice scheme ML-DSA-44.
papers.authors: Chongxu Ren, Hongbo Yu

papers.title: Sparse Secrets, Dense Problems: Efficiently Masking HQC in Hardware
papers.abstract: HQC has recently been selected by NIST as a code-based alternative to ML-KEM and is currently undergoing standardization. While multiple timing and power side-channel attacks against HQC have been presented, application of masking has so far only been studied for software implementations. As part of this work, we close this gap by first proposing a novel masking technique for the sparse-dense vector multiplication, one of the core components in all HQC operations. We manage to securely exploit the sparsity of the secret operand using a mixed Boolean and arithmetic masking technique and prove its first-order security in the transition- and glitch-robust probing model as well as its PINI-composability. With the same memory width, our configurable and highly parallelizable masked design takes only 3% more clock cycles than a previous unprotected HQC multiplier. Furthermore, our technique requires only 81 bits of randomness per cycle, irrespective of its parallelism. However, like previous Rotate-and-Add constructions, it is vulnerable to profiled horizontal side-channel attacks, which recover all support indices within ±8 positions from 200 traces of our FPGA implementation despite TVLA showing no signs of leakage after 10 million traces. To prevent such attacks, we integrate efficient hiding countermeasures natively into the architecture of the multiplier, resulting in only 1.7% additional latency and moderate area overhead. Together with efficiently masked fixed-weight samplers and a masked decoder, we present the, to our knowledge, first fully masked hardware implementation of HQC, supporting first-order masked key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation. Notably, our masked key generation is faster than a previous unprotected design from literature on an Artix-7 FPGA. Lastly, all modules of our complete designs show no signs of first-order leakage after 1 million traces.
papers.authors: Fabian Buschkowski, Niklas Höher, Tim Güneysu

papers.title: Analysis of the Multi-Key Optimization for SPECK
papers.abstract: SPECK has recently been introduced as a code-based digital signature scheme exploiting the similarities between the Permuted Kernel Problem (PKP) and the Permutation Code Equivalence Problem (PEP). By utilizing PEP as a trapdoor for PKP, SPECK achieves a significant speedup compared to LESS, replacing expensive Gaussian elimination with vector-matrix multiplications. This comes at the cost of larger signatures, since each round of the Zero Knowledge (ZK) protocol used in SPECK has soundness error $1/2$. A well known technique to reduce the soundness errors (and thus the number of parallel repetitions and, ultimately, the signature size) in ZK proofs based on group actions consists in giving multiple elements in the public keys. Despite being constructed around an instance of PEP, which admits a natural description as a code-based group action, the protocol employed in SPECK deviates from the traditional proof of knowledge used for group actions. As shown by the authors of SPECK, a naive use of the multi-key optimization may lead to concrete security concerns. Therefore, the question on whether such a technique can be applied successfully to SPECK remains open. In this paper, we give a positive answer to such a question. We revisit the multi-key optimization for SPECK and investigate the underlying security concerns in detail, identifying conditions and parameter constraints under which multiple keys can be securely integrated into the protocol. Even though, when instantiated with conservative parameters, the multi-key optimization leads to unappealing performance, we show there is wide room for improvements. Furthermore, we design a ring signature scheme based on the same underlying construction.
papers.authors: Marco Baldi, Michele Battagliola, Rahmi El Mechri, Paolo Santini, Riccardo Schiavoni

papers.title: Secure Compilation of Probabilistic Side-Channel Countermeasures
papers.abstract: Probabilistic countermeasures are a common means of protecting programs against side-channels. These countermeasures are hard to implement and are routinely broken by compilers. Proving that a compiler preserves probabilistic side-channel security directly would require reasoning about perfect simulatability of distributions, a challenging technique normally reserved for high-assurance cryptography in frameworks like EasyCrypt and out of scope for compiler correctness. In this paper, we present a language- and leakage-model-agnostic framework for provably secure compilation of probabilistic side-channel security notions. Our main contribution is formalizing a deterministic leakage-preservation relation that implies preservation of probabilistic security notions, including d-NI and d-SNI for masking and cryptographic constant-time. Our framework establishes the same guarantees without probabilistic proof obligations, reducing preservation to a per-pass simulation argument on deterministic traces. We use the Rocq proof assistant to prove that a model of the core pipeline and several optimizing passes of the Jasmin compiler preserve security in the value-probing model with glitches. We also show how to harden against transition leakage with lightweight annotations at the source level. On top of this, we build libmasking, an open-source library of arbitrary-order masked gadgets in Jasmin that securely compiles to ARM and RISC-V assembly, provides C language bindings, and is benchmarked on real hardware. Together, these contributions are a step towards programming environments in which masked code is written or generated, verified at the source level, optimized, and compiled without breaking security.
papers.authors: Gilles Barthe, Gaëtan Cassiers, Henri Dohmen, Marc Gourjon, Benjamin Grégoire, Nora Khayata, Thomas Schneider, Finn Schubert

papers.title: Efficient Two-Dimensional Representation Evaluation via Dual Isogenies with Applications to Isogeny-Based Cryptography
papers.abstract: The evaluation of two-dimensional isogeny representations is a fundamental operation in many isogeny-based cryptographic schemes, notably the public-key encryption schemes POK\'{E} (Eurocrypt 2025) and PIKE (PKC 2026), as well as the digital signature schemes SQIsign2D-West (Asiacrypt 2024) and SQIsign2DPush (Eurocrypt 2026). However, existing two-dimensional evaluation algorithms rely on time-consuming discrete logarithm computations and torsion-basis generation, creating a severe performance bottleneck for the entire protocol. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for evaluating two-dimensional representations by leveraging the properties of dual isogenies, thereby eliminating the need for costly discrete logarithms. We apply this methodology to significantly accelerate some isogeny-based protocols, including POK\'{E}, SQIsign2D, and their variants. We provide optimized C implementations for the speed-optimized variants of POK\'{E} and SQIsign2D using our proposed method. Experimental benchmarks demonstrate that the fast variants of POK\'{E} combined with our new techniques achieve computational speedups of up to $3.47\times$ in terms of CPU clock cycles compared to POK\'{E} at the NIST-I security level. Additionally, our explicit analysis and implementation results confirm that the signing phase of SQIsign2DPush (resp. the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization candidate SQIsign-v3.0), when using our method, achieves a performance improvement of up to $11.24\%$ (resp. $5.02$\%) across the three NIST security levels.
papers.authors: Jianming Lin, Saiyu Wang, Chang-An Zhao, Yuhao Zheng

papers.title: CHAMP: Cayley HAshing with Matrix Products
papers.abstract: Cayley hash functions hash binary strings by representing the bits of the message as elements of a semigroup and multiplying the corresponding elements. This gives Cayley hash functions useful homomorphic properties. Here, we propose CHAMP, a Cayley hash function based on products of $2\times 2$ matrices over a finite field, and discuss its security, implementation, and performance.
papers.authors: Alexander Demin, Alexey Ovchinnikov, Vladimir Shpilrain

papers.title: Power Analysis on SQIsign via Ideal Reconstruction from Quaternion Leakages
papers.abstract: SQIsign is an isogeny-based signature scheme, which is one of the Round-3 candidates for NIST's additional post-quantum digital signature standardization. NIST considers resistance to side-channel attacks as one important factor in evaluating digital signature schemes. However, side-channel analysis of SQIsign remains very limited. To the best of our knowledge, all existing studies target the Round-1 version, so their applicability to the substantially revised Round-3 SQIsign has not been established. Moreover, existing studies either provide experimental validation only for toy parameters or assume exploitable leakage without demonstrating its extraction in practice, leaving their applicability to realistic implementations unclear. In this work, we identify five side-channel vulnerabilities in the signing procedure of Round-3 SQIsign and provide polynomial-time algebraic algorithms that recover the secret key from the corresponding leaked intermediate values. Additionally, we further provide algorithms that enable the reconstruction of the complete secret key even when the side-channel leakage reveals only partial bits of an algebraic value, for each vulnerability. Finally, we further perform power analysis attack on the SQIsign source code, extracting the necessary leakage or its partial information for each vulnerability.
papers.authors: Won Kim, Jaeho Jeon, JeongHwan Lee, Suseong Lee, Young-Sik Kim, Changmin Lee

papers.title: Zippel: A Language, Compiler, Runtime, and Analyzer for ZK Proof Systems
papers.abstract: This paper introduces Zippel, a language, compiler, runtime, and analyzer for cryptographic proof systems. Zippel lets developers write proof systems with ease using syntax that mimics pseudocode in cryptography papers. It also eliminates entire classes of vulnerabilities by construction owing to its type system and runtime. For example, Zippel automatically synchronizes protocol transcripts and correctly applies the Fiat--Shamir transform. Zippel also has fully automated static analyses that confirm whether a protocol is complete and sound given only the protocol's description. We have implemented 35 proof systems in Zippel including Sumcheck, Schnorr, KZG, Groth16, Bulletproofs, Hyrax, Spartan, Dory, HyperPlonk, DeKART, and Pari. Our evaluation shows that Zippel programs are competitive with hand-written implementations on multi-core hardware, so Zippel's security and implementation benefits do not come at high cost.
papers.authors: Sebastian Angel, Sydnie-Shea Cohen, Eleftherios Ioannidis, Pratyush Mishra, Alex Ozdemir, Yuxiang Qiu, Alireza Shirzad

papers.title: AVX-512 Acceleration of SQIsign 3.0 Verification
papers.abstract: SQIsign is a compact isogeny-based signature scheme. We present a low-latency AVX-512 implementation of complete SQIsign 3.0 verification at security levels I, III, and V. Our implementation provides vectorized curve-side verification, including the Superglue transition, and introduces dynamic-programming strategies for the degree-$2^\ell$ and theta-model $(2,2)$-isogeny chains. The strategies account for batched point evaluation and the preparation of SIMD data. On an Intel Core i7-11800H running native Ubuntu 24.04, the complete verifiers achieve $2.14\times$, $2.08\times$, and $2.34\times$ speedups, respectively, over the SQIsign 3.0 Broadwell reference verifiers (the optimized 64-bit assembly implementation).
papers.authors: Yunqi Wen, Xuzhe Liu, Zhi Hu, Saiyu Wang, Chang-An Zhao

papers.title: SwiftAuth: Conditional Privacy-Preserving UAV Authentication with Multi-Source Credential Aggregation and Non-Interactive Authorization
papers.abstract: To address the challenges of interactive credential issuance and conditional privacy-preserving authentication for dynamic terminals accessing multiple third-party services, we propose an traceable and aggregatable tagged witness signature (TA-TWS). Building upon this scheme, we design an efficient and privacy-preserving anonymous authentication framework, termed SwiftAuth. SwiftAuth decouples the issuer’s authorization phase from the user’s credential acquisition process in traditional anonymous authentication systems by introducing an asynchronous credential distribution mechanism. This allows issuers to generate authorization components even when users are offline, while ensuring that only the designated user can derive the complete access credential. Furthermore, during the authentication phase, SwiftAuth reduces communication and verification overhead in concurrent multi-service access by compressing multiple credentials into a constant-size representation, and supports verifier-side batch verification across users. In addition, it provides conditional privacy by integrating a regulatory trapdoor, ensuring default anonymity for legitimate users while enabling authorities to trace malicious actors upon protocol violations. Finally, we formally prove that the proposed TA-TWS achieves unforgeability and witness hiding. Extensive experiments were conducted on multiple resource-constrained devices, and Aliyun servers, using the MIRACL Core cryptographic library, demonstrate the practicality and efficiency of our approach.
papers.authors: Mingwei Zeng, Qingyang Zhang, Jie Cui, Hong Zhong, Fengqun Wang

papers.title: safeRNSgcd: Accelerating Falcon key generation with RNS in SafeGCD
papers.abstract: The deepest level of Falcon's NTRU solver needs only one Bézout coefficient from two large integer resultants already represented in a residue number system (RNS). We give $\mathtt{safeRNSgcd}$, which computes this coefficient while keeping the large states in RNS. Its central insight is that centered explicit CRT can recover the exact low bits needed by SafeGCD batches using single-word fixed-point arithmetic. Integrated into $\mathtt{ntrugen}$, our C implementation reduces inversion and private-key basis-generation costs on a Raspberry Pi 5 and two x86-64 processors, compared with original $\mathtt{ntrugen}$ and a variant omitting the unused coefficient.
papers.authors: Cesare Huang, Bo-Yin Yang

papers.title: Byzantine Broadcast in $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ Communication
papers.abstract: We present a deterministic $n$-party Byzantine broadcast protocol secure against $t<n$ faults, with communication complexity $O(n^2\log^4(n)\lambda)$ and $O(t)$ rounds (where $\lambda$ is a security parameter), improving upon the seminal Dolev--Strong protocol from 1983.
papers.authors: Yuval Efron, Jovan Komatovic, Ling ren

papers.title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
papers.abstract: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(H)$ reaction queries, where $H$ is the entropy of the secret key. The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side. We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.
papers.authors: Song Bian, Hyeongmin Choe, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee

papers.title: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
papers.abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who does not know that randomness. The evaluator must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the $n$ parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a superlinear lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$. Our technique gives $Ω(n\log n)$ lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$ (with even $n$), and an $Ω(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$ when $q\leq(1-c)n$ for a fixed constant $c>0$. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$ and $MOD_q$ with prime $q$, the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors in the stated regimes. Under support privacy, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n)$ communication for every symmetric Boolean function. Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a $ω(n)$ lower bound for $OR_n$ using the same combinatorial core. Both works used AI assistance.
papers.authors: Marshall Ball, Peter Crawford-Kahrl, Vladimir Podolskii, Morgan Prior

papers.title: SMT-Boosted Security Types and Correctness for Low-Level MPC
papers.abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) is an important enabling technology for data privacy in modern distributed applications. We develop a new Hoare logic and type theory to automatically enforce correctness, confidentiality, and integrity properties of protocols written in the Prelude/Overture language framework. Both definition and automation of our analyses leverages SMT verification, supporting precision and efficiency. Our approach is compositional, scalable, and generalizes to arbitrary prime fields and secret sharing schemes.
papers.authors: Christian Skalka, Steven Baldasty, Yeonhee Yeh, Felix Walberg, Joseph P. Near

papers.title: Blind Watermarking of Software Repositories via Module Placement
papers.abstract: Source-code watermarking supports provenance tracking by embedding a recoverable identifier in a software artifact. Many existing approaches encode this identifier in tokens or program syntax, exposing the watermark to transformations that modify the source text. We present PlaceMark, a blind watermarking system that encodes a payload in the placement of modules within a repository. Each eligible module is identified by its filename and top-level definition names. A secret key determines its ordered candidate destinations and its position in the reading order; the module's location within its candidate list determines the encoded symbol. Embedding relocates selected modules and updates their import references. Extraction uses the distributed repository, the key, and agreed decoding parameters, without an original copy or placement ledger. Capacity measurements on ten Python repositories yield nominal capacities of 249 to 2,166 bits in nine repositories, while one provides no placement channel. In 216 trials of the evaluated text transformations, the payload is recovered exactly. Relocation degrades recovery gradually on Django, Airflow and Salt, while on Pylint a path-based exclusion in our implementation lets relocation change carrier membership, and we measure it for an untargeted adversary and for one that concentrates its budget on the public carrier set. Changes to filenames or definition names alter the identity input and are measured separately. Exact recovery also depends on placement feasibility. The results characterize module placement as a carrier that can complement watermarks embedded in source text.
papers.authors: Khadija Mohamed, Khaled Fathy, Mamdouh Farouk, Mohamed M. Darwish

papers.title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
papers.abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.
papers.authors: Nitin Jha, Prateek Paudel, Abhishek Parakh

papers.title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
papers.abstract: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.
papers.authors: B. Nancharaiah, Ramakrishna Kolikipogu, J. Sulthan Alikhan, Lakshmana Phaneendra Maguluri, Elangovan Muniyandy, D. Baburao

papers.title: GhostFaceMPC: Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition with Multi-Party Computation
papers.abstract: Facial recognition has become central to modern authentication systems, security frameworks, and personalized services. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by severe privacy risks, particularly surrounding unauthorized access to sensitive biometric data. To address these challenges, this paper presents GhostFaceMPC, the first end-to-end, privacy-preserving face recognition system to evaluate a deep convolutional neural network extractor and matching under secure multi-party computation. GhostFaceMPC enables secure processing of facial data across all stages of a face recognition process, from feature extraction and storage to matching, without exposing raw images or biometric embeddings at any stage. We introduce a multi-party computation-friendly quantization of the GhostFaceNet model and circuit optimizations that make face recognition under multi-party computation practical. The code is available at https://github.com/crypto-unict/GhostFaceMPC.
papers.authors: Davide Carnemolla, Dario Catalano, Mario Di Raimondo

papers.title: Benchmarking Post-Quantum Key Encapsulation in S3-Compatible Object Storage under Client Concurrency
papers.abstract: Data encrypted today with classical public-key algorithms could be decrypted once large quantum computers exist. Cloud object stores keep data for years, so the client-side encryption that protects it must move to post-quantum algorithms such as ML-KEM, which adds a key-encapsulation step and a larger ciphertext to every stored object. So far, the cost of ML-KEM has been measured for the algorithm on its own and for securing network connections, but not for encrypting each object in a storage system that serves many clients at once. It has therefore been unclear whether ML-KEM slows such a system, under which conditions, and why. We address this problem by measuring per-object ML-KEM against classical key exchange on an S3-compatible object store, with two client implementations, two processor types and up to 500 concurrent workers, using pre-registered experiments and statistical equivalence tests. ML-KEM reduced throughput only when the client's processor was at or near full load, with one unexplained exception, and then by 4.0 to 4.9% in our main client. Controlled experiments on one processor type traced most of that loss to the way the software library was called, and a second, native client showed that the size of the loss depends on the implementation. The lasting cost is storage: 1,056 more bytes per object than with classical key exchange. The results cover two clients, one single-node store and one cloud provider.
papers.authors: Revanth Reddy Lingala, K. Gangadhara Rao, Padigela Srujan, Saarthak Manocha, Vainavi Venkat

papers.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
papers.abstract: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.
papers.authors: Jason Anderson, Kaz Gunning

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
papers.abstract: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.
papers.authors: Jasleen Kaur, Chloé Cachet, Koray Karabina, Jean Belo Klamti, Philippe Lamontagne

papers.title: NOMAI: Scalable Federated Learning with Private Weights
papers.abstract: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.
papers.authors: Yiyi Sun, Mushtari Sadia, Amrita Roy Chowdhury

papers.title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
papers.abstract: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.
papers.authors: Khalil Ahmad, Omar Ansari, Mohsin Kamal, Asif Iqbal, Muhammad Naveed Aman

papers.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
papers.abstract: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences. A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
papers.authors: Jan Reineke

papers.title: MAppPrint: Robust and Real-time Mobile App Fingerprinting via Traffic Behavior Correlation Graphs
papers.abstract: Mobile apps have become ubiquitous in daily life. Despite communication encryption, app fingerprinting (AF) attacks can still enable adversaries to infer the apps in use by analyzing patterns of encrypted network traffic. However, existing AF attacks suffer from three critical limitations that hinder their practical effectiveness: (i) the inability to capture app-specific traffic dependencies, rendering traffic fingerprints fragile under dynamic networking conditions; (ii) the neglect of latency and throughput considerations, resulting in inefficient real-time user tracking; and (iii) the incapacity to handle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency. In this paper, we propose MAppPrint, a robust and real-time app fingerprinting framework. MAppPrint introduces a behavior-level traffic fingerprint, i.e., Traffic Behavior Correlation Graph (TBCG), which models app traffic by capturing unit traffic behaviors and their correlations, thereby providing reliable app fingerprints. To enable real-time fingerprinting, MAppPrint incorporates a fingerprint compression algorithm that transforms each TBCG into a compact graph by selectively aggregating redundant information. Furthermore, MAppPrint employs an unsupervised decomposition strategy to disentangle mixed traffic generated by multi-app concurrency, enabling unified identification of both single-app and multi-app traffic. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MAppPrint achieves 4.9~13.9% improvement in AF precision and 3~6 times improvement in timeliness over state-of-the-art methods. Meanwhile, MAppPrint is robust in dynamic networking conditions, while achieving a throughput of 10.5 GB/s and a prediction latency of 0.68 seconds.
papers.authors: Tao Duan, Junzhou Zhao, Jianglong Li, RongHua Li, Youqian Zhang, Nuo Xu, Pinghui Wang, Haibo Hu

papers.title: On the Robustness of Gossip Protocols in Modern Blockchains
papers.abstract: Modern platforms such as Ethereum and Polkadot nowadays execute Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus protocols over large validator committees, often comprising hundreds of nodes. At this scale, complete graph topologies for connecting nodes are impractical, leading systems to adopt various gossip mechanisms, often in an ad hoc manner. In this paper, we study the robustness of widely deployed gossip protocols used in committee-based blockchains against realistic network adversaries. We show, both analytically and through extensive empirical measurements, that the graph parameters commonly chosen to instantiate random graphs are insufficient to guarantee that enough honest nodes receive consensus messages for quorum formation in existing protocols. Motivated by this finding, we empirically assess the robustness of Bitcoin's Erdős-Rényi (ER) graphs, Polkadot's grid topology, Ethereum's GossipSub, and Solana's chunk- and tree-based disseminations. Our results reveal surprising tradeoffs: Solana's dynamic trees are bandwidth-efficient in benign settings but fragile under adaptive attacks; Polkadot's grid achieves strong robustness at the cost of high bandwidth overhead; GossipSub is both bandwidth-efficient and resilient to adaptive adversaries, yet highly sensitive to parameter choices; and ER graphs provide a strong robustness-efficiency tradeoff, e.g., when the (average) fanout degree exceeds 15 for networks up to 5000 nodes.
papers.authors: Wenting Li, Jannik Albrecht, Frederik Armknecht, Ghassan Karame

papers.title: Poisoning the Neighborhood: A Topology-Aware Topic-Level Attack on Large-Scale HNSW-based RAG Systems
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations and knowledge staleness in large language models using external knowledge. However, ingestion from public and third-party sources exposes RAG systems to poisoning attacks. Existing attacks are designed and evaluated under exact retrieval, where poisoned documents participate in global ranking. Deployment-scale systems instead rely on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW), where limited search budgets, graph-search reachability, and local benign-document competition invalidate this assumption and degrade existing attacks. We present a topology-aware topic-level poisoning attack against large-scale HNSW-RAG that generalizes to unseen topic queries. We organize poisoned documents into a Hub-Satellite structure: Satellites provide competitive entry points across semantic regions, while Hubs strengthen local cohesion and facilitate cascading retrieval. For generation, we propose an entity-claim promotion attack combining evidence anchoring and entity-claim coupling to promote the target entity via a target claim across different query regions. On 2M-document Wikipedia, our attack maintains over 72% retrieval success and reaches 31.29% attack success, substantially outperforming baselines; domain-specific experiments further support its effectiveness. Structural analyses show that the Hub-Satellite topology forms in HNSW, indicating that graph structure contributes to improved poisoned-document retrieval. Existing poisoning defenses cannot mitigate the attack, exposing graph-structural risks in HNSW-RAG systems.
papers.authors: Yufei Chen, Yao Wang, Haibin Zhang

papers.title: What Survives Self-Evolution: Provenance Marks in Copied Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses, the prompt and tool code around a base model, leak. Claude Code's 512,000 lines were mirrored within hours of a packaging error. A plagiarist can pass a leaked harness through a published self-evolver and ship the result as its own. We define this as a covert rewriting attack. No one targets a provenance mark, yet a large language model (LLM) proposer rewrites the file that carries it and a score keeps the better rewrites. We give the first measurement of marks under this attack, with three evolvers, five proposers and two environments. Published marks fail. KGW in the prompt survives GEPA's rewrites in 0 of 12 copies, AgentMark as released in 5 of 12. The proposer's habits decide survival, by two orders of magnitude across models, and selection protects a mark only when each decision sees enough games. We then build a mark for this attack. Its key is the order of near-tied entries of a table of where objects are found, built from public games, so deleting the table costs success, rewrites that keep its rows keep the order, and a customer reads the key from the agent's actions alone. On held-out games it is detected in 62 of 76 copies whose lineage rewrote its file. A scheme-aware plagiarist reshuffles the ties at no measurable cost, and a plagiarist who asks the proposer for more general code removes the key in 75-100% of rewrites.
papers.authors: Jieyu Li, Jingya Li, Sheng Li, Xinpeng Zhang, Zhenxing Qian

papers.title: When Rotation Bounds Nothing: Streaming Image Classifiers to Field Nodes Under Physical Capture
papers.abstract: Field nodes run image classifiers locally, exposing a first-class asset, the trained model, to theft. Trusted-execution enclaves, collaborative-inference splits, and encrypted storage assume the device owner is the adversary from deployment. Here the operator owns the node, and an adversary seizing it reads only what cold-boot capture finds resident. One answer stores nothing: a chunkable multi-exit model streams into volatile memory, rotating to bound residency. We characterise the capture envelope on real LTE traces across two victims of one architecture, against passive and adaptive adversaries. Neither survives a capable adversary; recovery cost alone differs. Against a from-scratch victim the uncaptured stages must be learned: the adaptive adversary gains most at shallow seizures, ends the CIFAR-10 envelope at every rotation, and stays rotation-bounded on CIFAR100, from 42.6% of usable seizures at 5 s to 86.8% at 30 s. Against the same architecture sliced from a public pretrained backbone, the adversary downloads those stages, recovering at least 90% of maximum accuracy at all depths, taking usable CIFAR-100 seizures from 0.0% to 97.3% at 5 s, given the victim's full labelled training set. Delivery-side secrecy raises a seizure's price; a public copy of the withheld stages erases it.
papers.authors: Daniel Gilkarov, Ran Dubin

papers.title: FedPix: Learning What to Share with Less Leakage in Federated Intelligence
papers.abstract: Existing federated intelligence paradigms primarily focus on how models are trained or aggregated, while overlooking a more fundamental question: \textbf{what information should leave the client?} Existing methods often share model updates that users cannot easily inspect, or data representations that may reveal sensitive information. Moreover, generating these representations can be computationally expensive for resource-constrained clients. We observe that image classification does not require all the visual details needed to reconstruct the original image. This suggests that clients could share less information while preserving task performance. However, learning what to preserve is challenging when the server cannot access raw client data. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedPix}, which learns to share compact, visually inspectable images instead of model updates or intermediate features. The key idea is to use the shared representations themselves to learn what information should be preserved and what can be discarded. By balancing task utility and reconstruction resistance, FedPix enables the server to improve the representations without accessing raw client data, while keeping client-side computation lightweight. Extensive experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, FashionMNIST, and MNIST demonstrate that FedPix achieves strong reconstruction resistance, with reconstruction PSNR as low as 6.87~dB and synthetic PSNR as low as 6.74~dB. Meanwhile, FedPix reduces client runtime by up to 96.0\% (from 1223~s to 49~s on CIFAR-10), while maintaining competitive classification accuracy of 99.18\% on MNIST, 89.97\% on FashionMNIST, 82.24\% on BloodMNIST, and 65.63\% on CIFAR-10.
papers.authors: Jingwei Zhao, Tiantong Sun, Yuanyuan Song, Jinhuan Guo, Zishuo Wei, Shengyu Huang, Ziyuan Ren, Wei Chen, Xiaojin Zhang

papers.title: CARE-SD: Explainable Reasoning Architecture for Local SLM Self-Disclosure Analysis in Textual Data
papers.abstract: Cybersecurity interviews uncover critical security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns often not fully captured by conventional technical assessments. Consequently, identifying genuine self-disclosures is challenging because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretations may introduce unsupported claims. Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) protect sensitive participant data by keeping processing within controlled environments, but their limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis. This study developed CARE-SD (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure), a novel four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. We evaluated three local SLMs, including Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, and Llama 3B, using 82 independently annotated cybersecurity interviews across five organizational sectors. Comparisons included conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, larger 8B--32B models, and architectural ablations. Two independent reviewers assessed disclosure labels, factual claims, and explanation correctness. CARE-SD improved the accuracy and evidence reliability of SLMs, increasing Llama 3B Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while reducing unsupported claims by 60\%. Remarkably, the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the architecture without requiring a larger model.
papers.authors: Aisvarya Adeseye, Adeyemi Adeseye, Mohammad Tahir, Jouni Isoaho

papers.title: Approve What, Exactly? Effect Binding and Trusted Rendering for Agent Step-Up Authorization
papers.abstract: AI agents now pause for approval before they send money, delete files or email outsiders, and that approval is usually treated as a second factor. We argue it is one only when compromising the agent cannot produce it and when it names exactly what it approves, and we test both conditions. We define twelve attacks on the approval path, including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting, and run them against the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), the Microsoft action-bound approval design and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. An audit of ten agent runtimes finds no third-party verifiable approval record, no flood limits where measurable, and post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes with measurable binding. As a reference defense we build ASU (Agent Step-Up), a gateway that renders the approval card from a canonical effect descriptor, has a passkey on the phone of the user sign its digest, and executes only the stored call. Tamarin proves its binding, single-use and key-level non-repudiation properties under three stated hypotheses (53 lemmas). Across 27,108 scripted trials and 609 AgentDojo attack pairs, ASU stops substitution, replay and grant stretching, and the trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03. With 15 current language models as automated approvers, the trusted card raises the attack catch rate from 0.30 to 0.98, at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses, mostly due to a placeholder artifact in our stimuli. A second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation in these experiments, flooding still succeeds 0.45 to 0.60 of the time against a modeled approver, and approval cannot stop effects that policy already allows. Code, data and proofs: https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/agent-step-up
papers.authors: Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty, Jaylen Cargill

papers.title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey of Thermal Side-Channel and Perception Attacks
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. These paths differ in mechanism and privilege; both exploit interfaces that AV stacks cannot disable without compromising Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF). Classical microarchitectural and cyber-physical systems (CPS) surveys address cache timing, adversarial machine learning, and camera or LiDAR spoofing; no prior survey jointly frames physical thermal IR attacks and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry as one residual-risk class. This survey systematizes thirteen representative works into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, comparing them by privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance. We distinguish attack family from adversary class and map defenses to residual risk while thermal management remains operational. A commodity proxy supports the software co-tenant branch only; physical IR evidence comes from cited literature. We identify open problems in on-target automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis, aiming to motivate co-design across sensors, operating systems, silicon, and automotive standards.
papers.authors: Harsh Aaryan, Ce Zhou

papers.title: Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models. Our results for the first time suggest that random projection can serve as a competitive and practical baseline for privacy-preserving RAG systems.
papers.authors: Dixi Yao, Tahseen Rabbani, Tian Li

papers.title: Subgraph Counting with Local Node Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: We study the problem of approximately counting subgraphs under local node differential privacy (LNDP), a recently introduced model that enforces strong privacy guarantees in analyses of distributed social networks. We design a noninteractive $(\varepsilon,0)$-LNDP algorithm that, given any public $k$-node template graph $H$, counts occurrences of $H$ in a sensitive undirected $n$-node graph with additive error $O(n^{k-\frac{1}{2}}/\varepsilon^{k-1})$, for any constant $k$.
