We also partially implement an RLWE-based post-quantum instantiation over a \(2^{128}\) sized index space for negligible collision probability among indices. A batch of 1024 messages uses approximately 0.89 MB per ciphertext and 20 seconds of single-thread decryption per server.
papers.authors: Amit Agarwal, Sourav Das, Babak Poorebrahim Gilkalaye, Benny Pinkas, Peter Rindal

papers.title: Worst-Case Hardness for Succinct and Decomposed Learning with Errors
papers.abstract: The succinct LWE (CRYPTO~'24) and decomposed LWE (CRYPTO~'25) assumptions are two recently introduced variants of the celebrated LWE problem, known to imply the existence of numerous new cryptographic primitives. Yet, the hardness of these problems has thus far remained poorly understood, since there is no known reduction to LWE. In this work, we study these lattice problems from a foundational perspective. Our main technical contribution is a worst-case-to-average-case reduction from \emph{superlattice SVP} (SuperSVP) to succinct SIS. We introduce SuperSVP as a variant of SVP for general lattices in which the solver is additionally given, as a hint, a short basis for a related superlattice. Combining this result with our quantum reduction from succinct SIS to succinct LWE, which is an analog of Regev's SIS-to-LWE reduction, and with our search-to-decision reduction establishes worst-case hardness for succinct LWE. Finally, we show that succinct and decomposed LWE are equivalent, extending this conclusion to decomposed LWE. Overall, our work places succinct and decomposed LWE on firmer theoretical ground and, as a direct consequence, establishes the \emph{worst-case} hardness of a variety of cryptographic primitives, known to be implied by these assumptions.
papers.authors: Damiano Abram, Gal Arnon, Valerio Cini, Paul Lou, Giulio Malavolta, Lawrence Roy

papers.title: Faster generic CCA secure KEM transformation using encrypt-then-MAC
papers.abstract: ML-KEM is a lattice-based IND-CCA secure key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) standardized by NIST in FIPS 203. ML-KEM achieves chosen-ciphertext security by applying the Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO) transformation to an IND-CPA secure public key encryption (PKE) scheme. The FO transformation uses de-randomization and re-encryption to ensure ciphertext non-malleability, but because ML-KEM's underlying PKE encryption subroutine is slower than the decryption subroutine, ML-KEM's decapsulation performance is dominated by re-encryption. In this paper, we revisit the ``encrypt-then-MAC'' paradigm as a generic KEM transformation: the PKE ciphertext is authenticated by a message authentication code (MAC) whose key is derived from the PKE plaintext. We prove that the transformation achieves IND-CCA security in the random oracle model when the underlying PKE is one-way under plaintext-checking attack (OW-PCA), and we introduce a fine-grained security notion, one-wayness under $q$-bounded plaintext-checking attack (OW-$q$PCA), under which the transformation achieves IND-$q$CCA security. In contrast to the tag-based IND-1CCA transformations of Huguenin-Dumittan and Vaudenay (Eurocrypt 2022), whose tag is a random-oracle hash of the plaintext and the entire ciphertext, our transformation applies the random oracle only to the short PKE plaintext, while the long ciphertext is processed by a standard-model MAC that needs only to be one-time existentially unforgeable. We present ML-KEM-EtM, an IND-$q$CCA secure KEM derived from applying the encrypt-then-MAC transformation to the PKE subroutines of ML-KEM, and McElieceEtM, an instantiation with Classic McEliece that achieves full IND-CCA security under the conjectured OW-PCA security of its Niederreiter PKE. We implement ML-KEM-EtM with a wide selection of MACs including Poly1305, GMAC, CMAC, and KMAC256. At the cost of minimal increase in encapsulation CPU cycle count and ciphertext size, ML-KEM-EtM achieves a substantial reduction of the decapsulation CPU cycle count.
papers.authors: Ganyu Xu, Kalikinkar Mandal, Guang Gong

papers.title: Software-Pipelining The Number Theoretic Transform on Neural Processing Units: A Loop-Fission Methodology
papers.abstract: Lattice-based post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) rely heavily on the number theoretic transform (NTT) for efficient polynomial multiplication. While GPUs and FPGAs have been widely explored for NTT acceleration, neural processing units (NPUs), a rapidly growing class of AI accelerators, remain largely unexplored for cryptographic workloads. In this work, we develop a methodology for accelerating the NTT on NPUs, using AMD’s AI Engine (AIE) architecture as a representative NPU to develop and benchmark it. At its core is manual loop fission, in which large and complex loops are split into smaller primitives, enabling highly efficient software pipelining and avoiding memory stalls or register spilling. Applying it, we develop efficient Barrett reduction primitives and use these to construct three high-throughput, low-latency NTT implementations (radix-2, radix-4, and radix-8), achieving significant performance gains over the AIE compiler and prior literature. On AMD’s first-generation AIE specifically, we achieve speedups of $8.27\times$ to $13.2\times$ in throughput and $2.44\times$ to $10.3\times$ in latency per AIE tile in comparison with prior work. Our implementations support arbitrary NTT-friendly moduli and polynomial sizes up to degree 4096 for 14-bit moduli and 2048 for 30-bit moduli. Finally, we discuss the portability of our techniques to other NPU architectures, and identify which architectural features are most beneficial for NTT acceleration.
papers.authors: Henri Vermeersch, Xander Pottier, Quinten Norga, Thomas de Ruijter, Ingrid Verbauwhede

papers.title: Leakage-Resilient Incompressible Cryptography: Constructions and Barriers
papers.abstract: We introduce Leakage-Resilient Incompressible cryptography, which simultaneously addresses two variants of side-channel attacks that have been tackled in theoretical cryptography. Leakage-resilience seeks to provide security against an adversary who learns a part of the secret-key and the entire ciphertext or signature; conversely, incompressible cryptography provides security against an adversary who learns the entire secret-key, but only a part of the ciphertext or signature. However, constructions in either of these security models can fail against an attack in the other model. In this work, we define a new model of security that subsumes both leakage-resilient cryptography and incompressible cryptography, and we present several non-trivial positive and negative results. On the positive side, first we present a transformation from incompressible symmetric-key encryption (SKE) to leakage-resilient incompressible SKE in the information-theoretic setting. Next, as one of our main results, we construct a leakage-resilient incompressible public-key encryption (PKE), combining an incompressible SKE and a new primitive that we call leakage-resilient non-committing key encapsulation mechanism (LR-NC-KEM). While an information-theoretic incompressible SKE suitable for use in both these constructions already exists in the literature (Dziembowski, CRYPTO 2006), we present a new construction achieving ciphertext-rate $\frac{1}{2}$ and compression-rate $\frac{1}{2}$, using an appropriate notion of invertible extractors; this leads to corresponding improvements in the final parameters we obtain in these constructions. We also construct a leakage-resilient incompressible signature scheme in the classical random oracle model, assuming $(\mathsf{DCR}\text{ or }\mathsf{LWE})$ and the Decisional Linear assumption, with signature-rate and compression-rate $1-o(1)$ and leakage-rate $1$. On the negative side, we show barriers to significantly improving the parameters we obtain, by showing impossibility of basing the security of such improved schemes on blackbox reductions. Apart from the general framework and the specific results we obtain, some of the intermediate tools that we define and instantiate, like LR-NC-KEM and invertible extractors, may be of independent interest.
papers.authors: KAARTIK BHUSHAN, Rishab Goyal, Venkata Koppula, Varun Narayanan, Manoj Prabhakaran, Mahesh Sreekumar Rajasree

papers.title: edaBits in the Exponent (edaBitE) and Issuer-Hiding Blind Signatures from ML-DSA and VOLE-in-the-Head
papers.abstract: Blind signatures let a user obtain a signature by interacting with an issuer that controls the signing key, while the issuer never sees the message. They form the basis of anonymous credentials, which are the centerpiece of privacy-preserving digital identification to be deployed widely in the coming years. Existing plausibly quantum-secure blind signatures rely on bespoke cryptographic constructions, instead of standardized ones. This is dissatisfying from a cryptographic perspective, and also leads to practical issues: secret signing keys are often stored in secure elements, in which case only signature algorithms supported by certified secure elements can be the basis for deployed protocols. We give the first blind signature whose issuer runs a NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme unmodified. Issuance is just an ML-DSA signature on a commitment, and the blind signature is a zero-knowledge proof of knowledge, using the VOLE-in-the-head zero-knowledge proof system, of the ML-DSA signature. Security reduces to the EUF-CMA security of ML-DSA and to the proof system, with no new assumptions. A blind signature is about $1$ MB and takes under a second to produce and half a second to verify. Issuer-hiding and selective disclosure of signed attributes can easily be added on top for a few tens of kilobytes, at a proof size essentially independent of how many issuers the list names. Underlying the construction is edaBitE, a novel batch consistency check between binary and prime-field commitments. In a non-interactive proof, the existing edaBits checks it replaces would be the single largest item in the blind signature. We believe that edaBitE is of independent interest.
papers.authors: Carsten Baum, Marvin Beckmann

papers.title: Refined Application of the XL Algorithm within the Algebraic Approach to the Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem
papers.abstract: The Syndrome Decoding Problem (SDP) is a fundamental mathematical problem underlying code-based cryptography, which is considered a promising candidate for post-quantum cryptography. The Regular Syndrome Decoding Problem (RSDP) is a variant of the SDP in which the error vector follows a specific block-wise structure. Recent developments in RSDP-based cryptographic schemes have led to a wider variety of parameter settings, making it increasingly important to evaluate the complexity of solving the RSDP over a broad range of parameters. One of the main approaches to solving the RSDP is the algebraic approach, which transforms a given RSDP instance into a polynomial system and solves it using algebraic techniques such as the XL algorithm. In this work, we construct and analyze algebraic algorithms for the RSDP by combining and extending techniques used in existing algebraic approaches. Our algorithms mainly follow the framework of the hybrid algorithm proposed by Wang et al., while allowing an arbitrary solving degree $d$ in the application of the XL algorithm. We further consider two variants: an XFL-based method that combines partial Gaussian elimination with variable guessing, and a WXL-based method that exploits the sparsity of the Macaulay matrix. Our complexity analysis for various parameter settings shows that, for some fixed values of $n$ and $k$, the WXL-based variant using a larger solving degree $d>2$ is particularly efficient when the block size $\beta$ is sufficiently small, while the original hybrid algorithm becomes more efficient as $\beta$ increases.
papers.authors: Hiroki Furue, Yusuke Aikawa

papers.title: Modulus Operandi: Round-Optimal Modulus Conversion for MPC and Threshold FHE
papers.abstract: In secure multiparty computation (MPC), modulus conversion turns a sharing of a value $x$ modulo $q$ into a sharing of the same value modulo $t$, without leaking anything about $x$. One important application of modulus conversion is in threshold decryption for lattice-based cryptosystems, where a sharing modulo the ciphertext modulus has to be moved to the plaintext modulus before it can be opened. The most efficient protocols so far (Damgård et al., Asiacrypt 2026) are in the preprocessing model, assume $x$ is bounded away from $q$ by a constant factor and take two rounds for a prime target modulus, three rounds for arbitrary moduli, and one round when all moduli are 2-powers. We improve upon this by constructing three new modulus conversion protocols in the preprocessing model: - Our first conversion protocol takes a single round for arbitrary moduli, consisting of just one opening. - Our second conversion protocol is a variant of the first protocol, where in the preprocessing most of the secure multiplications are replaced by private inputs, which are checked in a batch using fully linear interactive oracle proofs (FLIOPs). This makes the preprocessing cheaper (amortized over a batch of conversions) when the number $N$ of parties is small. This comes at the cost of making the bound on $x$ a factor $N$ stronger. - Our third conversion protocol avoids the bound on $x$ altogether but takes two rounds. All our protocols are stated in the arithmetic black box (ABB) model, so they can run on top of a wide variety of MPC protocols, inheriting their corruption threshold and security model. To allow the third conversion protocol to run in two rounds, we construct the first one-round comparison protocol in the ABB model for comparing a bitwise shared $n$-bit value against a public threshold with polynomial-size preprocessing. Concretely, the preprocessing size is $\mathcal O(n^2)$ in general, and $\mathcal O(n^2 / \log n)$ in our case where the secret value is fixed in preprocessing. We also construct constant-round ABB protocols without preprocessing for computing symmetric functions and comparisons of values shared bitwise modulo powers of arbitrary primes (e.g., $2^k$), at communication quasi-linear in the number of input bits. Previously, this required either a sufficiently large prime or polynomially larger communication. Finally, we give an impossibility result for non-interactive modulus conversion, demonstrating that a single round is optimal: unless $t$ divides $q$, every non-interactive conversion for inputs $x < q/\beta$ is incorrect with probability at least $\approx 1/(4\beta)$.
papers.authors: Ivan Damgård, Sebastian Hasler, Sebastian Kolby, Stanislas Pawlak

papers.title: A Black-Box Compiler from Static to Dynamic SNARKs
papers.abstract: Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge (SNARKs) for NP allow a prover to prove knowledge of a witness of an NP relation to a verifier with a short proof. The primary goal of a (static) SNARK is to make verification cheap: the proof should be short, and the verifier's work should be minimal. However, recent work has also focused on making SNARKs more prover-efficient: cheap verification should ideally not come at the cost of large prover overhead. One avenue for achieving prover efficiency is via Dynamic SNARKs, which allow a prover to efficiently update the proof when the witness is updated. For example, one may use a SNARK to issue a proof of a query being performed correctly on a database, and then issue a new proof of the query once the database is updated. If these updates are small compared to the size of the witness (only a single entry of a large database is updated), then the prover should ideally be able to use the old proof to generate a new proof in time proportional to the distance between the old and the new witness. While some constructions of dynamic SNARKs for NP have been recently proposed by Wang et al. [Eurocrypt 2026] and Zhang et al. [Eurocrypt 2026], they have many limitations, such as lack of post-quantum security, dependence on a setup by a trusted third-party, and poor asymptotic and concrete efficiency. In this work, we present a compiler for constructing a dynamic SNARK for Plonkish constraints (which capture arbitrary NP computations) by using a static SNARK for NP and a vector commitment scheme as black boxes. When instantiated with a state-of-the-art hash-based SNARK and Merkle trees, the compiler yields a dynamic SNARK that is post-quantum secure in the QROM, has a transparent setup, and achieves $O(n)$ initial prover time and $O(k \log^2 n)$ update prover time, with succinct proofs and verification, where $k$ is the Hamming distance between the old and new instance-witness pairs. Our Ligerito-based implementation achieves cumulative prover speedups of $147\times$ and $11.7\times$ over a static HyperPlonk baseline for 10,000 successive one-gate updates and 1,000 successive 128-gate updates, respectively, on a $2^{23}$-gate circuit, including the full dynamic initialization cost.
papers.authors: Anubhav Baweja, Charalampos Papamanthou

papers.title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
papers.abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.
papers.authors: Mingfei Yu, Chenglu Jin, Giovanni De Micheli

papers.title: Chosen Ciphertext and Trapdoor Secure Public Key Authenticated Encryption with Keyword Search
papers.abstract: For public-key encryption with keyword search (PEKS), chosen-ciphertext attack (CCA) security has been studied in settings where an adversary is allowed to access the test oracle. Notably, the CHK transformation (Canetti, Halevi, and Katz, EUROCRYPT 2004) does not yield CCA-secure PEKS. To address this limitation, Abdalla, Bellare, and Neven (TCC 2010/JoC 2018) proposed a generic construction of CCA-secure PEKS from CCA-secure anonymous and weakly robust identity-based encryption. However, CCA security alone is insufficient to resist keyword-guessing attacks (KGAs) arising from trapdoor leakage in PEKS. To mitigate KGAs, public-key authenticated encryption with keyword search (PAEKS) has been studied. In particular, Li and Boyen (IACR CiC 2024) proposed a generic construction of PAEKS. In this paper, we propose a generic transformation that converts a PAEKS scheme into a CCTA-secure one, where CCTA denotes security against chosen-ciphertext and trapdoor attacks. Our transformation can be viewed as a variant of the CHK transformation. The key observation is that, unlike in PEKS, the receiver in PAEKS identifies and specifies the sender when generating a trapdoor, enabling keywords to be used as tags. The transformation directly upgrades PAEKS instantiations obtained via the Li-Boyen generic construction under various assumptions to CCTA-secure schemes. As a result, we obtain the first fully CCTA-secure PAEKS schemes from both pairings and lattices. As an additional benefit, the transformation improves search efficiency. By leveraging verification keys embedded in ciphertexts and trapdoors, sender-receiver matching can be performed without cryptographic computation, for example, by using hash tables. Consequently, for a trapdoor associated with a particular sender, the search complexity measured in cryptographic operations becomes independent of the number of senders and is essentially the same as that of PEKS. Although improving efficiency is not the primary goal of the transformation, this benefit is of independent interest.
papers.authors: Tomoki Mori, Keita Emura

papers.title: Nowhere Man: Device Binding for Post-Quantum Anonymous Credentials
papers.abstract: Anonymous credentials are seeing widespread deployment. Notably, the European Commission plans to roll out age-verification solutions based on anonymous credentials by the end of 2026. Similarly, Google open-sourced Longfellow, a zero-knowledge proof system that lifts the standardized mobile Driver License framework into a full-fledged anonymous credentials, and is currently being integrated with Google Wallet. Any secure deployment of anonymous credentials must address two major challenges: 1) provide guarantees against credential sharing, and 2) support proof-of-personhood. The standard approach adopted by the industry to address both is device binding, which is mandatory for mDL and was only recently formalized for anonymous credentials by Friedrichs et al. (Eurocrypt '26). Simply put, the idea is to have the user's phone Secure Element sign a fresh challenge from the verifier, and to prove knowledge of this signature in zero-knowledge at each credential presentation. To date, all existing approaches, including Vega (S&P '26), have only considered non-post-quantum solutions based on legacy signature schemes. Crucial for near-term deployments and adoption is to work with standardized post-quantum signature schemes, such as ML-DSA, which were not designed for privacy. Because of this, solutions based on general non-interactive zero-knowledge proof systems (e.g., Longfellow) appear to be needed. This genericity, however, requires proving complex statements, significantly impacting proving time. In this work, we present a modular device binding protocol tailored to work with ML-DSA. We avoid the pitfalls of the generic approach by leveraging the structure of ML-DSA resulting in an efficient solution, but retaining the security underlying the post-quantum standard. Our most efficient variants additionally rely on a weak-MLWR assumption for unlinkability, which can be removed at the cost of lower efficiency. While tailored for ML-DSA and requiring no modification to the FIPS~204 signing interface, our solution is modular enough to be integrated with different anonymous credential schemes, allowing real-world solutions to pick the most efficient building blocks. To demonstrate the feasibility of our solution, we provide a proof-of-concept implementation.
papers.authors: Calvin Abou Haidar, Ryo Kikuchi, Octavio Perez-Kempner, Marcel Tiepelt

papers.title: On Secure Sorting and Its Application to Privacy-Preserving Graph Pattern Matching
papers.abstract: Sorting in secure computation has been studied almost as long as there have been implementations of multi-party computation (Wang et al., AsiaCCS'10). More recent advances include completely secure implementations (revealing nothing other than the list size) that have used Quicksort (Araki et al., CCS'21) and radix sort (Asharov et al., CCS'22). For the first time, we extensively compare the two variants across a range of parameters and for both honest- and dishonest-majority computation. We then apply secure sorting to improve sparse matrix multiplication without oblivious RAM based on recent work by Damie et al. (CODASPY'26). Our main contribution here is to produce an output in the same format as the inputs to the multiplication. This is needed for repeated multiplication of graph adjacency matrices, which we use to find cycles in graphs. Such cycles have been associated with money laundering, and this also applies to another graph pattern dubbed scatter-gather, which we can detect with the same approach. Our work therefore can be applied to privacy-preserving anti-money laundering detection.
papers.authors: Marcel Keller

papers.title: Confidential Error-Correcting Codes
papers.abstract: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. We formalize this primitive through three security properties: confidentiality, robustness, and soundness. To realize this goal, we develop a general framework for constructing CECs based on a Randomness-Security Separation (RSS) structure, which first encodes a nonce to introduce randomness and then masks the encoded payload with a pseudorandom function. Based on our RSS framework, we instantiate CECs, called Conc-CEC, using concatenated Reed-Muller and Reed-Solomon codes. The resulting Conc-CEC admits provable guarantees for all three properties. Notably, compared to PRCs (CRYPTO'24), another recent cryptographic primitive with error-correcting capability, CECs achieve significantly stronger concrete security guarantees under practical parameter settings. As a primary application of CECs, we further present CECMark, a watermarking scheme for AI-generated images. Our experiments on real-world generative image models show that CECMark consistently outperforms state-of-the-art watermarking methods, including Gaussian Shading (CVPR'24), PRCMark (ICLR'25), and T2SMark (NeurIPS'25). In particular, CECMark achieves higher robustness across all 56 evaluated perturbations and ensures a false positive rate below $10^{-5}$ without introducing side effects. Taken together, our work lays a novel cryptographic foundation for trustworthy watermarking schemes that, for the first time, unify provable security guarantees with strong practical reliability.
papers.authors: Tianrui Wang, Anyu Wang, Tianshuo Cong, Delong Ran, Xiaoyun Wang

papers.title: Hardware-Level Mitigation of Micro-Architectural Leakages in Embedded Processors
papers.abstract: Cryptographic software, with its inherent flexibility and adaptability, has become essential for meeting today’s rapidly evolving security requirements, despite offering lower performance than dedicated hardware accelerators. However, Side-Channel Analysis (SCA) complicates its secure execution on physical hardware, making robust protection a central challenge. While the masking countermeasure offers provable security guarantees in theory, its effectiveness is often undermined by the processor’s micro-architecture. In response, formal adversary models have been adapted to account for micro-architectural leakage under generic (but over-conservative) assumptions on the hardware. Consequently, achieving security under such a generic model requires compilers to produce less performant software. To bridge this gap, secure hardware-software co-design assumes a precisely specified hardware leakage behavior, enabling the specification of constraints for secure compilation. While this approach reduces the overhead required to counteract these effects, it does not entirely remove it. This work follows a more fundamental paradigm: instead of managing leakage in software, we aim at eliminating it at its source. Conceptually, we propose architectural changes to general-purpose processors at the Register-Transfer Level (RTL) that remove the root causes of micro-architectural leakages. The application of these changes enables the secure execution of masked software without introducing micro-architectural leakage under the Robust but Relaxed (RR) d-probing model, thereby removing the need for complex, security-aware compilers and hardware-specific workarounds in the software. While our countermeasures can be applied to many micro-architectures, we formally prove the security of each countermeasure individually and integrate them into the Ibex processor, whose security we evaluate as a whole through tool-assisted leakage assessment of the full netlist and physical experiments on a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA).
papers.authors: Niels Wieser, Nicolai Müller, Amir Moradi

papers.title: AegisAsync: Symbolic Async-Event Simulation for Risks in Python Asynchronous Programs
papers.abstract: Security and robustness risks in Python async programs depend on event order, object identity, and execution after exceptions or cancellation. Detecting these risks requires connecting related operations across function calls and tracking their effects along execution paths. We present AegisAsync, a bytecode-based analysis of Python async risks for CPython 3.10-3.14. Its Async Event Transition Graph combines bytecode control flow, resolved calls, async events, and symbolic object relations. Bounded path-local simulation tracks event order and object states and explores cancellation at await suspensions. Six detector plugins evaluate the resulting traces and states to produce candidates with supporting witnesses. On AsyncBench, our benchmark of 180 labeled risks, AegisAsync detects all labeled risks with zero false positives on each of the five versions. Across five path budgets on 2,500 PyPI package versions, source review confirms 457 of 910 AegisAsync candidate records (50.2%), representing 457 unique bugs; across three flake8-async samples, 70 of 2,187 review judgments are confirmed (3.2%). By submission, 166 PoCs reproduce AegisAsync findings, and we have reported 157 bugs to developers, of which 16 have been confirmed and fixed.
papers.authors: Baihong Chen, Wen Li

papers.title: $\mathsf{EFI}\Leftrightarrow\mathsf{1PRS}$
papers.abstract: A series of recent works has established EFI pairs as the "minimal" assumption for quantum cryptography. Recently, Cavalar et al. [CCC+26] showed that EFI pairs are equivalent to non-uniform expanding single-copy pseudorandom state generators (1PRS), and obtained a non-uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. We remove the non-uniformity in their construction and prove that EFI pairs are equivalent to expanding 1PRS. As a corollary, we obtain the first uniform meta-complexity characterization of EFI pairs. Together with the equivalence of statistically verifiable one-way state generators and commitments proved by Batra and Jain [BJ24], this gives a quantum analogue of the classical equivalence between one-way functions, commitments, and pseudorandom generators.
papers.authors: Rishabh Batra

papers.title: Optimal Threshold Implementations of all bijective 4-bit S-boxes and new Infinite Families
papers.abstract: Threshold implementations (TIs) are now an established class of side-channel countermeasures. Their underlying idea is simple and compelling: under mild, practical assumptions, they provide protection against glitches and allow composability. Yet our understanding of one-stage TIs with a minimal number of shares remains limited, both for cryptographically relevant families—particularly power functions—and for concrete small functions. In particular, until now, except for Feistel-constructions, no optimal TI had been found for families of mathematically well-structured and cryptographically non-trivial functions, especially power functions. In small dimensions, many functions - particularly cryptographically interesting ones — were not known to admit an optimal TI. This was especially true for the 4-bit S-boxes frequently used in practical lightweight ciphers. Optimal refers to share-optimal, direct one-stage, uniform, first-order TI. Here, we introduce new families of TIs, including the first infinite families of cryptographically nontrivial power permutations. Moreover, every four-bit permutation of algebraic degree t admits a direct, uniform TI with t+1 shares and no fresh randomness. Those results prove several previous conjectures and claims wrong. Since such permutations are widely used in symmetric ciphers, our constructions offer new implementation options. $\textbf{Note:}$ The threshold implementations presented in this paper are available at: https://github.com/enripicc/Optimal-Threshold-Implementations-for-3-4-and-5-bits-permutations
papers.authors: Enrico Piccione, Yevhen Perehuda, Gregor Leander, Patrick Felke

papers.title: Hybrid Quantum–Computational Key Distribution with Reduced Assumptions (Short Paper)
papers.abstract: The HM-QCT protocol, presented by Mazzoncini et al. in 2025, uses a unique feature of quantum information to achieve quantum key distribution (QKD) with secret-key rates beyond standard constructions. The protocol has been designed in the hybrid quantum–computational time-lock (QCT) security model which imposes two independent (but related) restrictions on the attacker: (1) a computationally secure encryption scheme which a successful attacker must break within a narrow timeframe and (2) an assumption that the attacker can only store quantum information with low fidelity. We first review the protocol and its two-assumption model by presenting, in explicit form, the two natural “harvest now, decrypt later” strategies against it, one using quantum memory and one using classical memory. We show how each is excluded by exactly one of the two assumptions, so that harvesting resistance rests on their conjunction and on the presumed existence of a technological gap: the adversary's quantum memory must decohere much faster than the time it takes to break the short-term encryption. Finally, we introduce HM-PRF, a variant that replaces the short-term encryption with a pseudorandom function (PRF), evaluated locally. By eliminating the transmission of enciphered classical information, the adversary does not need to race an impending expiry event. We compare the security of our construction against the original and argue that our PRF-based assumption yields a more realistic adversary. It simply requires the existence of one-way functions rather than a predicted lasting limitation of quantum computation and memory technology.
papers.authors: Jean Snyman, Ioana Boureanu, Daniel Gardham

papers.title: Tight End-to-End Accounting for Differentially Private Synthetic Data
papers.abstract: Differentially private (DP) pipelines often combine heterogeneous mechanisms, yet their guarantees are best analyzed using different notions of privacy (e.g., bounded range, zCDP, ADP). When composing them, we have to analyze the guarantees through a reduced common representation that loses accounting precision. This issue is particularly relevant in DP synthetic data generation, where data preprocessing, generation algorithms, and DP-SGD could appear within the same pipeline. We develop novel tools for tight end-to-end accounting of such compositions using privacy loss distributions (PLD), $f$-DP, and Gaussian DP (GDP). In particular, we derive PLD and GDP analyses of bounded-range mechanisms such as the Exponential mechanism. Building on these theoretical results, we introduce AIM-GDP, a GDP-native variant of AIM (a state-of-the-art DP synthetic data mechanism) that enables easy composability with complex pipelines via PLD, attack-aware risk calibration, and tight end-to-end auditing while consistently achieving better utility; and MixCal, an algorithm for calibrating adaptive mixed compositions using PLD accounting. Overall, our tools enable tighter end-to-end accounting and thus less noise at the same privacy level in DP synthetic data pipelines.
papers.authors: Georgi Ganev, Vadym Doroshenko, Arun Ganesh, Juan Felipe Gomez, Ryan McKenna, Bogdan Kulynych

papers.title: Breaking First-Order Masked Kyber with Belief Propagation Alone
papers.abstract: We recover the long-term key of a first-order masked Kyber768 implementation on an ARM Cortex-M4 from about 2200 decapsulation power traces, using only authentic ciphertexts that pass ciphertext-validity checks. The secret is freshly shared before every decapsulation, and the attack combines weak second-order leakage from both shares. Under the evaluated leakage model, even exact Hamming weights of both shares provide about 97% less mutual information about a decryption-noise coefficient than the exact Hamming weight of the unmasked coefficient. A profiled neural network estimates Hamming-weight distributions for the two arithmetic shares of each noisy message coefficient. We combine these distributions into likelihoods on the decryption noise, which is a known affine function of the secret and the public-key error. A belief-propagation (BP) solver accumulates these likelihoods across traces, preserving their non-Gaussian shapes while approximating the aggregate interference from other key coordinates by a Gaussian. An Onsager correction from approximate message passing corrects for feedback between each factor and the current beliefs. The solver recovers all 1536 secret and error coefficients without lattice reduction. At the evaluated trace budgets, least squares performs no better than the all-zero estimate, and a greedy inequality solver fails even with exact Hamming weights. The evaluated primal-lattice cascade does not reduce the trace requirement: below BP's recovery threshold, its output remains too diffuse to enable practical lattice recovery. At 2000 traces, BP-derived hints lower the estimated BKZ block size from 624 to 505, leaving the lattice attack impractical.
papers.authors: Vahid Jahandideh, Lejla Batina

papers.title: Purpose IR: Compiling User Purpose for Privacy-Preserving Agent Workflow State
papers.abstract: LLM-agent workflows routinely transform rich observations into plans, summaries, memories, handoffs, and other reusable state. This creates a privacy boundary that task relevance alone does not capture: an observation may be needed as evidence for a task without its full semantics being authorized to persist. We call this mismatch the purpose-to-state semantic gap. The key distinction is that evidence authority is not release authority. We introduce Purpose IR, a bounded typed intermediate representation that compiles natural-language user purpose into an executable semantic boundary for reusable agent state. A Purpose program is an acyclic semantic dataflow graph in which evidence leaves specify task-required semantics, typed dependencies constrain authorized derivations, and declared sinks determine which values or actions may cross the reusable-state boundary. A deterministic compiler constructs and validates the authoritative program, while a typed runtime reconstructs reusable state only from validated sink outputs. Under explicit execution contracts, this design yields release confinement and purpose noninterference, characterizing what factual semantics may be released and which observation differences must become irrelevant to reusable state. Across 1,200 cases spanning LangGraph, CrewAI, and MobileRun, Purpose IR achieves 99.6% Privacy, 83.3% Task, and 83.3% Privacy-Compliant Success (PCS), outperforming the strongest high-privacy baseline by 27.5 PCS points. On 493 PrivacyLens trajectories, it achieves the highest Safe Action Rate at 77.3%, 10.4 points above the next-best method, extending the same boundary from reusable state to downstream actions. These results show that privacy-preserving agent state requires more than filtering sensitive or task-irrelevant content: it requires an explicit, executable representation of what the user's purpose authorizes to survive.
papers.authors: Dongsheng Chen, Xiangyu Zhao, Lei Ma, Xin Yao, Xuetao Wei

papers.title: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
papers.abstract: Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher-enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher-held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier-phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release-specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key-preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance metadata with release-specific face verification and record-linked evidence for further assessment.
papers.authors: Chia-Ming Lee, Chia-Yu Lin, Hung-Kai Huang, Yi-Ting Ku, Yu-Chen Liang, Chih-Chung Hsu

papers.title: SkillMarker: A KGW-Based Watermarking Method for Agent Skill Ownership Verification
papers.abstract: Agent skills encode operational procedures and domain expertise as reusable knowledge assets, yet their distribution in plaintext exposes them to unauthorized copying and leakage. However, practical mechanisms for skill ownership verification and leakage tracing remain underdeveloped. Watermark embedding before distribution offers a potential solution, but structured, compact skill instructions impose stringent requirements for factual and procedural accuracy. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillMarker, a KGW-based watermarking method that jointly targets functionality preservation and strong watermark embedding. SkillMarker unifies quality-constrained rewriting with signal-oriented candidate search. The former separates essential knowledge from flexible expression to preserve instruction fidelity; the latter explores alternative expressions to obtain a stronger watermark signal under preservation constraints. We release an open-source toolkit that integrates watermark embedding, quality auditing, and detection to support the protection of agent skills. SkillMarker targets ownership verification and leakage tracing in distributed skill ecosystems, where content may be copied in whole or in part, or incorporated into other skills. Across four datasets, SkillMarker negligibly affects downstream task performance on average. In our copy-paste tests, window-based detection consistently identifies copied passages containing as few as 1,536 consecutive tokens. Even after merging with one or three background skills, SkillMarker retains watermark detection rates of 72.2--77.8\%.
papers.authors: Alan Tang, Lifeng Wang, Gang Wu, Tao Zhang, Yantao Jia, Xiaofeng Zhu

papers.title: Efficient Vectorized Implementation of MQOM
papers.abstract: Post-quantum signature schemes require efficient implementations to be viable in practice. MQOM, a third-round candidate in NIST’s additional call for digital signatures, is a promising target for SIMD optimization. This work leverages a transpose-enabled paired-matrix trick to develop a vectorized implementation of MQOM v2.1, corresponding to the Round-2 specification, with reduced wasted SIMD work and memory traffic. We evaluate MQOM v2.1 on Arm NEON, x86 AVX2, and x86 AVX-512, covering key generation, signing, verification, and memory; peak dynamic memory falls by up to 39.43%. We also include supplementary MQOM v3 experiments to assess how the matrix-layout optimization transfers to the Round-3 code.
papers.authors: David Santos, Julio López, Francisco Rodríguez-Henríquez

papers.title: FlatMerkle: Logarithmic-Space Inclusion Proofs over a Single Linear Hash Stream
papers.abstract: Merkle trees are the standard way to obtain logarithmic-size, logarithmic-time inclusion proofs over a large dataset, but they require a tree-shaped hash structure distinct from the ordinary, linear (Merkle--Damg\aa rd) hashing that most deployed systems -- including Bitcoin's own transaction and witness hashing -- actually perform. We present FlatMerkle, a construction that achieves the same asymptotic guarantees, $O(\log N)$ proof size and $O(\log N)$ verification time, over a single ordinary linear hash stream, by periodically re-injecting the hash function's own past internal states (``checkpoints'') back into the stream as ordinary message content. The result is a flat byte sequence whose digest is a single, unmodified invocation of the underlying hash function -- syntactically an ordinary digest of an ordinary byte string, not a distinguishable commitment format -- while still supporting compact inclusion proofs for any element, and compact proofs that a published file is malformed, so that an honest party can always answer a malicious committer in logarithmic space. We give the recursive construction, a closed-form formula locating any element in the structured stream, worked examples with illustrations, a security reduction to free-start collision resistance of the hash function's compression step, an optimal element-size analysis for both a flexible toy primitive and real SHA-256, a batched multi-element proof construction, a measured construction-speed comparison against Merkle trees, a concrete application to committing data inside a Bitcoin transaction annex (BIP-341), a design sketch using that application as a data-availability layer for an optimistic Bitcoin rollup, a from-scratch gas-cost comparison, on Ethereum, Rootstock, and Arbitrum, of an in-contract FlatMerkle commitment against an in-contract Merkle tree, tracing the three chains' differing verdicts to specific protocol design choices rather than to anything intrinsic to either construction, and a comparison against the closest prior art we are aware of, authenticated append-only skip lists.
papers.authors: Sergio Demian Lerner

papers.title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
papers.abstract: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.
papers.authors: Mayank Kabra, Phillip Widdowson, Harshita Gupta, Rakesh Nadig, Nisa Bostancı, Eirini Tzermpou, Rakesh Kumar, Spiros Galanopoulos, Ataberk Olgun, Abdullah Giray Yağlıkçı, Mohammad Sadrosadati, Onur Mutlu

papers.title: Pin It on Anyone: Certified Targeted Displacement of Multi-Bit LLM Watermarks Without the Key
papers.abstract: Multi-bit watermarking embeds a message, typically an account identifier, into LLM output so that harmful text can be traced to its origin. We show an attack technique that allows to alter the watermarking message. This allows to, for example, exchange the embedded account ID to an arbitrary different one. The attacker mainly needs access to a few accounts for generating LLM output and model logits, but crucially not the secret key used to watermark. The attacker then rewrites the text, keeping its meaning, so that the watermarking message decoder recovers the watermarking message embedded by the attacker. We are, to our knowledge, the first to propose such an attack, which we call a targeted displacement. Theoretically, we present upper and lower bounds on the probability of our attack succeeding. This bound depends on the number of accounts the attacker has access to, the length of the message and some characteristics of the given text. Our attack can succeed whenever we can bound the ambiguity of the generated text well enough. Empirically, we test our attack technique against five watermarking methods and four LLMs. Attack success tracks our predicted bounds, allowing us to alter watermarking messages in almost all cases with high accuracy, given enough accounts. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Batorskq/PinIt.
papers.authors: Paweł Batorski, Przemysław Spurek, Paul Swoboda

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference on Financial Transaction Graphs via Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) in financial networks requires modeling transaction patterns that span multiple institutions. In practice, however, banks cannot share account and transaction features due to strict privacy regulations. We propose a privacy-preserving graph neural network (GNN) inference framework tailored to this multi-bank setting. A central server holds the graph connectivity and pretrained model weights in plaintext, while each bank keeps its transaction features encrypted. Inference is then carried out entirely on encrypted features under the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme, so that no plaintext transaction features or predictions are exposed to the server. The key to making this practical is an edge-centric GNN architecture, wherein message passing is expressed through operations on node--edge incidence matrices. This formulation not only preserves the edge-attributed multigraph structure of transaction networks but also reduces every aggregation step to plaintext--ciphertext matrix products. Since CKKS can evaluate only polynomial circuits, we also approximate each nonlinearity with a composite polynomial of the sign function, which we calibrate per activation site. On the IBM AML benchmark, our model achieves performance competitive with plaintext baselines, and with a consumer-grade GPU, classifies each queried transaction end-to-end in as little as 5.31 seconds, while per-transaction latency can be amortized to 1.65 seconds when optimized for throughput.
papers.authors: H. Çağrı Bilgi, Kemal Mutluergil, Ceren Yıldırım, Kubilay Atasu, Erkay Savas

papers.title: Logit Leakage through Floating-Point Bias Addition
papers.abstract: Language model APIs can expose token-specific biases while withholding logits and token probabilities. Existing bias-based extraction recovers relative logits, leaving a common additive component undetermined in ideal arithmetic. We identify a numerical side channel in floating-point bias addition that exposes information about this component through token identities alone. The channel distinguishes score vectors with identical complete unperturbed log probabilities. Our method exploits changes in representable spacing at binary exponent boundaries. Under the stated binary32 arithmetic assumptions and a known reachable score interval, it recovers a logit pair and its unknown tie-breaking priority exactly in at most 52 token queries. Given complete relative logits, one recovered anchor determines the original logit vector. We evaluate recovery across 11 public checkpoints from seven model families and extend the local method with adaptive interval search and anchor selection. In end-to-end experiments with vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp, adaptive recovery succeeds on all 128 Qwen3-0.6B inputs per system, including 64 held-out inputs. A separate token-only experiment extracts a pretrained small model's complete output-head representation up to an invertible hidden-basis transformation. We also establish a sufficient condition for suppressing common-shift disclosure by subtracting the maximum before bias addition. In controlled experiments, this mitigation eliminates all observed distinctions between common-shift variants and preserves token decisions under the tested random biases.
papers.authors: Shaomin Chen, Xiaorui Gong

papers.title: Asymptotics of Random-Lattice Enumeration: Beyond HKZ via Dense Sublattices
papers.abstract: To bridge the gap between worst-case and heuristic analyses of lattice enumeration, we study the sizes of (unpruned) enumeration trees on $n$-dimensional Haar-random lattices. Writing $n^{cn+o(n)}$ for the tree size at the shortest vector radius, we investigate the asymptotic scaling of $c$, and which bases minimize it. For quasi-HKZ bases, we rigorously analyze the random-lattice HKZ geometry and establish $c=1/(2e)\approx 0.1839$. This matches the worst-case enumeration exponent of Hanrot-Stehlé and confirms earlier predictions for the geometry of HKZ bases on random lattices. Searching beyond quasi-HKZ bases, we prove that with high probability, the minimum achievable tree size exponent $c$ over all bases of a random lattice satisfies: \begin{align} 0.1464 \approx \frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4}\leq c<0.1474. \end{align} For the lower bound, we use Kim's mean-value formula for nested chains of primitive sublattices to rule out bases with small prefix determinants. This strengthens the earlier Rankin-based heuristic lower bound exponent $c \geq 1/8$, discussed by Nguyen and Hanrot-Stehlé, and rules out the existence of random-lattice bases with trees as small as predicted by the geometric series assumption. For the upper bound, we show that with high probability a dense primitive half-rank sublattice exists with determinant at most $n^{n/8 + o(n)}$. Combining dual HKZ on this sublattice with HKZ on its quotient gives a basis with $c \leq 1/(4\sqrt{e}) \approx 0.1516$. Recursively splitting each half lowers the upper bound below $0.1474$, and under a natural heuristic assumption we prove that the lower bound is tight. Combined with the collision search of Feng-Gao-Liu, our two-block construction gives a polynomial-space algorithm solving the closest vector problem with preprocessing (CVPP) on random lattices in query time $n^{0.0892 n + o(n)}$ for arbitrary targets.
papers.authors: Thijs Laarhoven

papers.title: Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication: A Lightweight Processor-Level Countermeasure Against Fault Injection
papers.abstract: Fault attacks exploit transient hardware faults to bypass software-level security checks in embedded processors. Processor-level redundancy can detect such faults, but duplicating the whole processor is costly for resource-constrained devices. This paper proposes Staggered Instruction-Fetch Duplication (SIFD), a lightweight processor-level countermeasure based on instruction-fetch redundancy. SIFD fetches each instruction twice in consecutive cycles, while fetching two different instructions in every fetch cycle. This staggered schedule detects inconsistent fetch results without full processor duplication, compiler support, or cryptographic hardware. We implement SIFD on a custom RV32I processor and evaluate it on an Artix-7 FPGA using clock fault injection (CFI) and electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI). SIFD increases slice utilization by 15.0% and execution time by 16.3%. It reduces the attack success rate from 0.86% to below 0.01% under CFI and from 0.32% to 0.13% under EMFI. It also detects 73.18% of CFI attempts and 11.44% of EMFI attempts. These results indicate that SIFD can convert many fault effects into explicit detections and reduce successful fault-injection outcomes, especially under CFI.
papers.authors: Shoei Nashimoto, Naoya Okada, Yuichiro Murachi

papers.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
papers.abstract: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.
papers.authors: Souvik Das, Ariful Azad, Nitesh Saxena

papers.title: Mitigating Black-Box Score-Based Query Attacks via Gradient Confusion
papers.abstract: Score-based black-box adversarial attacks pose a serious threat to deployed machine learning systems by exploiting repeated model queries to craft adversarial examples, requiring neither access to model parameters nor architecture. Existing defenses predominantly rely on stochastic output perturbations, which fail to prevent determined attackers from recovering stable gradient estimates by increasing query budgets or averaging over randomness. In this work, we propose the Gradient Confusion Defense (GCD), a retraining-free, deterministic test-time wrapper that actively shapes the probability vector returned to querying adversaries. By solving a constrained optimization problem grounded in the model's Jacobian, GCD aligns the exposed logit-gradient with a target confusion direction that is maximally misaligned with the true adversarial loss gradient---increasing the query complexity of attacks without sacrificing predictive utility or top-1 accuracy. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis demonstrating that GCD provably slows gradient-estimation-based attacks and induces systematic accept/reject errors in random search-based attacks, with the confusion effect amplifying as the fraction of defended queries increases. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across multiple architectures (ResNet-18, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16) and four state-of-the-art attacks confirm these predictions: GCD achieves state-of-the-art robustness, while incurring zero clean accuracy degradation. %Crucially, unlike randomization-based defenses, GCD's deterministic structure provides resilience against adaptive attacks that exploit stochasticity, making it well-suited for security-critical deployment settings.
papers.authors: Ali Javeri, Javad Hezareh, Radin Shahdaei, AmirMahdi Sadeghzadeh

papers.title: Genericity in multivariate cryptography
papers.abstract: The results in this paper establish the genericity of some properties of the ideals and varieties generated by UOV public keys, in particular the equidimensionality of the UOV varieties and the radicality of public key ideals. These genericity results justify the various regularity assumptions that are made on polynomial systems of equations arising in the cryptanalysis of UOV and its variants. We also provide examples in the recent literature showing how genericity questions arise in crypt- analysis and why genericity should be taken into consideration when de- signing cryptographic schemes. Lastly, we perform a retrospective study of various cryptographic schemes through the viewangle of genericity. We identify several cases in which non-genericity led to the cryptanaly- sis of the scheme, but also provide a counter-example of a scheme whose non-genericity does not seem easy to exploit.
papers.authors: Simon Abelard, Pierre Pébereau, Mohab Safey El Din

papers.title: Security and robustness analysis of encrypted communications for local home automation: ESPHome Native API and MQTT over TLS 1.3
papers.abstract: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) in residential and local automation environments has highlighted the limitations of considering the internal network as an inherently trusted domain. Man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks, such as ARP spoofing, can allow traffic interception or manipulation when communications lack appropriate confidentiality, integrity, and authentication mechanisms. This paper presents a systematized review of the security mechanisms used by two communication alternatives between ESP-family microcontrollers and the Home Assistant platform: MQTT protected through TLS 1.3 and the ESPHome Native API, whose encryption is based on the Noise Protocol Framework using the Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256 pattern. The analysis considers four dimensions: cryptographic robustness, attack surface, implementation complexity, and resource consumption. The review identifies significant differences resulting from the architecture and cryptographic model of each alternative. TLS 1.3 provides a standardized framework compatible with public-key infrastructure and formal identity management, though it introduces greater configuration complexity and computational overhead during session establishment. The ESPHome Native API employs a more specialized scheme with lower operational complexity, eliminates dynamic algorithm negotiation, and uses ChaCha20-Poly1305. The resource-consumption analysis relies on measurements published by the projects and manufacturers themselves, not on an experimental test bench, and this limitation is explicitly acknowledged. The results identify the conditions under which each mechanism is appropriate for local home-automation architectures and provide a basis for designing IoT systems that balance security, interoperability, and resource constraints.
papers.authors: Carlos Roberto Gonzalez-Escarpeta, Juan Eduardo Garcia Sanchez, José Antonio Hernandez Reyes, Ricardo Francisco Martinez-Gonzalez

papers.title: Beyond User-Side Defenses: Image Protection in Open-Weight Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Model providers can support image protection, but open-weight deployment introduces practical constraints. We propose four requirements: protection effectiveness, clean fidelity, compatibility, and tamper resistance. We incorporate long-horizon attack simulations to strengthen resistance to protection removal. Experiments with a single protection tool show improved resistance to re-alignment at a cost to clean fidelity, motivating further research toward practical model-side protection.
papers.authors: Jihye Kang, Jiwon Park, Namhyuk Ahn

papers.title: Digital-Twin-Referenced Belief-Guided Q-Learning for Jammer Identification and Beam-Power Control in a mmWave Model
papers.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) combined with reinforcement learning (RL) can support adaptive resource allocation and security-aware decision-making by comparing expected and observed network behavior. This paper presents a simulation-based DT reference and a belief-guided Q-learning (BGQL) for joint jammer identification and beam-power control in a site-specific 28-GHz network. For each action, the same channel simulator is evaluated under an attack-free and an attacked configuration. Receiver-level residuals are combined with spatial jamming footprints and accumulated to form a normalized suspicion vector. BGQL incorporates this vector into an aggregated state, a belief-concentration reward, and exploratory beam-selection rule. The BGQL scheme is compared with SARSA, Greedy, and Random under matched attacker sets. Across 30 paired Monte Carlo runs in four configurations, with the number of active jammers supplied to every method, BGQL achieves mean aggregate full-band link-rate scores of approximately 437.4--564.2~Mbit/s and rate-to-device-power scores of 60.37--76.79~Mbit/J. Its detection accuracy is 100\% in one-jammer configurations and approximately 78\%--81\% in two-jammer configurations. BGQL requires approximately 80--130~s per run, compared with 5--14~s for SARSA, reflecting evaluation of 625 beam pairs during exploratory steps. These findings provide a matched-model simulation proof of concept for DT-referenced belief-guided learning for security-aware beam-power control in 6G networks.
papers.authors: Parmida Geranmayeh, Onur Günlü

papers.title: ML-Assisted Power Side-Channel Attacks on ML Accelerators in Shared FPGAs
papers.abstract: Cloud providers offer on-demand access to Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), and multi-tenant FPGAs let multiple users share one device to improve utilization. This sharing introduces security risks: an adversary co-located with a victim on the same FPGA can mount power side-channel attacks against the victim's Machine Learning (ML) accelerator. Prior on-chip attacks on such accelerators based on Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) sensors have recovered only small, MNIST-scale grayscale inputs, including with ML-assisted reconstruction. This work is the first on-chip, TDC-based attack to produce full-scale color reconstructions of ImageNet-scale inputs, by combining ML-based upscaling and recoloring with TDC measurements of a remote victim's ML accelerator. We frame this as a proof-of-concept leakage study: the victim implements the first convolution layer of a CNN processing 224x224 ImageNet inputs on a shared FPGA, which we isolate to characterize the input-dependent leakage, and we quantify how much of each reconstruction reflects genuinely recovered information versus ML-generated post-processing. As a preliminary countermeasure, we study a pixel-substitution defense that replaces each pixel value, within a fixed intensity budget, with one of different Hamming Weight, producing a different TDC signature. We find that this transformation costs the victim's own model more accuracy than it costs the attacker and, because it applies the same fixed, publicly reconstructable mapping to every image, is largely defeated by an attacker retrained on the transformed data; robust defenses will require randomized or input-dependent transformations.
papers.authors: Anthony Etim, Kenan Erol, Jakub Szefer

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness of Camera-Radar Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving (AD) relies on multi-sensor perception to interpret the surrounding environment. However, the robustness of camera--radar fusion under adversarial conditions remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic measurement study of the robustness of camera--radar sensor fusion in AD. We construct a unified evaluation pipeline on the nuScenes dataset that simulates attacks on both sensing modalities, including eight camera-image perturbations and three radar point-cloud perturbations. We evaluate five camera--radar fusion algorithms across two perception tasks, 3D object detection and depth estimation, and quantify their performance under clean and attacked inputs using standard metrics. Our evaluation reveals a clear asymmetry in the robustness of fusion systems. Camera perturbations substantially degrade both object detection and depth estimation, and moderate attack strengths are already sufficient to cause severe performance degradation. In contrast, the evaluated radar perturbations produce smaller and task-dependent effects, with object-detection models showing particularly limited degradation. Our analysis attributes this difference to the strong dependence of existing fusion architectures on dense camera features, together with the filtering, association, and confidence-weighting mechanisms commonly applied to sparse radar measurements. These results demonstrate that sensor fusion does not inherently guarantee robustness and that the contribution and reliability of each sensing modality must be explicitly considered under adversarial conditions. Based on four empirical findings, we derive measurement-guided design implications for future robust camera--radar fusion, including modality-specific reliability estimation, cross-modal consistency checking, adaptive fusion, and graceful failover under severe sensor degradation.
papers.authors: Ce Zhou, Yubo Wu, Khang Nguyen, Liyang Xiao, Thomas Hou, Qiben Yan

papers.title: DelegateGuard: Purpose-Bound Capabilities for Delegated LLM Agent Workflows
papers.abstract: \textbf{(Context)} LLM agents increasingly delegate subtasks while holding authority over sensitive data, creating confused-deputy risks: an injected delegate can exfiltrate data, amplify its authority, or act after revocation. Existing leakage benchmarks expose these failures but do not constrain the authority a delegated agent may exercise. \textbf{(Methods)} We present \system, a reference monitor that converts the initiating user's authorization into attenuable capabilities over purpose, labels, operations, sinks, and delegation depth; every data-moving action is mediated outside the LLM, and revocation cascades through the delegation graph. We formalize a trace-level safety invariant and evaluate it with an adaptive within-authority adversary and four baselines, model-action and multi-turn ecological studies, and conformance and scale checks over deterministic traces and 517{,}401 Enron emails. \textbf{(Results)} \system blocks ungranted-sink exfiltration, authority amplification, revocation replay, purpose gaming, and intra-tool label violations, and dominates static allowlists on the revocation and intra-tool cases (10/10). Two open models proposed attacker-goal actions on 42/45 and 44/45 injected traces, all blocked at execution; a 90-run multi-turn study cut leakage from 0.844 to 0.20 with full task completion, at microsecond per-decision overhead. Proposition~1 characterizes exactly where attenuation-based authorization suffices, a boundary we also reproduce empirically across four observable-sink workflows. \textbf{(Conclusion \& Significance)} Purpose-bound runtime authorization gives delegated LLM workflows a model-independent execution boundary and a precise recipe for composing it with declassification and content monitoring on externally observable sinks.
papers.authors: Phat T. Tran-Truong, Ha Vo, Nhut Tran, Khang Vo, Thai-Minh Truong

papers.title: AutoSec-RAN: Specification-Grounded LLM Fine-Tuning for Automated Security Analysis of O-RAN
papers.abstract: This paper presents AutoSec-RAN, a specification-grounded large language model (LLM) framework for automated security triage of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) testing. Unlike approaches relying on static rule sets or privileged access to raw packet captures, AutoSec-RAN fine-tunes Mistral-7B-Instruct through two Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) stages over a curated corpus of 69 O-RAN, 3GPP, and adjacent standards documents, then selectively augments inference with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the same specification index. At inference, the model receives only an investigator-style question and a scenario metadata block, simulating an automated analyst operating without raw packet evidence. AutoSec-RAN is validated on a purpose-built 5G/O-RAN testbed across labeled fronthaul distributed denial of service replay scenarios. A Gemma-4-31B judge LLM scores each candidate's answer on faithfulness, correctness, and actionability relative to a reference authored from full packet capture and log evidence. AutoSec-RAN achieves a mean judge overall score of 0.713 across all 313 evaluation items (0.755 restricted to the five supervised taxonomy classes), clearing the 0.70 reporting threshold, and a blended score of 0.778 (0.808 supervised-only) when cosine similarity over Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI) General Embedding (BGE) is incorporated as a secondary semantic signal. The framework performs strongest on mitigation and threat-model reasoning (with a mean overall of 0.849 and 0.848, respectively) and identifies a measurable gap on the held-out attack-direction class (0.515), a controlled result that exposes a specific training data requirement. These results establish specification-grounded LoRA fine-tuning combined with RAG retrieval as a viable foundation for automated security validation of AI-native O-RAN.
papers.authors: Anoop Mishra, Joshua Moore, Aly Sabri Abdalla, Vuk Marojevic

papers.title: Secret Sharing from Non-Extractable Randomness
papers.abstract: Bosley and Dodis (TCC 2007) proved that a class of imperfect randomness sources that suffices for information-theoretic encryption of messages longer than the logarithm of the key length must admit deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits, and asked whether the same is true of two-out-of-two secret sharing. Aggarwal, Chung, Obremski, and Ribeiro (TCC 2022) gave a positive answer for schemes that are in addition leakage-resilient or non-malleable; the original question remained open. We answer it in the negative. For every $b\ge2$ we construct a class of flat sources on $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$, each of min-entropy at least $b$, together with a perfectly correct and perfectly private two-out-of-two scheme that shares a $b$-bit secret into two $(b+1)$-bit shares using any source in the class, and we show that every deterministic map from $\{0,1\}^{b+2}$ to $\{0,1\}$ is at statistical distance at least $1/6$ from uniform on some source in the class. This implies that sharing a long enough secret does not require extractable randomness. The proof is a short parity argument. The idea of the construction extends to other thresholds: for two-out-of-$n$ and $r$-out-of-$r$ sharing we give perfect schemes with $(b+1)$-bit shares, private for classes of flat sources from which no single bit can be extracted with error below $1/(4n-2)$ and $1/(2(2^r-1))$, respectively.
papers.authors: Divesh Aggarwal

papers.title: On the Hardness of Finding Permutation Automorphisms of Linear Codes
papers.abstract: We study the hardness of finding permutation automorphisms of linear codes. We look into three main problems: $\mathsf{AUT}$, $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ which, respectively, ask to find a non-trivial automorphism, a generating set and the order of the automorphism group. We give polynomial time reductions from $\mathsf{AUT}$ to $\mathsf{ISO}$ (the problem of finding a permutation isomorphism between two linear codes), and from $\mathsf{ISO}$ to $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$. This shows that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ and $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Count}$ are unlikely to be easy in the worst case, since all known solvers for $\mathsf{ISO}$ take exponential time if the hull dimension (the subspace given by the intersection between the code and its dual) is large enough. Furthermore, we give a reduction from $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ to the problem of finding generators for the automorphism group of a graph, which we refer to as $\mathsf{GraphAUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$. Up to some polynomial factors, the reduction runs in time $O(n^{h})$, with $n$ being the code length and $h$ the hull dimension: for $h = O\big(\log(n)\big)$, this implies that $\mathsf{AUT}$-$\mathsf{Gen}$ can be solved in worst case quasi-polynomial time. We also give a simpler version of the reduction, running in time which is exponential in the worst case (arguably, only for rather contrived codes), even for small $h$. However, heuristically, the algorithm is on average extremely efficient for small $h$. We use it as a concrete solver and show that a proof-of-concept implementation is significantly faster than the built-in implementations of Leon's and Feulner's algorithms provided by $\texttt{Magma}$ and $\texttt{Sagemath}$.
papers.authors: Michele Battagliola, Giuseppe D'Alconzo, Laura Mattiuz, Paolo Santini, Federica Zanetti

papers.title: Tamper Sensing Meshes in Payment Terminals and Beyond
papers.abstract: Card Payment Terminals commonly use tamper sensing meshes to deter physical attacks on devices handling sensitive data such as cryptographic keys. Although their use of such meshes is frequently referenced in research literature, the public record contains little research on their construction. Addressing this gap, in this paper we present the first comprehensive analysis of the practical implementation of tamper sensing meshes across a wide range of payment terminals, and some other devices such as ATM key pads and a data center HSM. We provide detailed photos of critical features. Based on our observations, we construct a taxonomy of mesh construction techniques. Our analysis reveals that most commercial devices use surprisingly simple construction techniques, and their structure size rarely approaches manufacturing limits. Based on our analysis, we identify a concise set of design patterns for the construction of secure tamper sensing meshes. We conclude that designing tamper sensing meshes that exceed the industrial state of the art is viable even using inexpensive and easily available manufacturing processes. Our set of design recommendations creates a foundation for both the practical tamper sensing mesh implementations and for future research into their design. Our results enable researchers to base test specimens on concrete evidence of industrial practice.
papers.authors: Jan Sebastian Götte, Björn Scheuermann

papers.title: Connecting Cryptanalytic Distinguishers through Divisibility
papers.abstract: Integral distinguishers can reveal more than a zero-sum property: the number of ones in an output component may be divisible by a high power of $2$, rather than merely being even. To exploit this divisibility, we relate linear, integral, differential-linear, and restricted differential sums through two-way conversions with explicit divisibility guarantees and data complexity, recovering established links as special cases. We derive exact random-permutation probabilities and rigorous bounds to quantify the distinguishing strength while accounting for dependencies between output conditions.
