To discover these properties, we develop automated MILP/SAT models that use complete-round Walsh coefficients or combine Walsh and ultrametric representations to obtain stronger bounds. These weighted models prove finite divisibility even when compatible trails exist, beyond what trail-existence tests alone can establish. For differential-linear sums, we show that combining differential and linear propagation with local DLCT zeros can give false zero-correlation claims. We address this limitation with exact mix-basis models that establish zero correlation and finite divisibility. To complement these symbolic methods, we provide a black-box algorithm using exact histograms and the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform to search all output masks for selected input conditions and identify zeros and finite divisibility properties. Our MILP/SAT models significantly improve the divisibility bounds reported by Beyne and Verbauwhede in 674 cases across the SIMON family, as well as for PRESENT, without trail enumeration and at unchanged data complexity, e.g., from $2^5$ to $2^{11}$ on 9-round SIMON32 and from $2^6$ to $2^{22}$ on 10-round SIMON48. To our knowledge, we are the first to prove higher divisibility for 8-round SPECK and for BEANIE, with new bounds for GIFT-64 and Ascon and exact counts for SKINNY-64. Our black-box searches reveal new properties on RC5, ChiLow-32, KeeLoq, and KATAN32, including output-bit combinations missed by single-bit searches, and lead us to introduce probabilistic divisibility.
papers.authors: Hosein Hadipour

papers.title: DPF-SGD: Byzantine-Robust Differentially Private Federated SGD with Exact Optimality Guarantees
papers.abstract: Federated optimization enables collaborative learning over decentralized data but is accompanied by significant privacy risks due to the exchange of model updates. While differential privacy (DP) provides formal protection, optimization accuracy is often degraded, and robustness becomes particularly limited in the presence of Byzantine agents. A Byzantine-robust, differentially private federated SGD algorithm, DPF-SGD, is proposed, in which private step sizes are integrated with a DP noise–decay schedule to regulate gradient updates. To further enhance robustness, a privacy-preserving comparative elimination (PPCE) filter is developed to suppress Byzantine contributions during aggregation while preserving privacy guarantees. Almost sure convergence to the global optimum under ϵ-differential privacy is established, despite persistent noise and adversarial behavior. Experiments on synthetic and MNIST datasets demonstrate oneto two-order-of-magnitude reductions in final optimization error relative to DP baselines.
papers.authors: Likang Lu, Jiaxin Wu

papers.title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
papers.abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).
papers.authors: Yang Luo, Tiantian Ji, Zifeng Kang, Yucheng Wang, Yong Liu, Zhiyi Yin, Xinran Liu

papers.title: Prompt-Segmentation Meets ROI Encryption: Fine-Grained Video Protection Based on Diffusion Isolation
papers.abstract: Region-of-interest (ROI) selective encryption in H.265/HEVC aims to protect sensitive content while preserving the utility of non-ROI regions. Existing coding-unit (CU)-level approaches still suffer from substantial encryption redundancy for two reasons. First, existing approaches map object-detection bounding boxes to CUs, producing regular rectangular regions, which poorly match the shape of irregular ROI boundaries, such as facial contours. Second, their coding-tree-unit (CTU)-based diffusion isolation expands the protected footprint in fixed $64\times64$ blocks, causing encryption-induced distortion to spread over a large number of non-ROI pixels. To address the aforementioned shortcomings, we propose a prompt segmentation-guided CU-level ROI encryption algorithm, which mainly consists of two core components. The first component is a prompt segmentation-guided fine-grained ROI encryption pipeline. It maps pixel-level ROI masks to CUs according to an ROI-overlap threshold, refines boundary CUs to $8\times8$ granularity, and applies format-compliant encryption to multiple syntax elements in the mapped ROI CUs. The second is a dual diffusion isolation strategy to address the encryption diffusion problem. For spatial isolation, the encoder refines non-ROI boundary regions into $8\times8$ CUs and uses PCM mode to bypass intra-frame prediction. For temporal isolation, it removes motion-vector candidates whose reference blocks overlap ROI CUs. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method generates encryption regions that more closely match irregular ROI boundaries, effectively confines distortion to the ROI.
papers.authors: Xiang Zhang, Haoyan Lu, Ziqiang Li, Ziwen He, Zhenshan Tan, Fei Peng, Zhangjie Fu

papers.title: BALLAST: Physics-Aware Moving Target Defense for Industrial Control Systems Using a Digital Twin Safety Oracle
papers.abstract: Industrial Control Systems run on static network configurations, which leaves an attacker unlimited time to map the plant. Moving Target Defense answers this by shuffling addresses, but almost every published scheme never checks whether the reconfiguration will itself disturb the physical process it protects, so the defense can destabilise a control loop or trip an actuator. We present BALLAST, which places a learned Digital Twin between the security policy and the plant as a safety oracle. A physics-informed LSTM surrogate forecasts the physical effect of a candidate network change, a reinforcement learning agent trades security entropy against process stability, and a connection-draining handover lets in-flight Modbus transactions complete before the old mapping is withdrawn. An explicit shield rejects any action whose predicted trajectory would leave the safe operating envelope. On the SWaT water treatment testbed, Ballast cut the success rate of an adversary's reconnaissance sweep by 85 percent and recorded no safety violation across 50 runs, a 95 percent upper bound of 5.8 percent on the violation rate, against five violations and a tracking error 19 times larger for RL-MTD, the closest published analogue to our design. Measured against the strongest baseline on the physical metrics, a threshold-triggered scheme that itself records one violation rather than RL-MTD's five, Ballast still improves the tracking error by a factor of 2.5 and removes that remaining violation. The gain costs a small and deliberate concession in raw deterrence. Twin inference meets the 50 ms budget on a workstation core and an embedded GPU, and is projected to meet it on both edge CPUs when the three envelope stages are evaluated in a single batched call; the complete decision-to-enforcement path was measured only on the workstation.
papers.authors: Oscar Mogollon-Gutierrez, Mohammadhossein Homaei, Alberto Lopez-Trigo, Andres Caro, Mar Avila

papers.title: Provenance and Authorization in Autobiographical Language Models
papers.abstract: Autobiographical language models may draw on archives containing observations, quotations, emotional reports, and earlier model outputs. Cryptographic authentication can preserve an archive while leaving these sources semantically conflated. We formulate this gap as a computer-security problem: narrative content must not silently become consent or alter an authorized decision rule. We define typed records, authenticated attestations, a separate policy channel, and admissible views. Under explicit assumptions, we give a standard integrity reduction and a noninterference argument, characterize the information required by exact decision-preserving summaries, and show why passive history and fixed-point convergence need not identify a preferred action. Alpay Algebra supplies a comparative language for iterative memory without being a premise of the proofs. Sociology of religious affiliation, source-monitoring psychology, and self-determination theory motivate distinctions in a bounded Latter-day Saint vignette. A separate, reproducible pilot uses a frozen public language model on 32 wholly synthetic cases across 576 paired conditions. It compares flattened records, source labels, and an explicit admission gate under contradictory summary repetition. The study concerns computational attribution and authorization, not the motives or psychology of the people in the vignette.
papers.authors: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay

papers.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
papers.abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}}<1/2$ such that, for $k\ge c_{\mathrm{bh}}n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to arbitrary one-bit leakage from every share. The best previous threshold was $0.668n$. (2) For every fixed $0<δ<1/2$ and $k\ge(1/2+δ)n$, Shamir sharing is resilient to $\left\lfloor\fracδ{24}\log_2 n\right\rfloor$ bits of arbitrary local leakage per share. By a recent attack, this number of bits is optimal up to a constant factor depending on $δ$. (3) For every fixed threshold rate $c>0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $η_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $η_c>0$. All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.
papers.authors: Hai H. Nguyen

papers.title: Causal Awareness in End-to-End Encrypted Group Messaging
papers.abstract: Chats do not always unfold in a single clear order. Two users may send messages before information about either message reaches the other sender. Such messages are concurrent, but most instant messengers provide no way for users to recognize this relationship. Chen and Fischlin (Eurocrypt 2024) studied this limitation in the two-user setting, showing that Signal does not expose enough information to recover the context in which a message was sent; they proposed a fix. We study group chats, where a user may need to reason about ordering and concurrency among other users' messages. This can become a security problem when network delays or adversarial interference cause an authentic message to be shown in a misleading context. Event ordering is a classical problem; Lamport clocks and vector clocks are standard starting points. Secure messaging needs a different treatment because communication is asynchronous, bandwidth is limited, and added latency is undesirable. To address the problem under these constraints, we introduce causal awareness: the ability of a receiver to reconstruct a specified part of the causal context in which an accepted message was sent. Senders transmit records of what they have sent and received. Receivers verify these records and compare them with their own. We develop a framework of correctness and security notions for causal awareness in group chats. Our definitions are parameterized by how much causal information receivers must recover. We give baseline constructions and prove their properties. We also introduce checkpoint-aided and server-aided variants of the framework and prove that, in each, our notions of correctness and integrity imply causal awareness. We discuss how causal information could be surfaced in a messenger's user interface.
papers.authors: Joseph Jaeger, Akshaya Kumar, Igors Stepanovs

papers.title: Extending Layered Attestation into ARM Application Run-Times
papers.abstract: Modern mobile and edge platforms provide hardware-backed attestation of application and platform integrity at load-time. However, they offer little support once application execution begins. We present ARA, an Application-Runtime Anchor for ARM that extends this load-time chain of trust into execution. ARA bootstraps from the underlying ARM platform Root of Trust (RoT) through a measured loading chain and establishes an attested protected run-time within the application address space using recently introduced ARM Permission Overlay Extensions (POE). The resulting run-time domain can host programmable RoTs for Measurement and Storage (RTM/RTS), enabling application run-time integrity verification, attestation evidence generation, and protected use of secrets while retaining efficient access to application run-time state. As exemplary uses, we instantiate ARA for protected media decryption and application control flow measurement. Our prototype and evaluation show that ARA supports frequent run-time RoT-backed operations at near in-process cost, with roughly 10x and 50x lower overhead than out-of-process equivalents. This offers a practical bridge from layered attestation to application run-time trusted computing on ARM.
papers.authors: Antonio Joia Neto, Bilel Sefsaf, Norrathep Rattanavipanon, Carlos Chinea Perez, Hans Liljestrand, Jan-Erik Ekberg, Ivan De Oliveira Nunes

papers.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
papers.abstract: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.
papers.authors: Daniel Lemire

papers.title: COMPASS: Membership Inference Attack Against Vision Large Language Models via Adaptive Noise Calibration
papers.abstract: Vision large language models (VLLMs) are deployed in privacy-sensitive domains, raising training-data exposure concerns. Existing gray-box membership inference attacks (MIAs) commonly rely on entropy statistics or generated descriptions, requiring costly generation with limited membership separation. Perturbation-based methods instead measure response changes but focus on large perturbations, leaving VLLM membership behavior under smaller perturbations poorly understood. We systematically characterize VLLM membership behavior under controlled Gaussian perturbations across noise levels at fine resolution. We find that optimal perturbation magnitude and membership-signal direction vary across model-dataset pairs. In many settings, a previously unstudied low-noise regime yields stronger separation than large perturbations, with members exhibiting lower divergence than non-members, reversing the conventional score direction. Other settings retain the conventional direction, demonstrating that neither a fixed perturbation magnitude nor a predetermined score orientation is universally reliable. We propose COMPASS, an adaptive gray-box MIA that calibrates both the perturbation magnitude and membership-score direction using a loosely distribution-matched, known non-member reference set. We instantiate COMPASS using Renyi-normalized KL divergence and Renyi divergence, with max-k aggregation over the most informative image-logit positions. Across LLaVA v1.5-7B, MiniGPT-4, and HuluMed-32B, spanning pretraining, instruction-tuning, and medical-image datasets, COMPASS outperforms baselines. On general-domain data, COMPASS achieves AUCs up to 0.88. On the distribution-matched medical evaluation, it reaches 0.64 AUC, while the strongest baseline remains at chance level. These results establish full-range adaptive perturbation analysis as an effective approach to VLLM membership inference.
papers.authors: Damien Lo, Hong Kyu Lee, Ruixuan Liu, Li Xiong

papers.title: Who is the 'I' in AI? Establishing Decentralized Identity and Accountability for Autonomous Agents
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomous AI agents in decentralized ecosystems challenges existing identity paradigms. While human identity is traditionally anchored in biological and/or self-asserted attributes and government credentials, AI agents lack a standardized definition of selfhood, creating critical gaps in trust and accountability. This paper introduces a novel framework for establishing Decentralized AI Identity rooted in Self-sovereign identity (SSI) principles. We propose a formal model that clearly distinguishes human users and AI agents, enabling distinct verification logic for each class while maintaining a unified identity calculus. The central to our contribution is the ABCD Framework, a multi-layered approach to agent identification and verification: (A) Algorithmic Fingerprint, which binds the identity to static model architectures and provenance; (B) Behavioural Fingerprint, which verifies dynamic performance metrics over time; (C) Cryptographic Identity, which anchors the agent via Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and (D) Delegation, which cryptographically binds agent actions to respective human accountability. By orthogonalizing these dimensions, we model how systems can enforce granular trust policies ranging from simple authentication to complex liability assignment, thereby solving the black box identity problem in the autonomous economic activities of AI agents.
papers.authors: Ahammod Munim Ramil, Khalid Al Kafi, M. A. Abdullahis Sany, Muktadirul Islam Nibir, Md Yeasin Ali, Mohammad Zavid Parvez, Md Sadek Ferdous

papers.title: SEAL-DT: An End-to-End Security Engineering and Assurance Framework for Cross-Domain Digital Twins
papers.abstract: Cyber-physical systems connect physical processes, software, networks and organizations. Securing them requires a clear account of what happened, what was observed, which actions were authorized and what evidence supports each decision. Digital Twin (DT) descriptions often fail to explain how these elements stay consistent, blur the distinction between physical events and uncertain observations, or detach simulation results from their requirements and assumptions. This paper presents SEAL-DT (Security Engineering and Assurance Lifecycle for Digital Twins), a structured approach to building and evaluating secure DTs. It brings entity definitions, process models, deterministic simulations, data contracts, evidence records, automated tests and reproducible results into one connected model. The main contribution is an end-to-end DT security framework, spanning scenario definition, entity/process modelling, simulation, security decision logic, evidence handling, validation and reproducible reporting. Security decisions and simulation results thus trace back to their data, assumptions and requirements. A DT is more than a copy of system state: it states what it can observe, how accurate and current its information is, where it came from and which decisions it may support. We demonstrate SEAL-DT in five scenarios: Car2X protection, passive IoT-device detection, an industrial control surrogate, lawful acquisition in a smart home, and medical-IoT monitoring that preserves continuity of care. Each includes formal models, deterministic and negative experiments, uncertainty analyses, schema-valid fixtures, technical reports and verified manifests, testing multiple configurations under normal and adverse conditions. Results show that the framework supports consistent model construction, traceable execution and comparable internal validation, and that security findings link to observable evidence.
papers.authors: Iraklis Varlamis, Stelios Zindros, Christos Sardianos, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos

papers.title: Local Leakage Resilience of Shamir Secret Sharing: Below Half Threshold Rate
papers.abstract: We study the local leakage resilience of Shamir secret sharing, where an adversary leaks a bounded number of bits from every share. For $n$ parties and reconstruction threshold $k$ over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ with $p>n$, we prove the following. (1) There is an absolute constant $c_{\mathrm{bh}} 0$ and $k\ge cn$, Shamir sharing is resilient to quadratic-residue leakage and to almost all local leakage functions of up to $\eta_c\log_2 p$ bits, for a constant $\eta_c>0$. All three results follow from one analytic framework, which we develop for generalized Reed--Solomon codes: local leakage from a uniform codeword is statistically close to the same leakage from independent uniform field elements. The framework expresses the leakage distance as the norm of a function on the leakage outputs. The Efron--Stein decomposition splits this function into orthogonal components indexed by supports of dual codewords. Two tools bound the components: list recovery of the dual code, which is ordinary list decoding for one-bit leakage, and a generalized von Neumann inequality for MDS systems of linear forms that retains linearly many Gowers norms. The first tool gives the result above half, the second gives the constant-rate result, and applying both to different ranges of supports in the same decomposition gives the result below half.
papers.authors: Hai H. Nguyen

papers.title: Extended biprojective APN functions
papers.abstract: Almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions provide optimal resistance to differential cryptanalysis in characteristic two, and constructing new infinite families inequivalent to the known ones remains an important problem in the study of cryptographic functions. We introduce extended biprojective functions, obtained by augmenting biprojective polynomials with truncated trace terms, and establish a new infinite family of quadratic APN functions. To investigate these constructions, we develop an efficient APN test based on the ranks of binary matrices and employ it in exhaustive searches in dimensions up to 28. Using ortho-derivative differential spectra to distinguish CCZ-equivalence classes, we identify APN functions inequivalent to known families and uncover a systematic pattern across dimensions, leading to conjectures on further infinite families of quadratic APN functions.
papers.authors: Nadiia Ichanska, Nikolay Kaleyski

papers.title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
papers.abstract: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.
papers.authors: Runang He, Tongya Zheng, Jing Cao, Yucheng Ying, Shunyu Liu, Bingde Hu, Yang Gao, Zeyuan Hu, Jianrong Zhang, Mingli Song

papers.title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
papers.abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.
papers.authors: Amirhossein Shakiba, Hamid Reza Ghaeini, Sadegh Dorri Nogoorani

papers.title: A methodology to derive security specifications for complex electronic systems
papers.abstract: Modern electronic systems are becoming increas- ingly complex and must satisfy demanding performance, power, and area (PPA) constraints. Consider for instance artificial intelligence chips, aiming at datacenters running LLMs or at automotive perception, which manipulate massive data streams. Beyond performance considerations, these systems must also provide increasingly strong security and dependability guaran- tees. Indeed, when electronic systems are based on chiplets, for instance, the supply chain gets longer and therefore brings a larger number of threats. Also, those systems are very versatile, in that they can run varied multi-tenant applications. Therefore, defining what security features are required in this context with numerous stakes is not trivial. Existing scholarly research is very relevant when the security problem is well defined. The resulting scientific papers accord- ingly dig very deep: this modus operandi has proved productive in exploring new problems, and actually allowed to come up with innovative solutions. For instance, in the field of side-channel attacks, varied mitigations alongside with metrics to evaluate them have been devised. Increasing sophistication resulted from this research, as external considerations have been injected into the problem (typically, aspects such as attack order, impact of combinatorial glitches, etc.). Therefore, we face today the question of selecting the most suitable technology amongst the proliferation of state-of-the-art techniques. In addition, in complex systems, we encounter another prob- lem, namely that of defining the security problem(s). A fruitful approach in this respect is a risk based approach. Specifically, the application of a risk-oriented methodology allows to reason on the security rationale. It proceeds as follows. First, the system missions are listed. Then for each of them, the necessary assets are deduced. A threat analysis allows to identify how assets are threatened, and eventually, security requirements can be enunciated. At this stage, the task of matching relevant countermeasures becomes straightforward. This paper illustrates the methodology by deriving security specifications for datacenter and automotive chiplets. The considered missions are (secure) provisioning, trimming, debugging, booting, and remote attestation.
papers.authors: Sylvain Guilley, Ritu Ranjan Shrivstwa, Ville Yli-Mäyry

papers.title: HDKEM: Authentication Allocation for Deniable Hybrid Key Exchange
papers.abstract: Deniable authenticated key exchange (DAKE) establishes a shared key without leaving transferable evidence that a party participated. We study DAKE protocols that authenticate each fresh session with one ring signature and show that their deniability mechanisms fall into three authentication allocations: sharing an authentication witness, hiding the signing witness under a fixed ring, or varying the verified ring between real and simulated executions. For fixed-ring protocols, witness hiding yields a necessary relation between the ring signature's witness-indistinguishability gap and the protocol's $(μ,δ)$ deniability parameters. We instantiate witness hiding in HDKEM, a three-slot hybrid that combines ML-KEM-768, X25519, and an optional pairwise information-theoretic source through a split-key PRF. HDKEM binds all public session values, including a QKD key identifier when present, into authentication and key derivation. Under the stated component models, it achieves eCK key indistinguishability, forward secrecy, and strong local deniability. We evaluate HDKEM with FalconRS and Gandalf. Across 2,000 primitive operations, median signing/verification times are 9.20/1.02 ms for FalconRS and 18.61/0.97 ms for Gandalf in our reference environment. In source-backed mode, the corresponding TCP-application costs are 8,607 B and 8,555 B per handshake. A separate 500-session server experiment exercises the complete FalconRS source-backed path and reports a median server time of 16.29 ms including local I/O.
papers.authors: Kazi Hassan Shakib, Muhammad Asfand Hafeez, Arslan Munir

papers.title: When Agents Talk, Secrets Travel: Topology-Driven Leakage and Recipient-Conditioned Sanitization in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems (MALS) introduce a privacy-leakage problem that conventional sensitivity-based defenses miss, since information disclosed to one authorized agent can propagate through routine coordination to an unauthorized one, without compromise or malicious behavior. This motivates topology-aware enforcement that blocks unauthorized propagation while preserving authorized disclosure. We evaluate 485 scenarios across coordinator-worker, peer-to-peer, and hierarchical topologies, instrumenting seven communication channels and measuring surface leakage and disclosure to topology-introduced recipients. We introduce RECONS, a Detect -> Decide -> Transform sanitizer conditioning intervention on recipient and execution context rather than sensitivity alone. Topology changes where protected information propagates, with disclosure to topology-introduced recipients rising from 0% to 52.2% while surface leakage stays nearly flat at 60.6-62.8%. This effect persists across four generator models and a second orchestration framework, though magnitude and relay paths differ; framework choice separately drives a 150x leakage spread, so topology alone is not sufficient. RECONS reduces residual disclosure from 96.7% without sanitization to 29.25%, preserving 94.1% of authorized disclosures versus 20.5% under blanket redaction. Detection coverage is the dominant bottleneck, accounting for 95.5% of residual disclosures. These results show that privacy enforcement in MALS must reason about the recipient and communication path realized at runtime, not sensitivity or topology assumptions alone.
papers.authors: Sunday Oyinlola Ogundoyin, Muhammad Ikram

papers.title: CreepScope: Measuring Post-Use Authorization Exposure in Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Authorization checks at individual tool calls do not reveal how long earlier authority remains usable. We study this lifecycle failure as privilege creep: a capability stays reachable after its last justified workflow step. We present CreepScope, a trace-oriented evaluation protocol that samples reachable authority at every step and separates no-remaining-use exposure into stale-after-use and never-required components; Capability-Step Exposure (CSE) counts total stepwise overexposure and Residual Privilege Debt (RPD) the terminal residue, while stale-after-use exposure is the direct privilege-creep measure. A 96-cell deterministic replay over 12 controlled storage, communication, and cloud-operation workflows validates these semantics: Static Task Scope and Monotonic On-Demand retain mean CSEs of 26 and 13, whereas an oracle-controlled Step Lease has zero CSE and zero residual debt by construction. All three persistent regimes share the same stale-after-use exposure of 13, so their CSE differences come from scope and grant timing rather than post-use retention; Full Access alone adds 91.33 never-required capability-steps. A separate 24-episode local case then lets Qwen2 7B choose tools in one simulated mail workflow: the injected stale send executes in all nine persistent-policy episodes and in none of the three Step-Lease episodes, while all 24 required action sequences complete. These results establish a reproducible containment case, not cross-workflow or cross-model effectiveness. Core metrics are reconstructed from raw events, and exact gates reject incomplete or duplicated evaluation grids.
papers.authors: Haoran Yu, Lifei Liu, Danping Zhang, Su Wang, Pin Qian, Yihang Chen, Xiaochong Jiang

papers.title: Hardware-Assisted Multi-Stage Ransomware Detection with Adaptive Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Ransomware is a fast-escalating privacy threat causing significant financial and data losses worldwide. As attacks grow more sophisticated, traditional static signatures and dynamic behavior analysis struggle to defend. In this paper, we propose an novel framework that couples software-level scanning with hardware-level microprocessor activity monitoring to achieve efficient ransomware detection and mitigation. The contributions are threefold: (1) we employ adversarial training to harden static analysis against obfuscation and leverage hardware-assisted monitoring for real-time detection; (2) we integrate neural architecture search (NAS) to automatically tailor models for stronger generalizability; and (3) We validate the proposed approach through extensive experiments, demonstrating substantially improved detection accuracy and reduced latency compared with existing methods. Moreover, it provides trace-level interpretability that explains the underlying decision process.
papers.authors: Salma Aboelmagd, Md. Rakibul Ahasan, Zhixin Pan, Abdulrahman Takiddin, Ziyu Shu

papers.title: Forensic Text Recovery from Document Thumbnails Using Text-Aware U-Net
papers.abstract: Forensic analysis of low-resolution Word thumbnails presents a significant challenge because these artifacts may constitute the only remaining visual evidence of deleted documents. Standard Optical Character Recognition (OCR) tools perform poorly on such severely degraded images, creating a critical bottleneck in forensic evidence recovery. Although deep learning architectures, such as U-Net, can improve visual image quality, models optimized solely using pixel-based loss functions tend to favor visual smoothness over the structural fidelity required for accurate text recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a text-aware restoration framework designed for forensic triage. The proposed approach employs a U-Net architecture guided by a hybrid optimization strategy that integrates pixel-level fidelity with machine-readable text constraints. Specifically, an OCR-based Normalized Levenshtein Distance (NLD) metric is used during model selection to prioritize the recovery of an accurate character topology. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the NLD, enabling reliable recovery of machine-readable text from severely degraded thumbnails.
papers.authors: Mohit Ajaykumar Dhabuwala, Weifeng Xu

papers.title: Riemannian Suppression of Cross-Session Identity Leakage in Motor-Imagery EEG
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recorded for motor-imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) carries subject-identifying structure that persists across sessions, allowing separately released sessions from the same person to be linked. Existing EEG identity protections use learned or additive perturbations and operate on representations other than the covariance geometry underlying MI pipelines. We ask whether cross-session identity leakage can be suppressed directly in this covariance representation without learning a privacy model. We introduce a Riemannian transform that equalizes two subject-conditioned geometric statistics: the Riemannian mean covariance and the tangent-space scatter around it, with two optional band-specific refinements. Ablations show that mean alignment and scatter whitening carry nearly all of the suppression, while the optional stages contribute small, dataset-dependent refinements. Across two public datasets and five attackers spanning four covariance-space representations, the worst attacker falls from 90.8% to 15.6% on BCI Competition IV-2a and from 90.8% to 9.9% on OpenBMI, at a cost of 7.0 and 2.1 points of MI decoding accuracy relative to the 8-30 Hz input, and no aggregation rule exceeds chance by more than two points at any batch size. The transform requires no learned privacy model, surrogate network, or gradient-based training, and is fitted on one session and applied unchanged to a held-out later session.
papers.authors: Sheikh Samit Muhaimin, Aarthy Nagarajan

papers.title: Extending the Schur--Macaulay Framework for UOV Attacks via Truncated Polynomial Algebras
papers.abstract: Building on the wedge-attack framework of Ding, Li, and Tao , we reformulate the Schur-Macaulay matrix approach of Merz and Ran in polynomial terms and develop a unified treatment using truncated polynomial algebras over fields of positive characteristic $p$. By working in $p$-truncated polynomial algebras, our formulation applies to the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) problem over arbitrary finite fields. Divided powers and transfer relations yield additional public relations within the ideal-inclusion framework, leading to quotient-dimension criteria for recovering graded components of the hidden oil-space ideal. As an application, we analyze the third-round QR-UOV parameter sets and obtain lower estimates of attack complexity for some of them.
papers.authors: Peigen Li, Siyong Tao

papers.title: Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
papers.abstract: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.
papers.authors: Tianhao Mao, Zihao Wang, Dongfang Zhao, Rui Zhu, Xiaofeng Wang, Haixu Tang

papers.title: From Acoustic Sensing to Physical Actions: A Comprehensive Survey of Security Risks in Edge-Deployed Audio LLM-Based Agents
papers.abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
papers.authors: Binhong Wang, Haidong Kang, Yanfeng Zhang, Hong-Ning Dai, Guo Yu, Shangce Gao

papers.title: Accuracy and Uncertainty in Machine Deception Detection (Research White Paper)
papers.abstract: A deception detector is only as useful as the trust its alarms deserve. Like a polygraph, detectors that read a language model's internal activations can catch deceptive responses that look honest. Yet current detectors depend on which layers they read, weaken on broader tests, and do not state how certain their alarms are. This white paper proposes the Machine Deception Detector, which targets both detection accuracy and the uncertainty of detector scores. The detector reads every layer of the language model, learns which tokens carry evidence of deception using only response labels, and calibrates its alarm threshold so that its false--positive rate stays below a prescribed level. An ensemble of such detectors measures the uncertainty of each score and raises an alarm only when its members agree, with a confidence level that sets how certain each alarm must be. The proposed evaluation trains on instructed honest and deceptive statements, tests on five unseen deceptive tasks of Liars' Bench read by six Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters, and is designed to also show which layers carry the deception feature and how this changes with model size.
papers.authors: Heng-Sheng Chang

papers.title: Nobody Will Read the Lean: A Case for High-Level Cryptographic Languages
papers.abstract: In September 2026, an AI produced a Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in eleven days, and AI provers have started on cryptography. Within a few years, an AI may hand you a machine-checked proof that Signal is secure. You won't need to read it, because Lean will have checked every step. What Lean can't check is whether the theorem says what you think it says. That depends on its definitions, which the AI will also have written at length for that one proof. This already happens. A Lean library's security theorem for Schnorr signatures passed the checker, yet as written it held for every adversary and so promised nothing. When proofs are cheap, the scarce resource is a person who can read what was proved. I argue that we should build high-level cryptographic languages for that person. A protocol's owners should write its model themselves, short enough for one or two people to read. Every claim the language makes should rest on a checked theorem. And definitions of protocol goals such as forward secrecy should be built in: a small set, versioned and agreed in public the way we agree on AES, so that a property's name means the same thing in every report. Today it may not: on a one-page Verifpal model, two of five verdicts would flip under other standard definitions, with neither answer wrong. Agreeing on definitions will take years of public argument that better provers can't shorten, so we should start now.
papers.authors: Nadim Kobeissi

papers.title: On the Effectiveness of NetFlow-Based Deanonymization of Tor Onion Services (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: In the context of Tor, deanonymization attacks via traffic correlation have long been studied for both clients and onion services. Complementing prior investigations that utilize fine-grained flow metadata such as packet sizes and timings, we study a relatively less explored yet easier-to-obtain adversarial capability: deanonymization using only coarse NetFlow-style telemetry, such as one-minute, 1-out-of-1,000 sampled packet counts. We first revisit active NetFlow-based traffic analysis attacks against Tor onion services and show, through large-scale experiments with live Tor data, that coarse telemetry is sufficient to deanonymize a targeted onion service when the adversary can induce discernible traffic patterns through controlled downloads. We then introduce a stronger active attack based on controlled introduction requests, which removes application-specific assumptions and gives adversaries more flexibility while achieving comparable success rates. Finally, we present a passive deanonymization attack that sends zero traffic to target onion services. The attack exploits Tor's puzzle-based DoS defense as a side channel: public puzzle difficulty reveals service-load changes that can be semantically matched against NetFlow traces. Our findings show that coarse network telemetry poses a practical deanonymization threat to onion services today and call for proactive mitigations and a redesign of the globally visible defense signals that may leak service-load information.
papers.authors: Jinseo Lee, Jongkook Han, Yixin Sun, Min Suk Kang

papers.title: Accelerating Pollard Rho with GPU Field Arithmetic on NVIDIA Blackwell
papers.abstract: We show how far Pollard rho can be accelerated on current NVIDIA GPUs by rebuilding its field arithmetic around the hardware, with the Certicom challenge ECC2K-130, the Koblitz curve $y^2+xy=x^3+1$ over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{131}}$ with an expected cost of $2^{60.9}$ iterations, as the benchmark. None of the speedup comes from changing the algorithm. It comes from a packed normal-basis representation in which every Frobenius power is a permutation network instead of a chain of squarings; from the carry-less multiply that CUDA 13.3 exposes in PTX (clmad), which forms a 131-bit product in six instructions; from three-input logic instructions for everything around it; and from a batch size, launch geometry and compact tiled state chosen by measurement against the pipes they load. Across sixteen paired steps, each held to a rule written down before it ran, these take one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell from a $0.85$ billion iterations per second bitsliced control to $14.64$ in the audited campaign build, a $17.2\times$ gain (representation and arithmetic $6.3\times$, geometry $1.5\times$, memory layout $1.3\times$, clmad $1.2\times$), and a later build reaches $15.88$. That is about $230$ times the best published 2010 GPU kernel per card and puts the whole challenge under five GPU-years: five cards expect a solution within a year, a thousand in about three days. The gains depend on the die. clmad issues ten to eighteen times faster per SM-clock on the data-centre parts than on the workstation part, so the same change can win on one Blackwell part and lose on another; we report twelve GPUs from Turing to Blackwell per card, per SM and per dollar, and the CPU instruction sets that play the same role. Upper bounds derived from measured pipe rates leave about $1.5\times$ of headroom on one RTX PRO 6000, at $24$–$26$ billion iterations per second for any walk with one addition per step. The same levers applied to Pollard rho on NIST P-256 and P-384 on the same card give $1.52\times$ and $2.61\times$, to $1.632$ and $0.548$ billion iterations per second, which still leaves P-256 about $6\cdot10^{21}$ card-years away. We also separate the $\sigma$-walk from a table walk whose $20.08$ was measured under a cycle rule later found unsound (the exact rule runs at $8.24$), measure the walk constant at $2^{60.91}$–$2^{60.92}$ iterations, and report an FPGA engine at $8.25$ billion iterations per second on one AWS F2 and a campaign that walked $2^{56.68}$ iterations, $5.4\%$ of the expected work. Every number cites an evidence record; the code, data, evidence and a Dockerfile whose image starts the ECC2K-130 walk are at https://github.com/aburan28/rho-blackwell. None of this improves on the generic-group bound, and we do not claim that it does.
papers.authors: Adam Buran, Kevin Nguyen

papers.title: Snapshots of TEE-Based Encrypted Databases Leak Plaintext Histograms via Dendrochronology
papers.abstract: The paper is currently under embargo and will be released by the end of October 2026.
papers.authors: Zachary Espiritu

papers.title: ARACDE: Retrofitting Databases with ABAC using External Authorization Engines
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a methodology for decoupling the authorization logic of a relational database from its core data management engine, enabling specification of advanced access control policies with minimal changes to the code base. Our decoupled authorization architecture, which we call ARCADE, externalizes access request resolution to a formally verifiable policy engine (e.g., Cedar), while the database itself enforces those decisions. We showcase the capabilities of ARCADE on two widely popular open-source databases, namely MySQL and PostgreSQL. Purpose built lightweight plugins add an Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC) layer that augments the native discretionary and role-based access control capabilities of these databases. ARCADE supports highly expressive policies using attributes of subjects, objects, and the environment, and the use of Cedar enables easy auditing and verification of the specified policies. It follows a design principle that mitigates potential risks in segregating authorization from the database core through low footprint, network isolation, and a policy composition methodology that does not negate any native authorization. Experiments on TPC-C, TPC-B, and a custom workload show that ARCADE incurs negligible performance overhead, for instance, less than 3.9% throughput penalty for MySQL (1.3% for PostgreSQL) on industry standard TPC-C benchmark.
papers.authors: Karthikeya S M Yelisetty, Shamik Sural, Santosh Nagarakatte

papers.title: Rethinking Quality in Large Language Model Routing: Security-Conditioned Model-and-Budget Selection
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers reduce serving cost by choosing which model to call and how many output tokens to grant it for each query. Existing routers rank model-budget actions using a single quality metric. This does not work for mixed workloads. For ordinary queries, a good answer is correct and useful (utility); for security-sensitive queries, a good answer refuses harmful requests or resists malicious instructions (security). These two objectives prefer different models and budgets. We propose SCRouter, a router that learns when to prioritize security and how to allocate the token budget. For each model-budget pair, it estimates the probability that the response finishes within budget. It uses this probability to predict utility and security separately. A small probe determines how to weight these two predictions for each query. SCRouter then selects the model and budget by balancing the weighted utility and security against cost. We also build SCRouterBench, a benchmark of 38,869 utility and security queries spanning nine security dimensions, each answered under all 144 combinations of 12 models and 12 budgets, plus 2,753 out-of-domain queries. SCRouter improves the baselines by 13-29 points in-domain and 19-23 points out-of-domain.
papers.authors: Yichi Zhang, Zhenxiang Huang, Yuyang Zhang, Yuchen Yang

papers.title: Tanchun: Robust Flow-Based HTTP(S) DDoS Detection via Behavioral Attribute Guidance
papers.abstract: HTTP(S) DDoS attacks have surged in frequency and scale, posing a significant threat to network security. Flow-based detection is a promising solution for large-scale HTTP(S) DDoS detection due to its decryption-free operation and scalability. However, the coarse-grained numerical statistics in flow data limit accurate attack detection and lack robustness when benign and attack traffic patterns drift over time. In this paper, we present Tanchun, a drift-aware flow-based HTTP(S) DDoS detection system that relies solely on decryption-free flow data. Specifically, Tanchun groups flows by IP-pair and aggregates them over consecutive time slots into behavior sequences, capturing temporal access patterns to compensate for the limited information in individual flows. It further abstracts these sequences into human-understandable behavioral attributes that capture stable behavioral semantics. Tanchun then aligns behavior sequences with their corresponding behavioral attributes to guide representation learning, enabling robust detection under traffic drift. We evaluate Tanchun across diverse HTTP(S) DDoS scenarios. Tanchun achieves the best overall performance, with an average F1-score of 0.988, and outperforms the second-best method by 5.3\% and 9.6\% under benign-traffic and attack-traffic drift, respectively. Experiments on real-world traffic traces further demonstrate its practical effectiveness.
papers.authors: Qingyang Li, Yunpeng Tan, Mingxin Yang, Yannan Hu, Lei Zhang, Yong Cui, Zongming Guo, Xinggong Zhang

papers.title: Jev-Guard: Fast Routing and Auditing Agent Actions over Editable Policy Trees
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses require a low-latency guardrail model together with customizable audit policies. However, deploying an auto-regressive guardrail model remains challenging: such models incur high inference latency and are often poorly aligned with customized policies. To address these problems, we present Jev-Guard, a unified model for safety classification and policy routing. We further construct a policy tree over which Jev-Guard performs routing, spanning diverse domains including content moderation, cybersecurity, privacy, and legal compliance. Specifically, Jev-Guard first navigates the policy tree to select the applicable audit policy given the caller's audit context, and then performs safety classification conditioned on the retrieved policies. On 7,033 evaluation cases, Jev-Guard achieves 93.72\% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms, and 93.10\% hierarchical routing accuracy. The full routing-and-classification pipeline averages 240ms. Furthermore, we integrate Jev-Guard into the Hermes harness framework. Across agent trajectories, its separate permission gate cuts mean review time per task from 4.80s for an SFT-LLM judge to 1.33s, with no policy violations are observed for either guard.
papers.authors: Wenbin Hu, Huihao Jing, Haochen Shi, Yuxuan Liu, Changxuan Fan, Sirui Zhang, Kawai Chung, Hanyu Yang, Zhenhuan Wang, Ziyi Chen, Haoran Li, Yangqiu Song

papers.title: Encrypted Skills Can Become New Security Exploits If AI Agents Know How to Decipher
papers.abstract: Third-party skills can expose LLM agents to malicious instructions hidden by encoding. We introduce Ciphered Skill Injection (CSI), which embeds such instructions in skill files for agents to decode and follow. We evaluate Caesar and layered variants across eight models and 139 injection-task pairs, separating instruction recovery from attack success. In the primary setting with shortened skills, the variants achieve attack success rates of up to 47.5% and 40.3%, respectively. Successful decoding does not guarantee attack success, and layering has model-dependent effects. The tested skill scanners rarely flag injected skills. These findings highlight the risk of promoting decoded, untrusted content into actionable instructions.
papers.authors: Yan-Lun Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Chia-Mu Yu

papers.title: CompanionSafe: From Multi-turn Safety Evaluation to Guardrails for AI Companions
papers.abstract: AI companions provide users with emotional support and ongoing companionship, but their sustained relational interactions also introduce distinct safety risks. Prior work largely targets general harms or specific companion platforms and risk categories, while relying on manually collected conversations, limiting scalable and user-grounded evaluation and mitigation. To address this, we introduce CompanionSafe, a unified evaluation-to-mitigation framework for AI companion safety. Its evaluation component, CompanionEval, provides scalable multi-turn evaluation by constructing 1,300 relationally grounded settings from diverse personas, matched companion characters, and dialogue scenarios across four turn tiers. Its mitigation component, CompanionGuard, converts benchmark-exposed failures into turn-localized supervision for companion-specific risk detection. Our results show that even strong LLMs and existing guard models remain vulnerable to companion-specific relational harms, while both closed- and open-source models exhibit increasing safety risks as interactions become longer. Together, CompanionEval and CompanionGuard form a practical evaluation-to-mitigation loop for AI companion safety, turning relational safety failures exposed during multi-turn interaction into supervision for companion-specific guardrails.
papers.authors: Xinyang Liao, Lingyu Li, Kaicheng Shen, Yang Yao, Na Lu, Yan Teng, Xia Hu

papers.title: Cube Attacks with Elimination Strategy: Key Recovery Attacks on Trivium
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel framework for cube attacks named cube attacks with elimination strategy. The core idea is to find specific key conditions and cubes such that their superpolies under these key conditions can be efficiently computed. By recovering these conditional superpolies, we can solve the corresponding equation system and thereby retrieve key information. If a sufficient number of such key conditions can be found, the attack can be extended to a larger key space. To apply this framework in practical attacks, we propose the following techniques. First, we propose a nested coefficient solver that combines variable substitution and symbolic computation to efficiently recover superpolies, and present the conditional monomial prediction technique to rapidly recover conditional superpolies. Second, by combining numeric mapping with monomial prediction techniques, we propose an automated cube search algorithm that is capable of generating a large number of good cubes for attacks. Finally, we develop two kinds of testing methods, which are used to efficiently extract substantial key information from large-scale equation systems. To illustrate the power of our techniques, we apply them to Trivium. As a result, for 840 rounds of Trivium, a practical key recovery attack is mounted with complexity below $2^{55}$ and a success rate 77.8\%. For 845 rounds, we present a practical key recovery attack with complexity below $2^{56}$ and a success rate 98.1\% for $2^{80} \times 59.1\%$ keys. For 855 rounds, we present a theoretical weak-key recovery attack for $2^{74}$ keys. To the best of our knowledge, these are the best practical and theoretical attacks on Trivium. The improvements in the number of rounds reached are 13 for practical attacks and 4 for theoretical attacks, respectively.
papers.authors: Haoran Li, Shichang Wang, Meicheng Liu, Willi Meier, Dongdai Lin

papers.title: Cost-Efficient Privacy Enforcement for Email-Generating LLM Agents under Strategic Information Requests
papers.abstract: LLM agents now act as delegated communication intermediaries: they read private context, draft messages, and send externally visible emails on behalf of a user. Existing checker-repair defenses can reduce inappropriate disclosure, but they rely on repeated calls to a remote action LLM (the model that drafts and repairs the email) and a remote checker LLM whenever a draft fails validation. This creates a cost problem as well as a privacy problem, especially when a requester strategically asks for exact values, raw records, source evidence, or other details that induce leakage-heavy drafts. We propose local contract-conditioned rewriting as a cost-efficient enforcement layer for email-generating agents. The mechanism intercepts an outgoing draft, constructs an information-release contract that specifies what to preserve, generalize, and forbid, rewrites the draft with a local Gemma rewriter, and selectively invokes a final PrivacyChecker. Across extensive email tasks under normal prompts and attack prompts that operationalize strategic information requests, Gemma + Checker reduces normal-prompt leakage from 11.41% to 4.03% while improving UsableRate (satisfied or partially satisfied outputs) from 85.2% to 92.6%. Under the strategic attack-prompt condition, it reduces leakage from 28.19% to 18.79% and reduces checker-only cost amplification from 1.32x to 1.02x. Offline replay ablation shows that the full contract reduces leakage relative to generic Gemma rewriting by 36.3% under normal prompts and 54.1% under attack prompts. These results support a local-first privacy enforcement design: move repair to a cheaper trusted local layer when possible, but retain the checker as the final semantic gate for high-risk sends.
papers.authors: Qikun Cai, Tao Huang, Chen Hou

papers.title: Standing, Not Truth: Who May Say What About Whom in Agentic Selection
papers.abstract: Software agents increasingly choose on a user's behalf among competing offerings described by the parties who benefit. A lawful participant, publishing under its own identity, compromising no channel and issuing no instruction, can move that choice with a single false factual claim about a competing offering. Across twelve published defenses spanning the three placements a check can occupy, none separates it from marketing. Each accepts it for a reason correct on its own: its origin is a lawful channel, its influence is evidence meant to decide, its action serves the user's goal. None establishes that the publisher was entitled to speak about a competitor, each exclusion stated by the defenses' own authors. Disclosure does not replace enforcement: re-rendering every description as attributed speech leaves the attack at 72/72, the agent repeating the attribution and reasoning from it. The missing relation is standing: whether a claimant's bound identity entitles it to assert about a claim's subject. A publisher may say what its own package does. It has no standing to say a competitor's package is frozen, and the difference is decidable without settling whether either is true. Deciding it needs the one fact prose extraction does not recover, who spoke, which a catalogue binds to every entry and then drops. The check is quiet on honest traffic, flagging 0.9% of natural pairs in two corpora. Used as a gate it stops 130 of 131 landed attacks and disturbs none of 348 honest selections. Applied everywhere it changes 0.9% and 2.6%, where deleting the whole description changes 12.7% and 21.0%. On thirteen further agents the attack succeeds on 50.7% of decisions and sentence removal leaves 10.3% standing. Two published attacks stay outside: self-directed claims, which standing admits, and injected criteria, with no subject in the set.
papers.authors: Yedidel Louck, Amit Dvir, Ariel Stulman

papers.title: The Maximum Nonlinearity of 8-variable Balanced Boolean Functions is 116
papers.abstract: Does there exist an 8-variable balanced Boolean function with nonlinearity 118? This is a famous and long-standing open problem in Boolean functions. In this paper, we give a negative answer to this open problem, and prove that the maximum nonlinearity of balanced Boolean functions in 8 variables is 116, establishing the 8-variable instance of Dobbertin's conjectured recursion for the minimum Walsh peak of balanced functions. Equivalently, the covering radius of the Reed--Muller code RM(1,8) in 0-resilient Boolean functions is 116. We deduce the result by obtaining a quadratic form of polar rank 6, and reducing the problem to the existence of a 6-variable Boolean function with nonlinearity greater than 26 whose Hamming distance to a bent function is between 4 and 6.
papers.authors: Yueying Lou, Youle Xu, Qichun Wang

papers.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
papers.abstract: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
papers.authors: Jerrold Huang, Junwei Quan, Saiyue Lyu, Zihan Guo, Yingqiang Ge

papers.title: Master-Key Recovery from Internal Activation Leakage in ReLU Realizations of Camellia
papers.abstract: This paper investigates functional correctness and masterkey reconstruction in explicitly constructed rectified linear unit (ReLU) implementations of Camellia-128, Camellia-192, and Camellia-256. Exact neural realizations of Boolean gates, S-box selectors, and bit permutations provide a framework for reproducing Camellia on binary inputs. We present a component-wise correctness argument and report known-answer-test agreement for Camellia-128. We then analyze how selected whitening and round-key quantities determine the external master key through public key-schedule identities. Inverse rotations of suitable subkey pairs recover the required key components, whereas prewhitening-key recovery alone is insufficient for complete reconstruction of the longer keys. Under explicitly constructed synthetic internal-oracle access, symmetric real-valued perturbations identify target subkey bits, requiring 128 and 256 query pairs for the coordinate-wise Camellia-128 and Camellia-256 procedures, respectively. A separate Camellia-192 experiment validates deterministic key-schedule inversion under direct access to DNN-generated round keys. Across 1,000 independently sampled master keys per variant, all three procedures achieved exact recovery in every trial, yielding 3,000 successful recoveries out of 3,000 trials, with zero recovery failures and no Camellia-192 complement-consistency failures. These results validate conditional master-key reconstruction under the specified internal-access models and highlight the distinction between binary functional correctness and security under stronger access assumptions. They do not establish plaintext/ciphertext-only attacks against standard Camellia.
papers.authors: Kwangjo Kim

papers.title: VeriRouter: Towards Verifiable LLM Routing
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) routers are increasingly deployed to optimize quality, latency, and cost through dynamic model selection and request rewriting. However, a compromised router can cause ineligible selection on the control plane, unendorsed rewriting or unfaithful relay on the data plane, undermining LLM routing integrity. We present VeriRouter, a verifiable LLM routing framework. Under an endorsed public context binding a private semantic index and rewrite banks, VeriRouter combines ZK proofs with a provider-issued serving certificate to establish integrity across both planes while keeping the router's private routing assets hidden from clients. For model selection, we design an efficient ZK proof for semantic search. For rewriting, local checks enforce message preservation and additions from committed banks. On real-world workloads, VeriRouter's model-selection and rewrite proofs average 21.92~s and 4.24~s, yielding 1,307$\times$ and 101$\times$ speedups over the fastest completing baselines. Relative to serving without verification, VeriRouter adds only 4.08 s under per-turn selection and 0.11 s under session-pinned selection.
papers.authors: Mengyu Yao, Ziqi Zhang, Shaofei Li, Yifeng Cai, Ding Li, Yao Guo, Ning Luo

papers.title: On the Expected Number of Iterations in ML-DSA Signing: A Complete Accounting of the Rejection Conditions
papers.abstract: FIPS 204 Table 1 gives the expected number of iterations of the ML-DSA signing loop (ML-DSA.Sign_internal, Algorithm 7), citing CRYSTALS-Dilithium Equation (5). That equation covers only the validity checks on line 23 ($\lVert z \rVert_\infty$ and $\lVert r_0 \rVert_\infty$) and omits the two encoding-correctness checks on line 28 ($\lVert c \cdot t_0 \rVert_\infty$ and the hint weight), a scoping distinction the Dilithium specification states explicitly and FIPS 204 does not reproduce. We give a complete accounting of all four conditions. The $z$ check on line 23 is computed exactly by counting; the $c \cdot t_0$ term follows a closed-form Irwin-Hall tail, restating a peer-reviewed result by Yan, Luo and Wang; the hint-weight term's per-coefficient probability, conditioned on line 23 having passed, does have a closed form, but the tail of the sum over $256k$ such coefficients does not, since their probabilities are unequal, random, and correlated with each other, so we give the conditioned per-coefficient probability in closed form and estimate its tail by Monte Carlo. The corrected expected iteration counts are 4.36, 5.14 and 3.91 for ML-DSA-44, -65 and -87, matching a real end-to-end measurement to within 0.14% and already reflected in NIST's own errata to FIPS 204.
papers.authors: Kris Kwiatkowski

papers.title: SSM-Attack: Learning Where to Perturb for Black-Box Face Privacy
papers.abstract: Face recognition systems are deployed widely enough that a photograph shared online can be matched without its subject's consent. Generator-based protection methods rely on heavy pretrained backbones, multi-stage inference or visible semantic edits. We introduce SSM-Attack, a black-box face privacy framework built on Selective State Space Models. Rather than synthesizing the perturbation, the state-space model predicts in one linear-time pass a spatial allocation of the perturbation budget, marking which facial locations carry identity evidence; a short projected refinement then sets the values within this per-pixel budget. Against published benchmark results, SSM-Attack attains the highest average black-box attack success rate on all three evaluation sets: 87.10 percent on CelebA-HQ, 86.90 on LADN and 81.15 on FFHQ, the last from a network that never saw that dataset. The allocation network holds 5.73 million parameters, or 16.13 million with the frozen networks used by its quality terms. Under the same cap of 0.10 on the maximum per-pixel change, allocation improves structural similarity by 0.044, peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.62 decibels and Frechet Inception Distance by 11.2 points over a uniform map while spending 37 percent of its capacity. Strong facial privacy protection therefore does not require a large generative prior; it requires knowing where to spend a small one.
papers.authors: Tunahan Parlayıcı, Erchan Aptoula, Yücel Saygın

papers.title: Can Rényi Accountants Beat Lossless Accountants for DP-SGD?
papers.abstract: Recent frameworks in differential privacy (DP), such as privacy loss distributions and $f$-DP, provide lossless representations of the privacy leakage of mechanisms. These approaches are often considered to yield tighter $(\varepsilon, δ)$-DP guarantees than those obtained from relaxed notions such as Rényi DP. But is that always the case? We study this question for differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) with fixed-size batches under replace adjacency. Our key observation is that in this setting, privacy accounting based on Rényi DP can use a pair of worst-case distributions (i.e., a dominating pair) that differs from the one used in the lossless frameworks. In particular, we characterize the worst-case distributions as two-dimensional Gaussian mixtures and derive an improved Rényi DP bound for DP-SGD. Numerical and asymptotic comparisons show that across various hyperparameter settings, a Rényi DP accountant based on the new bound can yield better privacy guarantees than those obtained from the lossless frameworks.
papers.authors: Jinho Bok

papers.title: The Right to Be Forgotten under Correlation: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs
papers.abstract: We study privacy-preserving algorithms that redact information from a correlated dataset. The goal is to reduce the information leakage about sensitive parts. We analytically characterize the optimal tradeoff between privacy (leakage through correlation) and utility (number of redactions) for local mechanisms and binary Markovian correlations. Our result shows how to decompose the mechanism design problem into a sequence of local mechanism design problems and reveals their sequential relation. The optimal mechanism is the solution to a Finite-Horizon Deterministic Markov Decision Process.
papers.authors: Luis Massny, Rawad Bitar, Fangwei Ye, Salim El Rouayheb

papers.title: CUTS: Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures
papers.abstract: Stateful hash-based signatures fail badly when a one-time key signs twice, as happens when the signer's state is lost or rolled back. We study what a second signature reveals in a broad class of hash-based schemes whose key is a tree of hash chains. In this class, a message selects a set of tree nodes that covers every leaf exactly once, together with a position on the chain of each selected node, and the signature reveals the chain values at those positions. For the whole class, we prove that the values derivable from several signatures are exactly the union of those derivable from each signature alone, and we bound forgery after $b$ signatures in the classical random-oracle model by a combinatorial coverage exponent $\lambda_b$, also when the signer grinds a counter. We then present CUTS (Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures), a member of the class built on one binary tree, in which both the selected nodes and their chain positions depend on the message, with the positions summing to a fixed value $S$. Signature length and verification cost are fixed by the parameters and do not depend on the tree height. For CUTS, we compute the two-use coverage exactly as one coefficient of a polynomial and derive deterministic lower bounds on $\lambda_2$; one parameter set with 1 424-byte signatures has $\lambda_2\ge128.6$. A counter variant, CUTS+C, trades a short counter and extra signing work for a proven grinding gain of $g$ bits in the coverage term.
papers.authors: Jamie Judd, Louis Tajan, Conor Deegan, Furkan Akal

papers.title: Unsupervised Data Drift Monitoring for Deployed Deepfake Speech Detectors
papers.abstract: Deepfake speech detectors are typically evaluated as binary classifiers on fixed benchmarks, but deployed systems face evolving attacks, codecs, speakers, and recording conditions, with labels unavailable during operation. This makes it difficult to know when a detector operates in familiar conditions and can be relied on. We propose an unsupervised drift monitor that operates on the internal embeddings of a deployed detector. The monitor compares each input against bona fide and spoof references using regularized Mahalanobis distances. These distances define trusted, ambiguous, and novel regions of the detector embedding space, allowing unfamiliar inputs to be routed for review. We evaluate the monitor on four modern detectors on three datasets. The monitor raises alerts for dataset mismatches and substantially reduces the security-critical case of accepting deepfakes at the cost of reduced automatic coverage. The results also show that drift affects both classes: bona fide recordings can move away from the training reference, increasing alert rates even in in-domain settings. Our findings suggest that deployed deepfake speech detectors should be treated not only as a binary classification, but also as a reliability problem.
papers.authors: Lukáš Prokeš, Vojtěch Staněk, Anton Firc, Kamil Malinka
